articles.title: LONDON TRADES
articles.text:
THE LONDON TRADES

AND
LANC NSIIIRE DISTRESS.

THE Trades of the Metropolis have well
responded to the call of the London Trades'
Council on behalf of their distressed brethren
in the cotton districts. On Tuesday evening
last, delegates from about forty trade societies
assembled, and after unanimously adopting a
resolution that it was the duty of every trade,
"either by special levy, or voluntary contribu-
tion," to aid the Lancashire operatives, standing
idle and starving, through bad and inefficient
legislation and cottonocracy cupidity, agreed to
form themselves into a committee, under the
title of "The London Workmen's Central
Committee for the Relief of Lancashire Dis-
tress," to receive, collect, and disburse the
subscriptions of their brother unionists and
fellow-workmen. Having had the privilege of
being present at the meeting, I am able to
testify, from personal observation, the deep and
earnest feeling existing amongst all present,
that all that was possible to be done should be
done by the working men of London, while a
just indignation was evinced at the shortcom-
ings of the great bulk of the cotton princes, and
the arbitrary and impolitic conduct of many of
the middle-class relief committees now exist-
ing, and an expression of astonishment at the ex-
traordinary conduct of the Mansion-house and
Manchester Central Committees. At a time
when the distress is augmenting daily, and
rendered more severe by the season of the
year; when pestilence is threatening to follow
close upon the heels of famine; when the
bodies of the factory operatives are denuded of
their necessary clothing, which is piled up on
the shelves of the.pawnbrokers ; when grown
men are existing, not living, upon the pittance
of two shillings and twopence per week,
received "from all sources "—this is the time,
of all others, the gentlemen who comprise the
Mansion-house Committee have the assurance
and audacity, I may say the:cruelty, to perform
an act which must, at least, so far as their
committee are concerned, materially affect the
flow of contributions into their exchequer.
These City almoners of funds sent to them
specially to relieve starving men, women, and
children, have shown their incompetency for
the task they have undertaken, by withdrawing
the sum of £40,000, accumulated from the
subscriptions entrusted to them, not for the
purpose of increasing the two shillings and
twopence per week relief; not for laying in a
stock of food, fuel, or clothing, for the use of
those persons on whose behalf these large
funds have been entrusted to them, but for
investment in Consols ! " They have not done
this impolitic act without warning of the
probable effect. A few days ago, Mr. Samuel
Morley, one of our wealthiest and best' City
reformers and philanthropists, waited upon
this committee, and in presenting them with
his subscription of £l,OOO, remonstrated with
them on the tendency they had shown to keep
a reserve fund. He told them it would neces-
sarily check subscriptions; and it was only
upon the understanding that this course would
not be persevered in that he left his £l,OOO in
their hands. "What is bred in the bone will
not come out of the flesh." There is nothing
so pleasant to these City "men made of
money," as the "dabbling in Consols ; " they
feel then in their element. A couple of
intelligent and independent working men on
this committee would probably have prevented
such an act of imbecility and disregard of their
true position as public trustees.
Working men on our committee! what as-
sumption! is the cry of the smug City mer-
chant, who gives a few hours per week to the
supervision of these funds—the real—the hard
work—being, of course, performed by a staff
of Mansion-house clerks, whose usual monoto-
nous duties must be thus agreeably diversified.
And why not, good man of the well-lined
money bags? You appeal to the working
class for their subscriptions, you receive them
largely in response to that appeal, and would
it be anything so extraordinary for a couple of
working men to sit on the committee, to have
some control over the distribution of those sub-
scriptions?

I trust my fellow-workmen will repair their
error in having entrusted their subscriptions
to the hands of
.men who have thus publicly
shown their incompetency to use them pro-
perly. A channel is now opened, by means of
the newly-formed "London Workmen's Relief
Committee," through which working men can
send their subscriptions, with the full con-
fidence that they will be freely...and fairly dis-
•tributed amongst those parties for whom they
were intended, and not "invested in Consols,"
or hoarded up, to form, at some future time,
the nucleus of a fund to be appropriated to
purposes, however good, quite foreign to the
object for which they were subscribed. Neither
should working men allow the proprietors of
newspapers to make personal capital out of, or
trade upon, their subscriptions, as is now being
done. I feel ashamed at seeing so many of
my fellow-workmen pandering to the pride of
such newspapers as the Daily Telegraph and
144, by swelling their subscription lists.
They show, by so doing, a lamentable
want of dignity an self-respect. Have
they so soon forgotten the manner in
which the Daily Telegraph reviled and calumn-
ated them and their ,unions during the
late struggles in the building trade, that they
are thus ready to "eat the leek," by- entrusting
their subscriptions to a newspaper proprietor who
proved himself a deadly and bitter foe to
trades' unions? And to whom does the Daily
Telegraph send the subscriptiens entrusted to
it? Why to the Manchester Central Commit-
tee, who are also hoarding up a large reserve
fund, while the money they distribute is handed
over to committees from which working men
are systematically excluded, and which com-
mittees refuse relief to members of co-operative
societies, or to those operatives who have made
themselves conspicuous in trade matters, in
opposition to the employers. One of
those conimittees the other day refused
relief to an operative, because he was
a member of a relief committee of operatives,
and another committee refused to admit a
respectable young woman into a sewing class,
supported partly by funds subscribed by work-
ing ,men, because her father was a member of
a trades' Union! Is there not spirit enough
left among Wol*king men to resent these insults,
or will they servilely go on supplying com-
mittees with their funds rather than trust their
fellow workmen? Lloyd's paper, again, parades
large subscriptions from trades' unionists,
While the proprietor is, and always has been,
an opponent of trades' un-
ions, and conducts'
his establishment, if not in direct opposition I
to the Compositors' Trade Society entirely by
boy labour, to the exclnsion of society journey-
men; and yetworking
men enable this person
to pay into the Mansion-bouseCommittee every
week, to be inve,sted onso/s, some £2OO or
£3OO, paidin, by the bye, not as subscriptions
.from workiug men, but from' the "Proprietors
of Lloyd's Newspaper!
The establishment of the." London Work-

men's Central Committee," does away with any
excuse for working men sending their contribu-
tions through any of the other channels above
alluded to. By making this committee- the
medium of their free-will offerings at the shrine
of distress, they will have a guarantee that the
funds will not be hoarded up in reserve, will
not be "invested in consols," but will be at once
devoted to the purposes for which they were
subscribed, the feeding the hungry, the clothing
the naked, the comforting the suffering,
amongst their fellow labourers in the north,
irrespective of creed or politics, unionists or
non-unionists, competitors or, co-operators. To
be an operative, willing to work, but compelled
to be idle from the cotton famine, will be a
sufficient guarantee to entitle him or her to a
share of the funds entrusted to the "London
Workmen's Central Committee." In wishing
it a hearty success, and God speed, every true
unionist, every working man who respects him-
self or his order, must assuredly join with
November 27. SCOURGE.

articles.title: CORkESPONDENCE.
articles.text:
CORkESPONDENCE.

THE POTATO DISEASE.
TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE.

Sin,—As there are few subjects which have caused
more uneasiness and alarm in the breasts of statesmen
and philanthropists than that of the disease in
potatoes, so I feel Impressed there can be no news
more welcome to the human family generally than that
which a remedy for that disease shall constitute or
suppy.

It is my privilege to make known on behalf of Mr.
Caesimer Hendriekx, a native of Belgium, this secret,
the result of years of travel and experiment in Russia,
Germany, France, Holland, and in our own country.
Mr. Hendriekx has been over six years in the
employment of a gentleman belonging to the
bench of magistrates for Westminster, on whose son's
property at Cheam, in Surrey, the chief part of the
experiments have been made.

appeares that this ground, three years ago,
yielded a sack and a half of potatoes, all diseased, and
that last year, on the same ground, the finest potatoes
ever seen were raised. I use the words of one of a
numerous party of neighbours, who were called in
to witness the result of Mr. Hendrickx's experiments,
and -who has himself been a grower of potatoes for the
last fifty years.

The ex-periments this year had reference more par-
ticularly to quantity, the result of which I had the
pleasure of witnessing on Tuesday week, in company
with a city merchant, who consents to be referee, and
also of two parties who had patches of potatoes planted
on the same ground beside that of Mr. Hendrickx's.
As to the size, I may observe that there were on each
root of Mr. Hendrickx's (which must have weighed
fully three times as much as any of those planted by
his competitors) potatoes four or five times as
large; and making allowance for the greater space occu-
pied by each root of his own planting, you will readily
understand that on measuring the three patches and
weighing the produce thereof, the result should be a
double crop, occasioned by Mr. Hendrickx's peculiar
mode of treatment.

It would appear that while in the Belgian army, he
received from his father a letter, describing the misery
and starvation the potatoe disease had inflicted in the
neighbourhood of his early home. From that moment
to the present time he has exhibited the zeal of an
enthusiast, in tracing out its cause and searching for
a remedy. His travels in the countries above named,
favoured his plans, but these were not brought to
maturity till he filled the situation of butler in
London.

Having three days' holiday allowed him on a cer-
tain occasion Mr. Hendrickx says, did nothing
day nor night but try potatoes. I stole out at ten
o'clock at night, and having brought a shovel full of
earth into the house, I found it stinking like rotten
potatoes.' He afterwards betook himself to prayer,
read from the New Testament the parable of the
Sower,' and received on that occasion what he justly
regarded as divine direction.

Mr. Hendrickx asserts that wherever he has travelled
it is the practice to neglect the ground from which the
crop a potatoes has been dug, and thus deprive the
soil during winter of that which it so much needs, and
which that season is so admirably adapted to supply—
revivication. The earth 'Ling in an exhausted condi-
tion, should be at once thoroughly turned over, so as
to receive the benefit of nature's restoratives, light,
heat, moisture, atmosphere, and frost.

_
_
Mr. Hendricks also contends that there is scarcely
ever sufficient 'depth of earth' allowed for the potato
to grow in, and that underlying the root, the soil is
generally caked; thus forming a resting place for innu-
merable vermin. The roots being thus obstructed,
travel out of their natural course and tend upward, and
the rain, also prevented passing through, settles to the
great injury of the plant. To complete
.the mischief,
another fatal plan is to use an implement to make holes
for the reception of the seed, the effect of -which is to
encase the seed as in cement.

After preparing the ground properly by guarding
against the errors indicated above, and employing
suitable manure and the ordinary plough, Mr. Hendrickx
would have a second plough, with prongs like human
fingers, to shake up the earth and prevent what may be
called constipation. The potato must then be placed
uncut into the earth, several inches lower than usual,
and protected against the use of manure of insufficient
age, and whatever would obstruct light, heat, moisture,
and the free play of the atmosphere; then, I doubt not,
having C?nalDlied with these conditions, the potato
disease will soon be eradicated and a double crop
secured.

When Mr. Ilendrickx returns from Belgium,
whither he has gone to test experiments made under
the eye of the Secretary of the Interior, I will supply
you with further particulars. In the meantime I trust
that what I have communicated may be turned to pro-
fitable account, and believing that the days of the
am, air, yours, &c.,
potato disease are numbered,

SAMUEL OWEN.
10, St. Germain's-teryace, Harrow-road.

DEATH OF A DWARF.—An inquest was held by Mr.
Walthew on the body of Caroline Clark, aged 17,
daughter of Mr. Clark, hair preparer, 22, Craven-
street, City-road. Deceased, when only a month old,
had a sefere illness, which had the effect of completely
checking lier growth, her body, when recently mea-
sured, being only twenty-four inches long. She had a
finely-tonedvoice, but was never able to speak so as to be
understood, and her memory of what was said to her
was defective. Dr. Simpson, who • attended her, said
he would have taken her for a child of two years,
diminutive of her age, and she had gone, during her
life, to a great many doctors, •none of whom could do
anything for her. Yerdict,,-Death from natural
cause,

LONDON, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER z 9, 1862.

THE FORGERY.AND ROBB A.RY ON
THE BANK OF _ENGLAND.

The examination of the six prisoners charged with
stealing the Bank paper, and also with forging Bank
of England notes, was resumed yesterday morning
before Mr. Alderman Cubitt at the Mansion-house.
Mr. Fresh&ld, the solicitor to the bank, again ap-
peared to prosecute; Mr. Pater, barrister,*appeareti
for the prisoner Buncher ; and Mr. Lewis, of Ely.
place, appeared for Brewer. There was a great deal
of additional evidence adduced, and the examination
lasted for a long time. Another remand took place.

articles.title: DESTRUCTIVE FII?ES.
articles.text:
DESTRUCTIVE FII?ES.

DESTRUCTION BY FIRE OF AUSTINFRIARS DUTCH
CHURCH.—This venerable edifice, probably one of the
oldest of the City churches, known as Augustine
Friars, situate between Austinfriars and Crown-court;
Old Broad-street, City, was destroyed by fire on
Saturday morning. The origin is attributed to the
overheating of one of the flues, which ran into the
northern wall of the church. The interior was
undergoing •repairs, and beautifying at the time,
and the place was closely watched both day, and night.
It was but partly insured.
FIRE IN THE WALWORTH-ROAD.—At a quarter before
seven o'clock on Sunday night a fire broke out in the
premises of Mr. Webb, bread and biscuit baker, 2,
Amelia-place, Walworth-road, which was not sub-
dued until nearly nine o'clock. By that time
,Mr.
Webb's shop and house were all but destroyed, and
the adjoining premises of Mr. Langton, oil and Italian
warehouseman, and Mr. Harvey, tobacconist, much
damaged.
FIRE AT CAMDEN TowN.—On Wednesday afternoon
a fire happened in the premises occupied by Mr.
Nicholas, pianoforte and organ screw manufacturer,
33, High-street, Camden Town. The fire began in the
workshops on the first floor, and in the course of a few
minutes the flames rushed through the roof and threat-
ened destruction to everything near. Several engines '
soon arrived, ani a good supply of water having been
procured, the firemen went to work; but they were
unable to get the flames extinguished until the workshop
was burned out.

FIRE AT A BEiLDER'S.—On Tuesilay morning a fire
broke out in the extensive premises of Mr. a J. Freak,
builder, situate in Onslow-square, Brompton. The
building in which the disaster commenced was, about
one. third destroyed.
FIRE AND 1.4,-)ss OF LIFE.—On Tuesday morning a
fire took place at 15, Edward-place, Seymour-street,
let out to several families. The fire commenced from
some unknown cause in the back room ground floor.
The engines were soon in attendance, but owing to the
exertions of the inmates and strangers the flames had
been previously extinguished, when a most distressing
scene presented herself, for an unfortunate aged female,
who had passed her sixtieth year, was found burned in
a most fearful manner. Medical aid was obtained, but
life was extinct.

FIRE AT 1•T-E-W-INOTON.—A fire happened on Tuesday,
on the premises of Mr. E. Derail (private), No. 118,
Howard-road, Stoke Newington. The lower part of
the premises was burned out and the upper part
severely damaged.
FIRE AT BROMPTON.—At a late hour on Saturday
night a serious fire broke out on the premises of Mr.
D. Rees, cook and confectioner, 11, Brompton-row,
Brompton. The premises were destroyed.

MURDER OF A POLICEMAN.—A policeman has been
murdered at Halesworth, in Suffolk. His .name is
Ebenezer Tye. He went on duty on Monday night,
and did not report himself at the station-house next
morning. This caused .search to be made for him,
and his body, with many bruises on it, was found in a
shalluw stream. It is supposed that he was murdered
while endeavouring to apprehend a man of bad
character. Two men and a woman are in custody,
suspected of being concerned in the affair.
FATAL OCCURRENCE TO A PAINTER ON THE LONDON,
CHATHAM, AND DOVER RAILWAY.—OD Thursday morn-
ing information Was received by Mr. Bedford, coroner
for Westminster, of the death of John Cooper' aged
25 years, who resided at 16, Addington-street, York.
road, Lambeth. The deceased, a painter, was in the
employ of Messrs. Lucas and Co., builders, and en-
gaged at work at the Brixton Station, on the London,
Chath ,m, and Dover Railway. While standing upon
• a scaffold only a few feet from the ground, he missed
his footing and fell, pitching on his head. In an insen-
sible condition he was at once conveyed to Westmin-
ster Hospital, and •expired in about a quarter of an
hour, his skull being frightfully fractured.
FRIGIIITPUL DEATH.—An inquiry was held by Mr.
Walthew, at the Lord Truro Tavern, Dalston, respect-
ing the death of Frederick Hepburn, aged 14, who was
killed while cleaning a window from the outside ledge.
It appeared from the evidence that the deceased and
another boy were in the employ of Dr. Williamson, of
Mildmay-street, Mildmay Park, and were recently
engaged cleaning the landing window, deceased stand-
ing for that purpose outside on the ledge. The other
boy kept cautioning him and, it appeared, made him
so nervous that he slipped off and fell on the iron spikes
of the railing, fourteen feet below. The spikes entered
the skull, and the brains protruded; but, singular to
say, he remained sensible enough to give the foregoing
account of the accident. He was removed to the German
Hospital, where he died.

THE POISONINGS AT Yons.—The recent wholesale
poisoning case at York was on Tuesday the subject of
inquiry before the magistrates of that City. Mrs.
Maria Cooke, a person of respectable position, and a
relative of the family, was charged with having admi-
nistered arsenic to the four children and two servants
of Mr. Cooke, of Bishophill. The only evidence given
was that of a person named Alice Clance.y, who up to
six weeks ago was in the service of the prisoner. This
woman says that some time last spring her mistress
came into the kitchen, remarking that she was 'much
annoyed with the conduct of the Cookes of Bishophill
towards her, and said she should like to Film up some-
thing for the witness to take and put it into the flour
bin at Bishophill. She said she would give Clancey
a£s note if what was done proved effectual.' The
witness of course refused the offer, and then her mis-
tress professed to give up the idea of doing anything.
Both were apprehended; and when before the magis-
trates, Mrs. Cooke simply protested her innocence of
the crime. The case was remanded until Monday next.

SIIIOIDE OF A WELL-IENOWN TILAFEZE PERFOILNER.
—Frederick Carini, known to the visitors to the Lon-
don Eldorado, Leicester-square, for his ability as a
performer on the trapeze, has committed suicide under
the 'following distressing circumstances :—lt appeared
that on the 24th of this month he parted from his wife
at the door of the London Eldorado, being at the time
in bis usual spirits, and, from that time: nothing was
seen of him. On Tuesday, however, his body was dis-
covered in the Thames, near Whitehall, and at once
taken to the dead-house of St. martin's Church. It is
stated that some time ago the deceased met with an
accident while performing, ad there is reason to be-
lieve it has affected his brain. The deceased was a
very handsome DM, possessed great mnpc,olar streAsth,
and his age is about thirt,y,three.,

articles.title: ATTEMP lED MU.!? )ER OF A WIFE BY HER HUSBAND.
articles.text:
ATTEMP lED MU.!? )ER OF A WIFE
BY HER HUSBAND.

On Wednesday, at the Leeds Town Hall, a young
man of 20, nlmed Edward Johnson Wylde, a labourer,
living in St. Mary's-lane, was charged with attempting
to murder his wife. About four months ago the
primer married Ann, the daughter of Mr. Carey, of
4, Wesley-terrace, Accommodation-road, but the union
appears to have taken place without the knowledge
and against the wishes of her father, though the
girl's mother was cognisant of the fact. After the
ceremony the wife continued to reside with her
parents, her excuse being that her husband had not
been able to provide a proper home for her. On Tues-
day night, shortly after eight o'clock, Wylde met his
wife in Est Field-street, and asked her to accompany
him, and live with him. The young woman refused,
Paying that it was better that she should reside at pre-
sent with her parents, until her husband could provide
a suitable home for her. This reply appears to have
exasperated the prisoner almost to frenzy, for he
exclaimed, Well, your father won't let me come to
see you, and I am determined that no one else shall;'
and then he drew a pistol and fired it at the poor girl's
heal By the explosion her bonnet was blown to
pieces, and a portion of the charge grazed the back
part of her head, but fortunately without inflicting
any serious injury. Mr. Cottam, surgeon, was imme-
diatelY called in to attend her, and though she was
unable to appear in court • yesterday, owing to. the
shock to her system, it is anticipated she will be able
to attend at the next hearing of the case. The
husband absconded after his attack, but he was appre-
hended early yesterday morning by Police constable
Ring. He stands remanded until the 3rd of December.

articles.title: FIGHT FOR TffE CHAMPIO.2I7
articles.text:
THE FIGHT FOR TffE CHAMPIO.2I7

SHIP.

The long-expected encounter for the champion's
belt and £4OO took place on Wednesday. The com-
petitors were James Mace, of Norwich, the champion,
and Thomas King, of London. Mace, who was born
, in 1831, stands 5 feet Bt,- inches, and weighed about
10st. 121 b. King is a line young fellow, standing
6 feet 21 inches, and weighing in condition about
12st. 121 b. He was born in 1836. A'great deal of in-
terest was excited in this affair, it being the second
time the men have entered a ring to contend for the
championship. For some time past the betting has
been in favour of Mace, 6 and 7 to 4 having
been laid, but as the time approached these odds
became lessened, and 5 to 4 was taken to money.
The start for the scene of encounter took place
at an early hour in the morning on the 'iron
road' to Tilbury, where the pugilists and their
friends stepped on board a steamboat that was await-
ing their arrival. The charge for tickets was £2, a
sum necessary to ensure comfort and safety to the
patrons of this sport, amongst whom the 'upper ten
thousand' mustered pretty strongly, notwithstanding
the chilly prospect before them. The event took place
in the neighbourhood of Thames Haven. The com-
batants entered the ring a few minutes past nine,
when, after fighting for thirty-eight minutes, during
which time twenty-one rounds were fought, mostly in
favour of Mace, King countered hint very heavily on
the nose and knocked him insensible. Previous to the
last round 6to 1 was offered on Mace. The winner
was seconded by Jaelt Macdonald and Bos Tyler, and
Mace by Bob Travers and Bob Brettle. The belt of
the Champion of England,' with whatever credit may
attach to its possession, has to pass from Mace and
King, his younger rival. After a much shorter
encounter than had been generally expected, and con-
trary, indeed, to most of the surmises and prochecies
of the cognoscenti, the late Champion—battered, bruised
and beaten—was led away by his seconds from the
crowd that cheered his antagonist with that enthusiasm
which success can always command.

ANOTHER CRINOLINE FATALITT.-011 We dn esday,Dr.
Lankester held an inquest at the Bank of England,
Cambridge-place, Paddington, on the body of Caro-
line Weedon, aged 14, daughter of a drover of
Southall, who lost her life by fire through an extended
crinoline. The jury returned the following verdict:
That the deceased, Caroline Weedon, died from ex-
haustion and inflammation of the lungs, coming on
after excessive burns through her clothing catching
fire by extended crinoline.'
FRIGHTFUL Occunazwcz.—A WOMAN IMMERSED IN
VrrnioL.—On Tuesday morning a shocking .occurrence
took place at the Bone Boiling and Crushing Factory,
Fore-street, Lambeth, to a young woman named Eliza-
beth Clarke, who was employed at the factory, when,
in crossing a platform, she slipped and fell into a vat
of vitriol which had been left uncovered, and she was
immersed in the burning liquid up to the waist. She
was carried, in excruciating agony, to Westminster
Hospital; where her clothes were found to be corn
pletely destroyed, portions of the skin and flesh coming
away with the remnants of them.

COLONIAL EMIGRATION.—The inaugural meeting of
the Colonial Emigration Society, recently formed, was
held on Tuesday evening, in the Town Hall, Birming.
ham. Mr. W. Scholefield, M.P., presided. Mr. Chil-
ders, M.P., moved a resolution in favour of a well-
arranged system of emigration, as promoting alike the
interest of the mother country and .the colonies, and
urged views strongly in concurrence with those of the
preceding speakers. Mr. Howe, from Nova Scotia,
addressed the meeting in support of the resolution,
which was carried, as was another resolution, declar-
ing that the objects of the society were well deserving
of general support.
MORE GAROTTING AND STR,EBT ROBBERIES. —On
Thursday morning information was received by the
police that between twelve and one o'clock, as Mr.
Otley, of Surrey-street, Black friars-road, musician in
the orchestra of one of the theatres, was returning
home, he was knocked down by a life-preserver, and
rendered momentarily insensible, when he was plun-
dered of a gold watch and chain, a valuable cornopean
and case £2 188. 6d. in money. Mr. Otley, on reach-
ing home, was attended by Dr. Catton, but from the
injuries inflicted it is feared some time must elapse
before he will be able to resume his professional
duties. On Wednesday evening, shortly before five
o'clock, as a gentleman was passing through one
of the passages on the north side of St. Paul's
Cathedral, which lead into Paternoster-row, he was
felled to the ground by a ruffian who had concealed
himself in a dark recess. Almost at the same moment
some persons came up, and the fellow took to flight.
He was pursued and captured, but it required the
united exertions of several policemen to take him to the
station. His victim was carried, bleeding and insen-
sible, to the hospital.—On Sunday evening a moat
brutal attack was made upon Mr. Girvan, a reporter,
from the effects of which he is at present confined to
his bed. He states that while passing, about seven
o'clock in the evening, from Whitefriars into Pnrset-
street; he was followed by three men, one a whom
spoke to him. Upon turning round he received a
terrifio blow from some blunt instrument, which ren-
dered him insensible. He was found, in that state by
the police, and conveyed to Bartholomew's Hospital,

articles.title: CAKILEIV' S DELEGATE HEETING.
articles.text:
CAKILEIV' S DELEGATE HEETING.

A general meeting of the delegates from the Metro-
politan Cab Drivers was held on Wednesday evening
at the BEEHIVE office, 2, Bouverie-street, Fleet-street.
Delegates were present from Highbury, Paddington,
Westminster, East London, South London, and
Eastern Counties Railway. Mr. Wise, of Westminis-
ter, occupied the chair. Mr. Bennett, the secretary,
read the minutes of the last meeting, which were con-
firmed. Mr. Bennett reported, that in pursuance of
the instructions of the sub-committee he had engaged
the large room of the Whittington Club for the
aggregate meeting of drivers, on Wednesday evening,
December 3, at which Lord Henry Cholmondeley had
consented to take the chair. He had also had inter-
views with several members of Parliament and others,
with reference to the bill fok the amendment of the
present Hackney Carriage Act, which was intended
to be brought into the House of Commons in ;the
ensuing session. It was then resolved that a recom-
mendation should be made to the public meeting, that
a deputation should wait upon Mr. Arthur Kinnaird,
M.P., to request that gentleman to take charge of the
new bill in Parliament. In was also resolved that a peti-
tion to Parliament should be submitted to the meeting
praying for an alteration in the present act, which was
both unjust and injurious to drivers. Various
arrangements with respect to the forthcoming
meeting were made, and amongst others it was
decided to recommend to the meeting that the
present delegates, or others, be appointed to sit as a
permanent committee until the termination of the
movement. The admission to the meeting will be by
tickets, charged 6d. each, the proceeds from which
will be devoted to paying the expenses attendant on
getting up the meeting, and any surplus will be paid
-over to the fund for carrying on the movement. Their
tickets can be obtained from any of the delegates at
all the houses generally used by babmen, at the delegates, at
Club Rooms, and at the office of the BEEHIVE
newspaper. A large meeting is expected, and many
influential proprietors have signified their intention to
be present.

MIDNIGHT MEETING OF CABMEN.—On Wednesday
night last, at 12 o'clock, a strong muster of cab-drivers
and their wives assembled at the Victoria-hall, Union-
street, Friars-street, Blackfriars-road, in response to an
invitation extensively issued by Mr. William Carter,
the popular lay preacher of Newington. About
three thousand persons were present. The pro-
ceedings were opened with prayer, after which a
hymn was sung, followed by a short address from
Mr. Carter. A plentiful supply of tea, coffee, and
sandwiches, were then supplied gratuitously to those
assembled; and, during the time occupied in disposing
of these refreshments, Mr. Carter delivered some
anecdotes connected with his personal experiences.
Ample justice having been done to the eatables and
drinkables, devotional exercises were resumed, and
continued until about 3 o'clock in the morning, when
the assembly broke up, much pleased with what had
taken place.

THE TRADES' UNIONS POLITICAL ASSOCIATIONS.—A
meeting of the Trades' Unionists Manhood Suffrage
and Vote by Ballot Association was held on Friday,
Nov. 21st, when the following resolution was proposed
by Mr. Howell, bricklayer, and seconded by Mr.
Cremer, joiner, and carried unanimously :—'That a
meeting of the association be held at the Brown Bear,
Broad-street, Bloomsbury, on Tuesday evening, Dec.
2nd, at 8 o'clock; and that the representatives and
members of Trades Societies be earnestly requested to
attend' GEORGE ODGERS, Chairman. THOMAS
GRANT FACET, Secretary.
MANHOOD SUFFRAGE ASSOCIATION.—At the ad-
journed meeting of the Central London, Tower
Hamlets, and Lambeth Manhood Suffrage Associations,
held at the Barley Mow, West Smithfield, on the
23rd inst., Mr. Thlvis in the chair, the address of the
Trades' Union Political Union having been read, a
discussion ensued, and the following resolutions were
carried That a deputation be appointed to wait on
the Trades' Union Political Union, to learn from them
their mode of action the deputation to consist of
Messrs. Bligh and Davies.'— That a circular be
drawn up and sent to all the known advocates of
manhood suffrage to invite them to take part in trying
to obtain a complete reform in the representation of
the people.'—R. S. Cock, J. Bligh, Secretaries.
SECESSION ?Rost THE CHURCH OF ENGLAND.—On
Sunday evening the Rev. William Lincoln, of Beres-
ford Episcopal Chapel, Walworth, announced to his
congregation his intention of seceding from the Church
of England. He stated that, when he viewed the
connection of the Church with the State and the world,
he was convinced it was that Babylon out of Nvhich
real Christians were commanded to come.' He in-
tended to join a free Church, which should be partly
Independent, partly Baptist, and partly Plymouth
Brethren.
EMPEROR LIFE AND FIRE ASSURANCE SOCIETIES.—The
annual wires of these societies was held on Monday
evening at Radley's Hotel, Bridge-street; Mr. Ebenezer
Clarke, sen., in the chair. The chairman having briefly
addressed the company, the secretary, Mr. Clarke, jun.,
read an elaborate report, which was of a very favourable
character. From it it appears that although the civil
war in America has greatly injured trade and commerce,
and consequently lessened the power of the people to
invest in life assurance and other provident institutions,
1431 new life policies have been issued during the year,
assuring upwards of £83,000, and the net premiums
received have increased upwards of 40 per cent, over
those of the previous year.' The claims paid during
th% year amount to £3,058 16s. A dividend of 5 per
cent. has been paid to the shareholders upon the paid- .
up capital from the commencement of the society, and
no call has been required beyond the amount of the first
deposit of £l, paid on the allotment of the shares. The
remaining unallotted shares therefore offer a goodinvest-
ment for capital, especially as the directors have special
opportunities of profitably investing it in freehold and
other good securities, and at the same time increasing
the number of their policies. The fire insurance busi-
ness also continues to increase: 4,412 proposals have
been received to this date, amounting to £1,492,954;
and 3,297 policies have been issued, insuring property
to the amount of £1,193,139.
Two FATAL ACCIDENTS.—Mr. W. J. Payne held two
inquests at Guy's Hospital, on the bodies of John
George Ashford and William Summers, who came to
their deaths in consequence of the following accidents:
—ln the first case Ashford was engaged at a building
at Blackheath, and on the 30th of October he was
pulling a truck from the road towards the building
when his foot caught against the leg of the truck, by
which he was thrown to the gr Bind, and in his fall
he fractured his right thigh. He was taken to the ,
hospital, but died of exhaustion produced by the I
injury. In the second case, tbe deceased was a jour-
neyman baker in the employ of 31.1 r. Miller, of Warner-
Street, Old. Kent-road, and between eight and nine
o'clock on the night of the sth of November he had
gone ui a, ladder to a loft that was over the bakehouse,
and cithen he had got to the top his foot slipped and he
fell to the ground, on the flags outside the bakehouse
door. The house surgeon said in this case the man
was brought in with a fracture of the right thigh, and
he died from exhaustion consequent on the injuries oa,
Saturday last, The jury in each cue Tetwile4
diet c Acoident4l death,'

articles.title: DISTRESS rAT LANCASHIRE.
articles.text:
DISTRESS rAT LANCASHIRE.

EAST LANCASHIRE CENTRAL EXECUTIVE
. RELIEF COMMITTEE.
The usual weekly meeting of the executive met at
the,Committee Rooms, Speak-buildings, Padiham, Mr.
James Denbigh in the chair. Present: J. Haworth,
Wm. Wilkinson (treasurer), Joseph Peacock (sec.),
John Pinder, Charles Sutcliffe, Lawrence Shackleton.
(Burnley), George Hargreaves, J. Heap, H. White-
head, J. Hartley (Habergham). The minutes of the
last meeting were read and confirmed.
The Chairman said applications had been made from
divers places to know the principles on which relief
was given, and it could not be too publicly known that
relief was granted by the local relief committees in
connection with this Central to all working men in
distress, whether connected with co-operative mills or
stores, with benevolent societies, trade associations,
factories, and workshops, without distinction of creed,
politics, or opinions. This Central, therefore, appeals
to all trades, because it relieves all trades. (Hear,
hear.)
The Secretary delivered in his report, after which the
meeting resolved that 'its best thanks be tendered to
the proprietors of the BEEHIVE, and Mr. George Potter
in particular, for their generous advocacy of our
funds.' Also to Mr. Watson, of the Shipwrights in
Newcastle, for his remittance of £l. 11s. id. Also to
Mr. Dyson, of the Spennymoor Colliery, for a Post-
office Order of 14s. 2d. Total received this week from
Mr. Potter, £35. (Cheers.) The thanks of the
meeting were passed to the Rev. Mr. Morley, rector of
Spilsby, for a parcel of useful clothing,
Mr. William Wilkinson expressed an opinion that
blanketing was a chief want in many families, und was
severely felt during the present frost.
Mr. Peacock stated that one of the local committee
applying for clothing to the middle class committee,
was refused because he belonged to the working man's
Central. (Cries of 'Shame !')
The deputation to Birmingham gave in their report.
Their reception by the pretended Working Men's
Committee meeting at the Town Hall was respectful,
but Mr. Bishop was evidently biassed in favour of the
Manchester Central. They asked for a portion of the
collections, but were refused. They had been to many
working men's committees, but never before saw so
strong a bias in favour of employers. (Hear, hear.)
Mr. Shackleton said that this week the London
Trades' Council would meet, and he hoped to see a
real working men's committee speak on this subject.
The distress was so vast that it N$ ould behove all
trades to help if Lancashire was to be saved, and a
National Working Men's Relief Committee established
in London to collect subscriptions from all quarters,
will be required to meet the crisis. (Applause.)
Mr. Hargreaves gave little encouragement to the
poor operatives if they had to depend upon middle-
class relief,—it was partial, grudgingly given, and in-
adequate. (Hear, hear.)
A deputation was then agreed upon to be sent to
Liverpool, to stir up the trades there.
Mr. Heap thought it strange that the Liverpool men
who had met to consider their claims had not yet pro-
nounced. He believed every artifice was being tried
to prevent working men from supporting their own
Central. (Hear, hear.)
After some discussion, the usnal grants were made
to Burnley, Padiham, and Habergham.
Mr. Wilkinson said that coals, clogs, as well as food,
were being distributed by the president, and a sewing-
class would be this week commenced at Habergham
with the victims of the middle-class relief committees,
—girls who were rejected by the other relief boards
because their fathers were connected with trade dis-
putes. (Hear, hear.)
Applications for grants from Great Harwood, Rams.
bottom, Bacup, and Accrington were deferred from
want of funds.
The treasurer said he had great hopes of being ta
possession of greater funds next week.
The meeting then separated.

The following letter has been addressed to the
editor of the Daily Telegraph upon the extraordinary
conduct pursued by the Mansion House Committee.
Will working men continue to send their subscriptions
to this committee to be thus invested by them while so
many thousands are perishing ?--‘ SlR,—Can you tell
me, Sir, for what reason on earth the Lord Mayor's
committee, whilst thousands are dragging out a half-
starved existence, on a pittance of about 2s. a week, in
the operative districts, have invested £40,000 in Con-
sols that has been entrusted to their care to relieve
these poor people? If they have too much money let
them double the allowance they are now doling out, as
though they were afraid London had no more money
to give. Until that £40,000, now lying by whilst half
a million of people are in want of bread, is realised and
distributed, I shall not subscribe another penny
towards the Mansion House Fund, but shall send my
contributions either to you, or the Central Committee
in LancaShire.—Limmo, Nov. 22.'
[Meetings have been held in several of the London
parishes and other places during the week, in aid of the
distress fund. The important meeting of the delegates
of the London Trade Societies, held on Tuesday even-
ing last, will be found reported in another column.]

articles.title: CATHOLIC DEHONST.RATION AT
articles.text:
CATHOLIC DEHONST.RATION AT

BLACKHEATH.

On Sunday last a demonstration in favour of the
Pope was held at Blackheath, attended by about 2,000
Irishmen, principally resident in Bermondsey, Dept-
ford, Greenwich, and Woolwich. There were at least
5,000 spectators, but unlike the hired Irish 'roughs'
in Hyde-park a few weeks back, they allowed the
conveners of the meeting to hold it and express their
opinions in peace. Me business of the meeting com-
menced by a Mr. Looney coming forward and asking
all Irishmen present to take off their hats, and give
three cheers for the Pope. This appeal was responded
to, amidst loud cheering, by about one-forth of the
crowd, and was followed by loud hisses from another
portion. Mr. O'Leary having been called upon to preside,
Mr. 'Wylie, of Deptford, came forward and said
he stood there as an Irishman and a Catholic
to maintain the temporal power of the Holy Father
against all assailants. He then went on to
denounce the late attempt of Garibaldi to conquer
Rome, and praised the conduct of those of his country-
men who had signalised their devotion to the Pope in
Hyde-park. He concluded by proposing That this
meeting expresses its opinion as to the necessity of
maintaining the temporal power of the Pope, and
offers its utmost sympathy to the Holy Father in his
present troubles and. sorrows.' Mr. Looney seconded
the resolution in a violent speech, in which he stigma-
tised Garibaldi as a tyrannical, heretical, buccaneer-
ing, unprincipled, and piratical filibuster, well deserving
the fate he met with in his late unholy expedition.
This opinion was received with tremendous cheering
from the Irishmen, and by loud hissing and laughter
from the other portion of the crowd. Several other
speakers supported the resolutions in speeches abusive
of Garibaldi and. his principles; the chairman was
about to put it to the meeting, when several of those
around him suggested, as it was evident they would be
in a minority, on a show of hands, he should put it to
the meeting by calling for three cheers in its favour.
Just at this moment considerable confusion was created
by a person in the crowd calling out 'Three cheers
for Garibaldi,' and a rash of Irishmen being made
towards him, in the midst of which the chairman called
for a show of hands in favour of the reselution, which
being heard only by the Irishmen immediately in
front of the mound, was only responded to by them,
the bulk of the meeting being unaware that the resolu-
tion had. been put. The chairman declared the reso-
lution carried unanimously, and. immediately declared.
the meeting dissolved. The Irishmen then reformed
in procession, and proceeded homeward.

THE DENS OF DEURY-LANE.-Dr. Lankester held

articles.title: CENTRAL CRIJMV.AL COURT.
articles.text:
CENTRAL CRIJMV.AL COURT.

At the opening of the November Sessions the
Recorder made the following remarks:—
The Recorder, in charging the .grand jury, said he
was very sorry that he could not congratulate them
upon there being a small number of cases to be brought
before them, for, although the interval that had elapsed
since the last session was somewhat less than usual,
there was a very considerable number of prisoners to be
tried, and there appeared to be a great increase of crime,
particularly of one class of crime coining under the
designation of street robberies, there being no fewer than
27 persons who were charged with highway robbery or
with assaults with intent to rob. When a state of
things like this occurred with regard to any particular
offence, it was always a difficultthing to discover whether
it arose from an actual increase of the crime or film
increased diligence and watchfulness on the part of the
police.; and he certainly found that in many of the cases
that appeared in the present calendar the police did
appear to have exercised agreat deal of diligence in watch-
ing and detecting suspicious persons, and this would,
no doubt, account to some extent for the increase in the
number of those charges, on the present occasion. The
result of his experience in that court was that formerly
these garotte robberies were in most cases committed
upon persons who were in a state of intoxication, and the
reason for this was obvious, as persons in such a condi-
tion were more liable to become the victims of such an
attack, and were also not likely to give correct evidence
afterwards so as to lead to the detection of the guilty
parties. Of late, however, this was undoubtedly not the
case; and the persons who appeared to have been made
the subject of attack were not open to such an observa-
tion ; and if this very serious offence was really on the
increase, he could only express a hope that the police
would continue to exhibit the same watchfulness and
vigilance which they certainly appeared by the deposi-
tions to have exhibited in many of these cases. On the
part of the,Court he would also say that in every case
where persons were proved to have banded themselves
together to commit this offence, and a conviction took
place, a punishment would undoubtedly be inflicted of a
character that would be likely to cause considerable
terror to persons engaged in such offences. There were
two cases of child murder, in one of which it appeared
that the prisoner was suspected to be in the family-
way, but she declared that this was not the case. She
was, however, no doubt, afterwards delivered of the
child in question, and, according to the medical evidence,
the child was alive when it was born. The body was
found concealed in a chimney, and it appeared that a
piece of string was tied tightly round the neck; and it
would be for them to consider, after hearing the evidence
of the surgeon and the other facts in the ease, whether
the death could have arisen from any other cause than
the wilful act of the prisoner. The second charge of
wilful murder was one of a similar character, the
prisoner, it appeared, having denied that she was in the
family-way, although she was taxed with being in that
condition and not having made any preparation for the
birth. The cause of death in this case appeared to be
injuries to the head of the child, the skull being fractured,
and the only point they would have to consider was,
whether these injuries were inflicted accidentally by the
prisoner at the time of the birth of the child, or whether
they had been wilfully inflicted by her, in which case it
would be their duty to find a true bill against the
prisoner for wilful murder.

articles.title: GEIVERAL BUJ2iY2IDE.
articles.text:
GEIVERAL BUJ2iY2IDE.

General Burnside, who has been nominated, some say
temporarily, others permanently, to the command, is in
his fortieth year, a soldier by education, and one of the
most popular commanders whom the war his produced.
He is not prominent as a politician. He has twice before
tleelined the appointment, basing his refusal mainly on
the fa: superior fitness of M'Clellan, and partially on
personal ni,.+-ives of private friendship for that general.
'Unless he shall gain a speedy victory, which is so un-
likely as to be all but impossible, he too, will have to go
into winter quarters and suffer week by week, and day
by day, a dripping of the little rain drops of detraction
on the rock of his popularity, which will wear it away
before the spring. But if, contrary to expectation, he
should attack and conquer,—or should he, by force of un-
controllable circumstances, of which the early winter is
not the least, be prevented from striking a blow,—the
result of non-result will be equally conclusive to the
aggrandisement of M'Clellan, who is the real hero of the
hour. The complaint against M'Clellan was that he
was slow and inactive. But at the time when he was
superseded his army was in motion, as he had actually
gained a succession of small victories; so that if Burn-
side win a large battle, M'Clellan's friends will assert
that he prepared the way for it, and that he also would
have triumphed, and perhaps more splendidly, if the
President had not dismissed him at the critical moment
when his plans were ripening into maturity. If, on the
other hand, Burnside fight and be defeated, or if the
enemy escape his pursuit, the friends of M'Clellan will
be equally ready with the reminder that if their
favourite had been left in command the result would
have been different,--that Richmond would have been
taken, and the 'backbone' of the rebellion broken.
Thus, in either case, the Democratic party will turn
rortune to the advantage of their candidate, and the
President, as well aft Secretaries Chase and Stanton, and
all the other great and little people who aspire to the
perilous honour of the chief magistracy, will have the
mortification of reflecting that they have made the man
whom they attempted to unmake, and weakened their
own chances in attempting to ruin those If their rival.
General Burnside is, of course, quite aware of the
danger in which the army is placed by the sudden
removal of its commander. The Confederates are not
likely to miss the opportunity of striking a blow, if the
weather and the state of the roads and rivers will allow
and should he be induced by the clamour of the 'On to
Richmond' fanatics to follow the retreating army of
General Lee towards Gordonsville—which it is Lee's
evident intention he should do—General Stonewall'
Jackson anti General Stuart may appear before Wash-
ington and again alarm the country for the safety of the
capital and the person of the President. Such a hocus-
pocus as the simultaneous occupation of Richmond by
the Federals, and of Washington by the Confederates,
would be an amusing incident in this dreary war, and
might incline men'sminds to ideas of pacification by the
sheer force of its absurdity.

A CELEBRATED PARISEL—The Registrar of Tomintoul,
Banffshire, in his note in the Registrar-General's
qu'lrt-,rly report of births, deaths, and marriages, speak-
3ng of his parish, says :—‘ Owing to the general poverty of
the district, there are now very few residing in it who
have married within the last seven years. In no part
of the country are there more old, settled-down bache-
lors.'

LONDON TRAFFIC.—Notice of application to Parlia-
ment in the ensuing Session has been given by the city
authorities for power to regulate the several routes to
be followed by the omnibuses, cabs, and other public
carriages for the conveyance of passengers, or to ply
for hire, and by all cArts, waggons, and other vehicles
adapted or used for the conveyance of goods &c.,
passing into, through, or cut of the city of London and
the liberty thereof, and the speed at which they shall
be driven; to regulate the periods between which carts,
waggons, &c., may stop in any street, lane, &c., for the
purpose of being laden or unladen, and the time which
any such cart, waggon, &c., may so remain; to regulate
the height to which carts, waggons, and other vehicles
for the conveyance of goods, wares, and merchandise
may be laden, and the breadths between the outsides
of the wheels of any such vehicle and the maximum
width of the load of any such vehicle, to determine
the particular streets, lanes' roads, &c., and the period
of the day through which carts, waggons or other
vehicles, wholly or partially laden with timber, scaffold
and other articles, consisting of wood, metal, or other
material exceeding 20 feet in length, be allowed to pass
or be prohibited from passing; to regulate the mode in
which cabs or hackney carriages shall be distinguished
when empty, and when actually plying for hire; to
regulate the manner in. which 'barrows, trucks, and
hand carts, &c. may be driven, pushed, or wheeled,
and the particular streets, &c., and the particular time
of the day in which the same may be allowed to 4tand,
or be prohibited from standing; and lastly,_to_authorise
the making of by-laws and regulations.

LANCASHIRE DISTRESS.—We learn that the Poor Law
Board have issued orders authorizing the Guardians of
two of the Lancashire unions, those of Preston and
Blackburn, to borrow money under the provisions of the
Union Relief Aid Act, 1862. The order in each case
recites that the Guardians had found that the aggregate
expenditure in and about the relief of the poor of the
whole union, for the quarter ending at Michaelmas last,
exceeded the rate of 3s. in the pound per annum on the
annual rateable value of the property comprised within
the union by the sum of L-; that the Guardians had
resolved that an applicaticn should be made to the Poor
Law Board for power to enable them to borrow the
amount of such excess; and that the Poor Law Board
bad made due inquiry into the circumstances of the
union, and found that the total amount of such excess
was the sum Then the Board, by the order,
give authority to the Guardians to borrow the amount,
and to charge the common fund of the union with its
repayment in the manner provided by the Act. The
order to the Preston Union is dated the 10th November,
and authorizes the borrowing of £3,517 Os. ; and
the order to the Blackburn Union is dated the 21st
November, and authorises the borrowing of 18,89 Q.
The Union Relief Aid Act has been thus found to supply
a ready and inexpensive means of enabling boards of
guardians in the distressed cotton districts to borrow all
the money that they may expend in and about the relief
of the peer in excess of 33. in the pound.—Glo3e.

articles.title: BEE-HIVE, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 29, 1862
articles.text:
THE BEE-HIVE, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 29, 1862

THE SMITEFIELP CLUB CATTLE

BHO At

As the time for the opening of this great show draws
rapidly near, there is redoubled activity on the part of
its managers. Much yet remains to- be- done, but there
ie still a fortnight in which to do it; and if we may
judge from the rate at which the preparations are now
advancing, that time will be amply sufficient. There
can be little doubt that the show will be one of the
largest and most successful ever witnessed. It is not
so generally known as it should be, that the Smithfield
Club never had possession of all the premises at the
Baker-street Bazaar. Even when the shows were
being held in one part of the building, other portions
of it were occupied by dealers in ironmongery, glass
and china, and furniture, and by the Ladies' Bazaar.
The space at the disposal of the dull was simply that
which was generally devoted to the carriage trade,
and so much inconvenience was caused to the proprietors
by the temporary removal of this, that they were by no
means anxious for the show still to be held in their
building. Accordingly, when the club issued advertise-
ments inviting tenders for new premises, the proprietors
of the bazaar did not compete. Since last year they have
largely increased their accommodation in a manner
which was impracticable while the lease of the club
was still in force; and to prove that the parting was in
all respects &friendly one, it deserves to be stated that
they have rendered the authorities of the Agricultural
Hall Company very valuable assistance, by the advice
and the suggestions which their long experience enabled
them to offer. On Saturday, many of the agricultural
implements which have recently been exhibited atSouth
Kensington were removed, direct from the Exhibi-
tion to the New• Hall. The display of these will prove
one of the chief and rriost attractive features of
the corning show; but there will, in addition, be a sepa-
rate exhibition of machinery and implements of a general
character. The ample space which is now at the dis-
posal of the duly will thus be-tutned to sccount in more!
ways than one. Not only will the shop of cattle ancf ,
of farm- implements' be on z settle or nuppecedeated—
magnitude, but the general interest and the practical
utility of the exhibition will be materially increased by
the addition to the display of many articles for which,
in the confined premises at Baker-street, there was no
room. Our readers will remember that a five-shilling day
is now to be introduced; and the reasons given for this
seem sufficiently weighty. The change is not prompted
—at any rate, it is not entirely caused—by any desire
of the Club for self-aggrandisement; but it must be
confessed that, under the old system, the crowd of
visitors was too thick to allow those most interested in
the show to make such a leisurely examination of its
lontents as was desirable. Hustled along by: those who
same merely as sight-seers, the practical agriculturist or
grazier could often catch but a hurried glance at objects
which he really needed to study. Again, this crowd
was found to deter many of the upper classes—and more
especially ladies—from attending the exhibition. Recent
experience, in the case of the Dog Show, has sufficiently
proved that the experiment of introducing a five shilling
day is by no means hazardous, but rather one which may
confidently and reasonably be expected to prove a com-
plete success. The charge of five shillings for admission
will, as we have already stated, be made only on the
opening day—Monday, December B—and, during the
remainder of the show, the charge will only be one
shilling.

The-applications for space for the display of implements
have been, as was naturally to be expected, very nume-
rous; and it is fortunate, indeed, for the committee of
the club that they have secured such spacious premises.
Every specimem of this kind will have to be in its place
before Saturday, the 6th December; whilst animals and
other stock must be in the yard before twelve o'clock on
the night of Friday, the 6th. The means of public
access to the show will be ample, for whilst arrange-
ments have been made with the London General, and
with other omnibus companies, to run to the hall
from all parts of the metropolis, it has further been de-
termined to set aside a certain amount of space, on the
northern side of the building, into which the omnibuses
can turn for the purposes of taking up passengers. A
recess has accordingly been made in front of the
main entrance in the Liverpool-road, so that visitors
can be driven up to the very doors of the building with-
out in the least interfering with the general traffic. On
Saturday night the hall was partially lighted. The annual,
dinner of the club will take place on Wednesday, Dec.
10, at the Freemasons' Hall, when the president of the
association for the present year, the Earl of Faversham,
will occupy the chair: A certain gloom has been cast
over the coming show by the recent death of Mr. Jonas
Webb, the chairman of the Agricultural Hall Company;
and at the last meeting of his brother directors an
address of sympathy -vas unanimously adopted and
ordered to be forwarded to the lamented gentleman's
family. With this exception, however, there is no cloud
upon the prospects of the undertaking; and a success as
complete as must be desired by every one who is
interested, whether directly or indirectly, in the agri-
cultural industry of the country, appears almost kure to
be attained.

A court-martial assembled on board the Victory, at
Portsmouth, on Saturday morning, to try James Kent,
private of the Royal Marines, late of her Majesty's
gunboat Janus, for desertion from that vessel on or
about the 28th February, 1861, while at Shanghae,
China. The court comprised Captains Coote (President),
Connolly, Hire, Lacy, and Commander Bonham, with
Mr. E. Hoskins as officiating Judge Advocate. Prisoner
was granted leave to go on shore; he never returned,
and there was an entry made on the leave-book as
follows, '66th company, James Kent, Feb. 22, 1861,
deserted to Chinese rebel army, from leave at Shanghae.'
The usual It was placed against his name. He was
afterwards arrested under singular circumstances. While
the allies were capturing Tsing-poo, Kent was just
about to be thrown from the battlements and shot as a
Chinese rebel, when he declared that he was an English-
man. In defence he entered into a statement, showing
that he went on shore and got intoxicated, and on regaining
his senses, found himself on board a junk, about thirty
miles up the river from Shanghae. Ho was taken be-
fore a Mandarin and ordered to fight for the rebels but
he refused. His captors then put a band round him
next his skin, and chained him to a wall, where he was
kept, almost starved, for fifteen months. He made three
unsuccessful attempts to escape. On the city being
taken, he was made prisoner, and taken to where the
breach had been made where he saw some English
soldiers, whom he told he was a marine. He urged
these facts in his favour, and begged the court's consi-
deration on account of his long imprisonment and ill-
treatment. He used every exertion to return to his
ship but failed. The court cleared to deliberate, and
on returning found the charge of desertion not proven,
but were of opinion that prisoner was absent without
leave on the day referred to in the charge, for which
they sentenced him to six weeks' imprisonment, with
hard labour, in Winchester gaol, and to forfeit two days'
pay._ _

--NVAR OFFICE Cracur.art.—The subjoined circular in
reference to accidents occurring at rifle ranges has
been recently issued from the 'War Office: 'War
Office, Nov. 14.—Sir,—The attention of the Secretary
of State for War has been drawn to certain fatal or
serious accidents which have lately occurred at rifle
ranges belonging to volunteer corps, and he regrets to
learn, from the reports which he has received, that in
several cases those accidents arose from neglect of the
precautions prescribed by the regulations for the in-
struction and practice of musketry by the officers and
non-commissioned officers whose duty it was to enforce
them. Sir George Lewis, therefore, requests that you
will impress upon the adjutant and sergeant-iustructors
under your command the necessity of observing strict
regularity and discipline when in charge of firing
parties; and that you will point out to them that they
will be in future held seriously responsible for any
deviation from the regulations of the service in which
they may be concerned. lam also to inform you that,
while Sir George Lewis desires that every facility
should be afforded to persons of all classes to acquire a
knowledge of the use of the rifle, he is of opinion that
the safety of the public requires that indiscriminate
private practice at volunteer rifle ranges should not be
permitted, and he therefore requests that you will take
steps to regulate the practice at the ranges under your
control, so as to ensure the presence of an officer or non-
commissioned officer on all occasions when firing is
going on. lam further to observe that the practice of
employing boys as markers at butts is highly danger-
ous and improper, and to request that you will take
care that none but non-commissioned officers, or ex-
perienced volunteers, act in that capacity at the ranges
belonging to the corps under your eoramand.—l have,
Ice., DE GREY AND RIPON.'

A NEW USE FOR CRINOLINE. —The lady with the
marsupial crinoline has experimented on its girl-con-
cealing qualities once too often. Just before the
starting of the mid-day train to Melbourne, an un-
usual amount of fidgety whisperings among the porters
on the platform, resulting in repeated peeps, which
seemed very rude, in at the door of a first-class car-
riage, where sat the lady of the ample skirt, the neatest
little boots in the world (military heels), planted on
the opposite cushion. This—though not an extraor-
dinary position for a lady to assume when fatigued
during the journey—seemed odd at the station. A
porter thought he saw a pair of juvenile trotters on the
carpet, just under the graceful folds of the lady's dress,
but could hardly believe his eyes. Another and
another looked; there could be no mistake. A polite
hint was given to the lady that two passengers could
not travel on the strength of one ticket: The insinua-
tion was indignantly repelled; but, alas! the unsenti-
mental porter laid hold of the juvenile's ankle, and out
the young lady walked from her hiding-place. An
additional ticket was procured, and thp pair proceeded

The Duchess (Dowager) Of Norfolk has taken for a
term of years a mansion in Grosvenor-square, late the
residence of the Duchess of Cleveland.
The medals awarded to the Australian colonies at the
International Exhibition were as follows :—To Yictoria,
115 ; New South Wales, 74; New Zealand, 33; Queens-
land, 28 ; Tasmania, 26 ; South Australia, 24; and

Tire EASTERN FISHERIES.—The larae deliverTes of
herrings at Great Yarmouth reported a week since have
now fallen
.off in consequence of a change in the wea-
ther. On one day last week 1;000 lasts, or the immense
quantity of 13,200;000 fish, were landed. The herrings
received show an improvement in quality, and prices
have in consequence improved, good cargoes having
realised £ll, £l2, or £l3 per last. At Lowestoft the
receipts have averaged from 90 to 300 lasts per day; and
although prices have fallen remunerative returns have
still been obtained. On the whole, there is every rea-
son to suppose that the season will prove a lucrative
one. The fish salesmen at Yarmouth have agreed—at
any rate for the present—not to sell fish on Sundays.
A new mode of engraving and priaiting bank-notes
has been brought forward by Messrs. Ashby and Co.,
which are asserted to possess the recommendations-1.
That they cannot be photographed, as the black print-
ing is interlaced, in an extremely complicated manner,
with another colour; 2. That the note plates cannot be
copied, the ornametal engraving being executed by a
machine from a matrix arbitrarily formed and made
intricate by transposition in kaleidoscope fashion, and
3. That note plates engraved by such a matrix cannot
be produced again by the engravers without the matrix,
so that if that is destroyed, or handed to the custody of
the bankers, they hold their own security.
A Hrianoo PAPER ON THE BIBLE.—The Bengali
papers seem to be becoming more liberal in their views.
The Sajjoua Rajana, advocating the introduction of the
Bible into Government schools, describes it, in remark-
able language, as coming from a heathen, as the best
and most excellent of all English books, and there is
not its like in the English language. As every joint of
the sugar-cane from the root to the top is full of sweet-
ness' so every page of the Bible is fraught with the
most precious instructions. A portion of that book
would yield to you more of sound morality than a thou-
sand other treatises upon the same subject. In short, if
any person studies the English language with a view to
gain wisdom, there is not another book which is mere
worthy of being read than the Bible.'
BURGLARS SHOT AT BY A LADY.—A. somewhat ex-
citing encounter between a woman and a couple of
burglars took place in the garden of a house in Sum-
mer-street, Birmingham, early on the morning of
Saturday. It appears that Mrs. Bellamy, who lives at
No. 16 in the above street, retired to rest somewhat
early on Friday night, and that at about one o'clock
on Saturday morning she was awakened by hearing
footsteps in the garden in front of her house. She at
once got up, and, taking with her a loaded pistol, went
to the window, which she threw open. Seeing two
men huddled together near an arbour in her next door
neighbour's garden, she asked them what they wanted.
No answer was returned ; and,
,judging that they were
there for no good purpose, she fired her pistol at them,
without, however, doing them any injury. The pair
immediately took to their heels, ran rapidly across the
garden, made for the road, and were lost to sight.
Police-constable Withey, being on duty near, and hear-
ing the report of a pistol, hastened to the spot, and,
learning what had happened, searched around the
garden. The result was the finding of a mask and a
gimlet, which had evidently been dropped by the two
men. All traces of the men themselves were, how-
ever, lost. The premises were again examined by day-
light by Mr. Layton, the owner of the house, when a
razor was found. Either the same men or others, it
seems, made several unsuccessful attempts at burglary
in the neighbourhood on the same night.
WRECK OF A FRENCH VESSEL.—Palling, Norfolk,
Saturday night.—At 5.15 this morning, during a strong
wind from the N.N.E., and in a heavy sea the French
schooner Josephine, of Dunkirk, coal laden, came on
shore about a mile to the northward of Palling. The
crew of the lifeboat of the National Lifeboat Institution
on this station was immediately assembled, and, horses
having been attached to the carriage of the boat, she
proceeded along the beach a distance of three-quarters of
a mile. At daylight it was observed that the vessel was
a derelict, having been abandoned before she came to the
beach. The lifeboat was, consequently, taken back and
placed in the boathouse. From the strong wind blowinoca
there is every appearance of the vessel becoming a total
wreck. This valuable lifeboat was instrumental, in March
last, in rescuing the crew of ten men of the wrecked brig
Ann, of Shields.

A 'STRANGE VISITOR.--011 the night of the 3rd inst.,
as the bark Dimbrody, of New Ross, was on her home-
ward passage from Quebec, 950 miles from land, long.
30 W.., one of the seamen observed a strange .looking
bird attempting to roost among the shrouds. After
many unsatisfactory efforts, it at length found a brief
resting•place on the main topsail-yard, to which one of
the sailors quickly ran up and effected a capture. The
bird proved, on examination, to be a very large owl, and
created much surmise as to what unlucky wind could
have blown it so far out of its latitude. The commander
of the ship, Captaim W. Williams, treated his strange
visitant with the tenderest care, and nursed it in his
own cabin, but in vain,--the bird of Minerva pined
amid the sons of Neptune, and died on the third day
after its capture. The skin was skilfully removed by
Mr. W. Fortune, the sf-cond mate of the Dunbrody, and
temporarily stuffed with oakum. It is now the
,pro-
perty of Mr. Graves, the head of the wealthy and
highly resiectable firm of Graves and Son, New Ross,
and the owner of the ship on which the unlucky bird
alighted. For, the benefit of your ornithological readers
I append a description of the owl. Its length from
the point of the beak the extremity of the
tail is 21 inches; from wing to wing extended, 55
inches; the wings are white, and mottled beautifully
with pale chocolate colour, in crescent-shaped spots';
the beak is one inch in length, and jet black; the eyes
are bright amber and black • and the claws and naiLs
inches long.—lrish Times.

JAMIE --'1•01I.ER, THE CALF.— We dare say most of our
agricultural readers are aware of a pretty general cus-
tom among many of the farm servants in Perthshire, of
calling any cow or calf that their masters may purchase,
either by the name of the farm from whence it came or
by the name and surname of its previous owner. The
following is a very good illustration of this practice.
Once on a time a farmer lived not very far front the
village of St. Martin's. This worthy gentleman bought
a calf from an elderly neighbour named Storer, but be-
fore he reached home with his purchase the shades of
evening had closed around him, and his family and
domestic -servants had retired to rest. Disdaining
to disturb either family or servants, he proceeded to the
byre and bound the calf with his own hands. On
entering the house he informed his eldest son of what
he had done, and observed that he would see it in the
morning. On the following morning the son went to
the byre, but was surprised to find that the calf was
dead. He immediately went to his father, and, with
great seriousness in his face, informed him that Jamie
Storer was dead. 'Oh! never mind,' said the sire,
Jamie was an oddish sort of a man; you couldna look
for anything else. In fact, I ave thocht he wad gang
awa like the snuffing o' a candle. Never mind, never
mind.' 'Aye, father,' exclaimed the son, its Jamie
Storer, the calf, that's dead!' 'Jamb Storer, the calf!'
shouted the venerable sire; that alters the case. Bring
me my slippers,' an order which was speedily obeyed.
In company they reached the byre, only to find the sad
tale verified. Poor Jamie had been rather slackly bound,
and, in his struggles to free himself, he was choked.
The old man left the byre, muttering to himself, 'Ah,
weel—ah, weel ; its but warld's gear. It's maybe better
the way it is. Auld Jamie is a nice kind V a child r—
