articles.title: PRESTON.
articles.text:
PRESTON.

A deputation from the board of guardians, appointed
at their last meeting to wait on the Charitable Relief
Committee in order to confer with them as to a proposed
new arrangement in the mode of administering relief to
persons in receipt thereof from both sources, have just
held the conference. The• deputation consisted of Messrs.
Hewitt, C. R. jacson, Dixon and Cooper; and they
were received by Mr. Joseph Livesey and about a dozen
members of the General Relief Committee. One of the
objects sought to be attained by the interview,, it was
stated, was to come to such an understanding as should
the more effectually prevent imposition on the funds,
both of the Union and the charitable committee. The
Relief Committee said, if that was their sole object,
they would be glad to asist them all power;
but if, as had been rumoured, their wish was to
lessen—the- ametuate-sitf relief granted-from'. the cha-
ritable fund, the. 'Relief Committee- 4uld—decidedly
object to
.any course,. which might, have that effect.
The eleputaion intimated that that VaS not their object.
Mr. Jaeson said he wai-decidedly opposed to the making
of any reduction in the amount of relief granted by
the Board. Mr. Hewitt saidthat every source of income
of the applicants for relief should be taken into account
by the guardians when dispensing it. The committee,
however, replied that the contributors to the fund placed
at their disposal desired to raise the condition of the
people to a better standard than the allowances by the
Board of Guardians wonld secure, and that if any
reduction should be made in the allowance from the
parochial source the contributors to the Relief Fund
would be dissatisfied. Mr. John Cooper said it had
been a moot-point among the guardians whether the
plan adopted at Blackburn could not by advantageously
set in operation in Preston —viz., for the Board of
Gualailians to take sole charge of the relief of the constant
or usual paupers, and the Relief Committee to provide
for the occasional poor—i.e., those thrown out of em-
ployment by the cotton famine. This difficulty,
however, presented itself to the minds of the committee
—that persons were paupers one day and perhaps not
paupers another day, and that the condition of that class
was constantly fluctuating; the people on the list of the
Board of Guardians would be under-supplied with relief
if the amount they received from the Union were
not supplemented from the other sources, for the small
pittance which they received from the Board was really
not enough for their maintenance. The Relief Com-
mettee even had been found fault with by the London
Mansion-house Committee because a higher rate of relief
was not granted by themselves, and it was promised that
if they would but expend it the money required should
be forthcoming. They would, therefore, not venture to
become responsible for the consequences of any such
attempt to divide the classes of persons in receipt of
relief. They believed, indeed, that at Blackburn, and
also at Chorley, where there had been such division, the
system would be found not to have worked well; and
that even if the principle on which the Preston Relief
Committee carried on their operations were wrong, it
would be found impossible—at any rate, attended with
immense difficulty—to reorganise tkeir mode of opera-
tions in .their present stage and extent, and such re-
arrangement would doubtless lead to great dissatisfaction
on all hands. The public press reported that the system
adopted by the charitable committee was inferior to none
and superior to most, and it should be borne in mind
that neatly every letter received which contained sub-
scriptions urged them to increase, and on no account to
lessen in any way, the amount which they expended in
relief. The deputation then withdrew, one or two
members of them expressing themselves as being exceed-
ingly dissatisfied with the result of the interview.
The Committee of the Relief Fund on Saturday
issued their usual weekly report of operations, it
shows a further increase in the number of cases on the
relief list.s-iThere are now on the books 9,410 cases,
comprising 37,075 individuals. The cost, owing to the
distribution of coals (for which seven yards are opened
in different parts of the kingdom), is considerably aug-
mented, and amounts to £1,200, besides £5OO given out
in bedding and clothing. During the week 31,648
loaves of 41b. :each, weighing in the aggregate 56 tons
10 cwt. 1 qr. 4 lb. were distributed. The soup, scouse,
and coffee distributed has amounted to 43,646 quarts.
A large quantity of clothing has arrived during the
week, and the distribution of bedding 'and clothing
among the poor unemployed operatives has been made,
with great advantage to themselves; and their expres-
sions of gratitude have even overwhelmed those who
have superintended the distribution with tears, in
common with tears of thankfulness from themselves.
The fever has during the last few days broken out in
new parts of the town, some of the cases being very
bad ones. The fever ward is very near completion;
indeed, the erection has been finished, and all is ready
for the internal fittings and bedding. Patients are to
be admitted on Tuesday or Wednesday next. We re-
gret to have to record that Miss Jane Parr (sister of the
Rev. Canon Parr, vicar of Preston), who has been
assiduous in her aid of the movement for the 'relief of
the roor, has fallen a victim to the fever. It is
arranged to hold a series of free entertainments for the
amusement of the working classes now out of employ-
ment.

articles.title: BURNLEY.
articles.text:
BURNLEY.

The Mayor presided at the weekly meeting of the
Relief Committee held last Thursday. After the trans-
action of some formal business, the committee agreed to
raise the relief administered from Is. 9d. to 2s. per head,
and make a grant of £457 6s. 11d, for the relief of 6,323
individuals. They also granted £45 ss. in behalf of the
sewing classes.

articles.title: BLACKBURN.
articles.text:
BLACKBURN.

At the meeting of the Board- of; Guardians on Satur-
day it appeared that there were receiving out relief in
the Blackburn Union 22,500, an increase of 659 in the
week and one of 91,019 on the corresponding week of
1861, and at a cost of £1,223 3s. 2d., £65 2s. id. more
than the previous week and £1,053 9s. 2d. more than
that of the corresponding week of last year. Of the
22,500 relieved 17,861 belonged to the district of Black-
burn, and were relieved with £1,009 10s. 9d. and the
rest in the districts of Damen and Os cValdtwistle.

articles.title: WIGAN.
articles.text:
WIGAN.

The returns of the relieving officers to the board of
guardians show that during the past week 4,869 persons
are now in receipt of outdoor relief from th,,m—an
increase of 80 on the last return and one of 2,520 on the
corresponding week of last year. The expenditure has
been £343 ss. Bd., against £339 is. 6d. last week, and
against £l2B Ils. Bd. in the corresponding week of 1661.
In Wigan alone there are 3,235 persons in receipt of
relief from the officers—an increase of 132 on last week.
The return of the numbers relieved by the relief com-
mittee shows a very large increase. There are now on
the books of the committee 4,331 cases, representing
11,909 persons—an increase of 355 cases or 975 persons
on the week. The expenditure has in the same period
risen from £537 4s. to £589 Is. for food alone, a large
sum being also paid for clothing. Adding the numbers
in the workhouse to those given above as relieved by the
two bodies, a total of 17,222 is obtained. This is an
increase of 969 on the last return, when the total was
16,253. This shows that more persons were added to
the relief-lists during the last week than in any week
since the commencement of the distress.

GAROTTING IN THE PROVINCES. -- The infamous
system of garotting has, we are sorry to find, found its
way into the country, and it is much to be feared that,
unless the police are very vigilant, many of these
atrocities will be committed during the coining winter.
It appears that an attempt at garotting occurred recently.
Shortly after six o'clock Mr. H. Usher, of Boddicote, was
returning home from Banbury, and when nearly opposite
the first milestone he was accosted by a man who
solicited alms. On being refused he followed Mr. Usher,
cursing both loud and deep.' Mr. Usher continued
on his way; but, fearing an assault, he drew his pocket
knife and opened it. Scarcely had he done so when he
was attacked by a man who sprang from the hedge and
attempted to throttle him. A short struggle ensued;
Mr. Usher succeeded in inflicting a wound in the
scoundrel's right shoulder, and in knocking him back-
wards by a tremendous blow with his fist. The fellow
screamed out to his 'Pal,' using a frightful oath, 'Jem,
he has knifed me! Mr. Usher, not knowing whether
there were any more of the vagabonds in the neigh-
bourhood, deemed it prudent to make off as quickly as
possible.
Wisc SAWS.'—It is always term-time in the Court
Conscience.—The vicious reproving vice is like the
raven chiding blackness.—lf you wouldn't have afflic-
tion make you a second visit, listen to its teachings at
the first.—Peace gains her victories with spears of grain
and blades of grass.—The richest man on earth is but a
pauper fed and clothed by the bounty of heaven.--The
miser isn't vain; he thinks a penny better worth saving
than his soul.—Women are apt to make darlings of
their ugliest thoughts, 48 they. do of their deformed
children.

articles.title: ADDRESS OF THE EMANCIPATION • 4OCIETY:
articles.text:
ADDRESS OF THE EMANCIPATION
• 4OCIETY:

Fellow Countrymen,—The abolitiort of negro slavery
—always an object of earnest desire to the Rhilanthro-
pist—has become now an urgent political necessity.
Thirty years ago England found it impossible any
longer to tolerate the existence in her colonies of
800,000 bondmen. Since that time France, Holland,
and Portugal have decreed the abolition of slavery in
their colonial possessions. Slavery in the United
States of America has at length produced a crisis as
much more terrible than that which threatened us, as
the extent of the system is greater and the strength of
the slaveowner more formidable. If; in our own
country, slavery had occupied half the soil, had counted
as votaries or as victims a third of the population, had
for many years controlled the government, and had
diffused the poison of its influence through, all our reli-
gious and social institutions, we should not have got
rid of it by so easy a process as the payment of
£20,000,000 sterling. It would probably have pro-
voked a civil war, and have threatened to destroy the
commonwealth it could no longer rule. Thus has
slavery in America armed in its defence the States that
proclaimed themselves an independent Confederacy, and
demand European recognition in that capacity.
The government of the United States has tardily but
decisively advanced from the principle of free soil
territory to that of free labour throughout the Union.
It has proposed and earnestly recommended voluntary
emancipation, offering partial or entire indemnity from
the Federal exchequer. To the States and slave-owners
in arms against its authority it announces the cessation
of their legal title to property in human beings; and
appoints the first day of the next year as the epoch of
emadipation through all ,the States flievein rebellion.
The Southern slave-holders respond by the denun-
ciation of this measure as a violation of the laws of war,
and threaten acts of retaliation that imply a rooted
resolve to hold the negro race in the deepest degradation
is well as the hardest bondage.
_ _ _ _

To such a struggle England cannot be indifferent.
Neutrality must be to the end, as it has been from the
beginning, the rule of our governmental policy. But
our people cannot regard with unconcern a conflict the
origin and issues of which are so closely allied to the
question of personal slavery or freedom to four millions
of human beings.
To make more plain this connection, to make it every-
where perceived and confessed, by the force of indisput-
able testimony, that the South is fighting for slavery,
whilst the North
.is fully committed to the destruction
of slavery—is the principal object for which this society
is organised. Its promoters do not believe that English
anti•slavery sentiment is dead, or even enfeebled. They
are confident that when the demands and designs of the
South are made clear there will be no danger of your
being enticed into complicity therewith. They trust
that an unequivocal expression of English feeling in
favour of the Republican North—of its free soil platform
and its free labour proclamation—will powerfully en-
courage the friends of negro freedom in America, and so
hasten the satisfactory termination of the war that-now
devastates the New World and afflicts the old.—By order
of the committee, WILLIAM EVA.IIB Chairman.
F. W. CHESSON:Hon. Sec.
Offices, 65, Fleet-street, London, E.C.

articles.title: TERRIBLE COLLIERY EXPLOSIOA AND LOSS OF LIFE.
articles.text:
TERRIBLE COLLIERY EXPLOSIOA
AND LOSS OF LIFE.

Between five and six o'clock on Saturday morning an
explosion occurred at Walker Colliery, situate about
three miles from Newcastle. There were about thirty
men in the pit at the time of the occurrence, of whom
fifteen have been brought up alive, though they are
injured from the effects of gas. Seven are known to be
dead, and eight more are in the colliery, and have not
been seen, but there is not the slightest chance of their
being got out alive. The pit has two shafts, the upcast
shaft being about a quarter of a mile distant, near
Walker factory. Before seven o'clock three men were
brought up at the upeast shaft. They were named
Chamber; Knox, and Collins. They were all alive,
but each was suffering from the effects of gas and fright,
as well as from the shock they had received by being
thrown down when the explosion occurred. From
their statements it seems that there would be about
thirty men in the pit, some of whom were working
bye,' at a considerable distance from the mouths of the
shafts. It is supposed that some of these men had been
at work in a trouble,' and had fired-shots, from which
the explosion may have occurred. The injured men are
likely to recover. They describe the first warning they
had of the explosion as like the sound of a hurricane,
and its effect on themselves was to throw them violently
down. The stoppings, brattices, &c., in the colliery
workings are all destroyed, and the mine is thrown into
confusion; some of the coal in the further workings of
the pit is on fire, and men an) employed in carrying
water to extinguish it. Mr. Cole, the resident viewer,
was among the first to descend the pit, and since that
time parties of miners had gone down to explore the
workings, at great risk to themselves. Mr. Jobling, the
principal engineer, and one of the owners of the colliery
(which is the property of Messrs. Lambert, Nicholson,
and Co.), has also descended; and shortly before the
dispatch of our parcel, Mr. Matthias Dunn, Inspector
of Coal Mines, and Mr. Potter, of Cramlingten. mining
engineer, has been lowered down the shaft. Those who
have walked as far in the workings as they possibly
could had seen three dead bodies, and it is feared that
several others had shared the fate of their unfortunate
comrades. It is to be feared that these men who have
not yet been brought out of the pit are dead. The miners
who descended to explore the mine come up, much ex-.
hausted, and state the air to be very bad. A small crowd
is assembled at the pit mouth, but there is very little
excitement. The pit workings are very extensive, and
those men who have been brought up alive were at a
great distance :rom what is believed to be the seat of
the explosion. The whole of the horses and ponies
down the pit were killed, and were very much
cha-red. There were about 10 horses and 24 ponies
down in all. The stables had been on fire. When
Mr. Dunn and Mr. Jobling were down, several
of the stoppings had been restored, and the air was much
improved. By the time we left, the whole of the stop-
pings had been temporarily restored, and the pit made
safe for the men to go down and bring the bodies to
bank. A large hand barrow had been provided for that
purpose. We may mention the providential escape of
George Mitford, who, at the time of the explosion, was
working in another part of the pit. As soon as he
heard the concussion, he ran for his life as hard as he
could, but was overtaken by the after-damp and was
struck down like a shot. He gave himself up for dead,
but was fortunately rescued by some men sent down to
save the lives of as many as they could. A considerable
time elapsed before he came about a little, but he is
likely to expurience the baneful effects of the after-
damp for some days yet. Up to midnight twelve of the
bodies had been recovered and four were missing.

LATER PARTICULARS.
The following is a description of the interior of the
pit after the explosion, and the discovery of the
bodies The first news of the catastrophe produced
gre.it alarm among the colliery people living in the
village, and the distress of those whose relatives were
known to be down the pit was most poignant. The
high platform of the pit, where the work of the down-
cast shaft is carried on, was kept clear by a force of
the Nortumberland county police, and the work
of exploring and clearing the pit of gas was conducted
steadily and with despatch. It was not, however, until
about 7 o'clock that the task of identifying the dead
and bringing them to the bottom of the shaft become
Practicable. At this time the work of recovering the
bodies commenced in earnest. The party then peram-
bulating the recesses of the mine witnessed sad and awful
scenes. Four of the men were found in their respective
'boards,' or long narrow spaces of working. One man,
Moore, had been blown a distance of about 30 yards
from the face of the seam; he was much scorched, but
not considerably injured in othet ways, and he was
easily recognised. In the second board, T. Miller, a
man about 40 years of age, was lying near the face of
the board, and seemed as calm as if in life. He was
neither scorched nor wounded, and did not seem to have
been moved from the place where he had been working.
Thos, Kenny was the man in the third board, and he had
been carried by the force of the blast about 46 yards from
the place where he would be working when the explo-
sion occurred. One of his legs was broken below the
knee; he was sadly burnt about the head, and was so
much disfigured as not to be easily recognised. John
Ellerton' who was in the fourth board, was thrown
about 16 yards from the face of the working, and was
much scorched. His body was almost buried among an
accumulation of flat stones, and he was disfigured.
William Burrell was found in the west way leading
to the juds.' He was lying flat upon his face, and
appeared to have been struck dead by fire. Juds 'is
a name applied by miners to broken workings, and
in one of these juds, about one hundred yards from the
unbroken workings or boards, five men were found.
John Mitcheson, George Barnes, and William Barnes
were discovered lying over each other in the corner of
the jud, and it was remarked as a curious fact that a
watch found in the pocket of William Barnes was still
going and indicating the correct time. A watch found•
in the pocket of George Barnes had stopped at 10
minutes past 6 o'clock. In the west jud Thomas
Atkinson was lying on his back upon some coal, where
it was inferred he had been resting at the time of the
explosion. Barnes seemed to have been struck on the
face as he was lying in a similar position on the coals.
An expression of intense fright was observable on his
countenance and in his eyes. Thus 12 men were brought
to the foot of the shaft. Five coffins, bping all that were
then ready, received the remains of five men.

Her Majesty has commissioned Mrs. Thornycroft to
make a bust of the Princess Alexandra of Denmark. and
her Royal Highness is giving, daily, the necessary
sittings for the model.
The Russian Embassy at Paris has contradicted for-
mally the rumour that the Duke de Lenchtenberg was
to come to Paris for the inauguratioa of the Boulevard
du Prince Eugene.
,
Her Majesty (says the West Surrey Times) is expected
to pay her usual visit to Sir James Clark, at Bagshot
Park, during the present month.
A dentist in one of our large citieq advertises that he
inserts teeth cheaper than anybody else. He might find
a bulldog who would do it still, cheaper. Curiosities
wassted.—A handle for a blade of grass, a letter written
with a cow pen, and a feather from the wing of a hospital.
—Western Australia Inquirer.
The good tradesmen of Brussels are making free with
the late Exhibition. Numbers of shops in that city
display the medal, and very many others announce the
fact that they have obtained one at the Exposition de
Londres.' Nine out of every ten of these medals are
said to be impostures.
A letter from Memel (Prussia) states that the trade in
amber, which has been limited for some years, has re-
cently received a fresh impetus from the discovery of
several rich veins in that neighbourhood. Most of the
amber found near Memel is sold to merchants at Dantzic
and Leipsic, who export it to Turkey.
Mr. W- H. Stephenson, of the Treasury, has 'been
appointed chairman of the,Board of Inland:Revenue, in
the room of Mr. Pressly, who has resigned. Mr. Ste-
phenson has been long recognised as one of the able:st of
toe permanent Treasury officials, and no better head
coulde be chosen for the department over which he is
about to preside.
Stonewall' Jackson's admirers in Europe have
testified their regard for that brave chieftain by sending
over to him, from Paris, a silver-mounted revolver of a
new pattern, which is constructed to throw balls as a
cannon throws grapeshot. With this weapon it is cal-
culated that a person can destroy half-a-dozen enemies
at a single discharge of the revolver. The presentation
was made by General Beauregard.
A full-length portrait of the late Prince Consort has.
just made its appearance in Windsor, published by Mr.
Mitchell, by command of, and dedicated, by special, per-
mission to, her Majesty the Queen. It is 'engraved by
F. Rolf, from a coloured drawing by E. Corbould, after
a photograph by Miss Day. The Prince appears in the
dress of a private gentleman, leaning against the outer
walls of Osborne, in the act of reading a dispatch, with
a roll of others in his hat, placed upon a garden seat. It
is certainly the most faithful and pleasing likeness of the
Prince Consort that has yet been published, as well as
one of the finest specimens in the sat of line engraving
of the present day.
Manhattan,' the amusing correspondent of the
Horning Herald, writes as follows :—' We are a great
people. We yesterday dispatched the Rev. Levi D.
Chapman and his wife in the barque Lye-ee-Moon for
Shanghai, China. The cost of the expedition will be
about 12,000 doll.; but it will be cheap:if it succeeds in
converting the 365 millions of Chinese from their
wooden Joss arrangements to any of our numerous
faiths. I think the man and wife mission are Presby-
terians of the new light school, and not of the old
school, though I do not suppose it will make much
difference to the Chinese.'
Apropos of bubble-betting,' one of the best 'sells'
of the present day is to bet as to the number of five-
pound-notes required to weigh down a sovereign.
Another is to bet that a man cannot mark the exact
height of your hat from the ground; the probability is
that he will mark far above the spot to which the hat
will reach.
An anecdote is told of Leighton which strongly indi-
cates his vivacious amiability of disposition, not without
a dash of humour, and which deserves a place by the,
side of the story of Sir Isaac Newton and the dog Dia-
mond. He had a ne'er-do-well sort of young fellow for
his man-servant, whose thoughtlessness and idleness he
bore with the utmost equanimity. We may be very
sure, too, that the good Leighton did not fail to give
him serious and solemn counsel. One day it so happened
that this- young fellow took it into his head that he
should like to have a day's fishing; he accordingly
started off, locked the door, and took the key with him,
Leaving his master a prisoner. His occupation proved
so interesting that he did not think fit to return till
evening, and all that the kind Bishop s tid to him for
the bad behaviour that might justly have caused his
dismissal was, John, when you next go a-fishing, re-
member to leave the key in the door.'
The following absurd canard is mentioned in. a Paris
letter Besides the Boulevard Prince Eugene plot,
almost every one you meet inquires, Have you not
heard of the Emperor being shot down at Compiegne ? '
A man assured me solemnly on Monday that one of the
Cent Gardes was killed-lit Compiegne by. a ball in-
tended for the Emperor, and that the assassin was exe-
cuted on the spot! In order to enforce the truth of the
anecdote, he assured me that he had seen a lady who.
' had seen a sister of the slaughtered Cent Garde, in deep.
mourning for hira! Moreover, he said that the bullet •
was of a particular description, and made on purpose to
penetrate the coat of mail which the Emperor wears!
The improbability of such an affair being hushed up is,.
however, so great that one cannot swallow it. But it is
very curious that so many tales of plots and assassina-
tions should. be in the air. There is no doubt at all
aboutthe increased activity of the secret police, and the
terror among the class of political suspects.'
The intelligence of the premature death of her Ma-
jesty's godson, the youthful heir of Kamehameha, King
of the Sandwich Islands, has just arrived. The first
duty of Bishop Staley on his arrival at Honolulu was to
be to baptise into the Anglican faith the heir to the
crown; the Bishop was to be the tutor to the boy for a
few years, after which time he was to receive the edu-
cation of a gentleman at Eton School. He was taken.
ill of brain fever on the 19th of August, and. on the 24th
it was deemed expedient not to delay the performance of,
the ceremony of baptism. In the absence of a clergyei
man, a dissenting minister, Mr. E. W. Clarke,performedl
the rite, using strictly the Church's baptismal service.
Mr. Commissioner and Mrs. Synge represented the
Queen and Prince of Wales, and the other sponsor was
Prince Kamehameha ; the names given being 'Albert
Edward Kanikeanli Leiopupa a Kamehameha. On the
following Wednesday, the 27th, the Prince died.
The grand total of visitors to the Exhibition of 1862
is now, in round numbers, 6,198,000; the result or 171
exhibiting days. The grand total in 1851 was, also in
round numbers, 6,039,000; the result of only 141 ex-
hibiting days, or thirty less. The daily average of
visitors in 1851 was therefore about 42,800 ; whale the
daily average in 1862 has only been 36,246, or over -
6,000 a day less. Mee receipts in 1862, from pure ex-
hibition sources—that is, from season tickets and
payment at the doors—are at least £B,OOO less than the
corresponding receipts in 1851.
A whole family in York of the name of Cooke have,
had three narrow escapes frora death by poison. Hav-
ing all been taken alarmingly ill after their ordinary
meals, an analysis of the food took place, and arsenic
and tartarised antimony were discovered in large quan-
tities mixed with the salt and flour that had been used.
The case is involved in the greatest mystery. It is sup-
posed that the mixture of the poison with the salt and
tour has been the work of some one who designed. the
death of those who partook of it, but there is neverthe-
less an absence of all ground of suspicion against any
particular individual. The domestic servants in the
house appear to have suffered in a similar manner to the
family.

articles.title: BRITAIN _LAT 1861.
articles.text:
BRITAIN _LAT 1861.

I '\
One of the most interesting portions of the census of
' 1861 is that which relates to the progress of the people
in point of numbers since the commencement of the
present century; and the manner in which these numbers
are distributed throughout the country. •
It appears that the population of England and Wales,
which stood at 8,892,596 previoui to the 10th March,
1801, the date": of the first- iafficial census had
increased. to 20,066,224 at the date of the last (BthApril,
1861), being an increase of 11,173,688 persons, or 126
per cent., during the 60 years. Scotland, in the same
period, had increased from 1,608,420 to 3,062,294 being
an increase of 90.32 per cent. Both sets of returns
exhibit a degree of similarity with respect to the rate of
increase per cent. hi each decennial period, viz., an
increasin
,rate in the period from 1811 to 1821, ,and a
decennially decreasing rate afterwards; the rate for Eng-
land and Wales rising from 14 to 18 per cent. in the first
period, and• gradually falling to 12 in the last, while
that of Scotland rises from 12.27 to 15.82 in 1821, and
\ falls to 6 per cent. in 1861. The rapid increase in the
.earlier period is probably attributable to the return of
peace after the battle of Waterloo; while the perceptible
diminution since would seem to indicate that where no

extraneous circumstances occur to materially affect the
question of population, the increase will gradually
settle down,to a certain fixed rate per cent. The county
which stands pre-eminent in respect of its increase of
population is Glamorganshire, in Wales. This county
has increased no less than 348 per cent. since 1801,
viz., from 70,879- persons to 317,752., The next in
order is I)lonmouth6hire—the adjoining quasi-Welsh
county—l-which has increased 238 per cent. ; while
Lancashire, which most persons would have expected
to find at the head of the list, merely comes in for the
third place, its increase being only 261 per cent.
Durham claims fourth place, at 241 per cent. ; Stafford-
shire fifth, at 208 per cent. ; Middlesex sixth, at 170 per
cent.; the 'West Riding seventh, at 164 per cent.; and
Cheshire eighth, at 163. It will be seen therefore,
that the coal and iron districts of the country have been
- 'beating the cotton districts in the Matter of population,
and with far less display. The most striking instance in
thetables is that of Glamorganshire, for it .alone has
gone on advancing in its rate of increase whilst all the
other counties have fluctuated. Its rate of increase
during the six -decennial periods has been respectively 19,
20,24, 35, and 37 per cent.; the corresponding figures
for Lancashire being 22, 27, 27, 24, 22, and 20. This
last series of figures, it will be , observed, presents a re-
markable agreement with the law of increase, which we •
have already mentioned as obtaining in the country
generally, viz., an increase to a -maximum in 1821, and
a gradual diminution afterwards. The county which
exhibits the -minimum rate of increase is Merionethshire,
viz., '32 per cent., and, consequently, Wales supplies
both the highest and the lowest rates on the
hat The maximum, so far as the absolute number
of persons is concerned, is, however, attained by
Lancashire, whose increase in the 60 years amounts
to '1;755,954 persons. Next in order is Middlesex,
with 1,388,356 increase, and the West Riding (935,628)
-occupies the third place. All the other counties fall far
short of -these numbers. Surrey, the fourth on the list
(and including, as it does, a considerable portion of the
metropolis), only exhibits an increase of 562,860 persons.
The minimum increase, in point of numbers, is Rutland
—5,561; but this number, small as it is, represents an
increase of, 34 per cent during the century. London
itself has very nearly trebled its population during the
same period, having inci eased from 958,863 in 1801, to ,
2,803,989 in 1861.
It is a somewhat singular fact that the populations of
London, Lancashire, and Cheshire, and Scotland,
.approach very near tneach other in point of numbers
notwithstandingthe great difference in the areas which
they respectively inhabit.

'Three nninths 'ago we considered it our duty to draw
:the attentien of the public to the sad condition of the
neratives in Glasgow connectedowith the cotton spin-
ning and weaving trade; then, from statistics we pub-
lished, it. was shown that the distress amongst the cotton
factory operatives, although pressing most heavily upon
those of Lancashire, was not confined to them, but that
in this city and neighbourhood, sufferings of a very
poignant nature were being endured. The statement
we published on the 18th of August showed that there
were '4,417 persons totally out of work, 4,118 working
half time, 1,664 working two-third time, 1,628 working
three-quarter time, and 4,380, fall,- employed. Soon
after that statement was published the Lord Provost
called a meeting, and an influential committee was
aPpointed to collect subscriptions and relieve the neces-
sitous. That it was appointed not an hour too soon has
been shown ever since its appointment; and this
fact • will be made more apparent from a survey
of the statistics collected during the present week.
The executive relief committee, since their appointment
on the 2nd of September, have given weekly assistance
to between 1,800 and 2,000 individuals. One day this
week a member of the committee had himself no fewer
than between forty and fifty applications for schedules.
Of course all.of those who had got relief are now on the
list, as from various causes -a number have dropped off or
been struck out. The paucity in the number of appli-
cations for relief, when compared with those who are
actually unemployed, is accounted for by the fact, which
has been proved by the domiciliary visits of the sub-
committees of relief, that applications are never made
until sheer want compels them. The quiet suffering
that has thus been endured is beyond recital. The execu-
tive relief committee are fully aware of the whole circum-
stances of the sad case, and are doing all they can to
cope with its exigencies. They were invested with full
powers frcm the general committee appointed at the
public meeting in September, and accordingly at once
set about organising means for the collection of subscrip-
tions and the distribution of relief. Although they are
by no means out of funds yet, still undoubtedly more
money will be required during the coming winter if the
applicants for relief increase in the ratio they have latterly
done.—Glasgow Paper.

STORMS AT NAPLES.—A Naples letter of the 16th
says:—` For several days we have had the worst of
weather. Storms and whirlwinds have rooted up trees,
and blown down the heavy scaffolding of the new port
arches. Many boats have been picked up on the sea-
shore this morning, and a large vessel (American) laden
with merchandise, was literally broken in two, and
thrown on shore; four of the crew were killed. The
sight was fearful. The weather has nowmoderated, and
we hope the worst is over.'

THE FEDERAL FINANCES.—The following hopeful
view of the future of the Federal finances is from.a
recent circular of Mr. Sattherthwaite. It is only fair
that as the English public have the black side in all
American matters presented to them so frequently, they
should occasionally catch a glimpse of the views enter-
tained by practical persons who do not believe that the
whole nation is drifting rapidly and helplessly on the
road to 'universal ruin ' and financial chaos.' The
arrival of the American Government at this latter stage
was predicted six months ago, by a certain financial
writer, as sure to occur at the expiration of 'ninety
days'—another proof of the folly of prophecy. Mr.
Satterthwaite says The total _debt of the Federal
Government is stated to have reached 660,000,000 dols.,
and the expenses of the war are estimated at not over
1,000,000 dols. per day, so that if the war should conti-
nue another twelve months the debt would be about
1,000,000,000 dols.; now, supposing this to be funded
in a five per cent. stock, the annual interest would be
60,000,000 dols., or say £10,000,000 sterling—a sum
which need not be difficult for a powerful and wealthy
nation of about twenty millions of inhabitants to raise,
even supposing the burden to rest on the Northern and
Western States alone—Money Market Review. .

2ellow, who was nearly eaten out of house and home by

CIIAILLU AND THE GORILLAS.

Mr. Winwood Reade and the famous Indian hunter
known as The Old Shekarry,' who went out to the
Gaboon about a year ago, arrived in the early spring,
and went over the ground described in M. du Chaillu's
book. The Athenown publishes the following letter
from ,Mr. Reade

Loanda Sept. 7.
Having spent five active months in the Gorilla
country, lam in a position to state that M. du. Chaillu
'has shot neither ;leopards, buffaloes, nor gorillas; that
the kula-kamba does not utter the cry of kooloo,' or
, anything like it; that the young gorilla in captivity is
not savage; and that while M. du Chaffin affects to have
been 'a poor fever-stricken wretch' at Canama (June 1,
1859), he was really residing in health at the Gaboon.
Mongilomba, who is not a native hunter at all, and who
was in my service three months as steward and natural-
history assistant, duped Mr. R. B. Walker in asserting
that M. du Cha.illu had .killed two gorillas; nor did Ife
ever accompany that gentleman except in the above
capacity. From the Balengi of the Muni, from the
Shekani and Fans of the Gaboon, from the Commi Ba-
• kele, &c., of the Fernand Vaz, upon the banks of which
rivers I have hunted always unsuccessfully) gorillas,
examining those only who were hunters, and reserving
alone such evidence as was corroborative, I have gleaned
the following facts respecting this ape of contention
The gorilla dwells only in the densest parts of the
forests; he feeds exclusively on vegetable matter,
and one kind of grass is a slue indication of his
proximity; at noon and eve he approaches the vil-
lage plantations for the sake of the plantains, occa-
sionally uttering a wild kind of cry, but which in
rage• (as imitated by Etia) becomes a quick sharp
bark. By day he moves along the ground on all-fours
(as, having crawled for hours or their tracks, I can tes-
tify), sometimes ascending the trees. night he
chooses a large tree to sleep in. He is exceedingly wary
and keen of scent. When the female is pregnant, he
builds a nest (as do also, the kulu-kamba and the chim-
panzee), where she is delivered, and which is then
abandoned. These nests, several of cvhich I have seen,
are simply rude layers of dry sticil, and of small
branches evidently torn off the live tree by the hand.
With regard to his ferocity, as a rule, when missed or
wounded he will charge. His charge, from which the
natives often escape, being themselves nimble as apes, is
made on all-fours. Etia, whose left hand has been
severely crippled, informed me that the gorilla seized his
wrist with his hind feet, and dragged his hand into his
mouth as.he would have done a bunch of plantains.
Two things are at least certain—that-the gorilla is less
feared than the leopard; and the story of a man killed
by a gorilla at Camma is a complete fabrication.
Traditional accounts of such an incident exist,
but nothing of the kind has happened within the
memory of Man. The tale of the gorilla assuming
a boxing attitude, and beating his breast like a
drum, originated from Quengueza, and was unanimously
refuted by all hunters from the Muni on the north to
the Fernand Vaz on the south., Thus, in an obscure
African village an old savage could tell a lie which
has blazed through Europe. The Apingi 'country,
which is the Ultima Thule of M. du Chaillu's explora-
,tions, is distant from Gumbi (Nguinbi) lour foot-days'
journey, in a southerly direction. In tracing the
course of the Rombo, however, he adopted a longer
route. His description of the Fans (Bafanh), whom he
visited in company with Mr. Mackey, of Corisco, is
very good. In ascending the Gaboon to its rapids in
the bosom of the Sierra del Crystal, I advanced some
distance into their country, and found them gentle,
hospitable but -cannibals undoubtedly, as -one of
them confessed to me. Even the account of their
ghoul-like propensities is in one case supported
by evidence which I find it impossible to disbelieve.
This book, so strange a melange of truth and fiction,
was prepared by a gentleman well known in the New
York literary world, from copious notes made by M. du
Chaillu, when engaged in these expeditions. And I
must do the latter the justice to confess, that from, the
same sources which afforded me proof of his impostures,
learn that he is a
.good marksman; possessed of no
common courage and endurance; that he has suffered
many privations and misfortunes of which he ,has said
nothing; that his character as a trader hasbeennnjUstly
blemished; that his labours as a naturalist have been
very remarkable;, and that during his residence in
Africa he won the affection of the natives and the
esteem of those who most merit to be esteemed—the
missionaries. And a fellow labourer, though an humble
one, may be permitted to regret that, actuated' by a
foolish vanity or by ill advice, he should have
attempted to add artificial flowers to a wreath of laurels
which he had fairly and hardly earned.

In cases of poisoning by phosphorus the luminosity
of this substance in the dark is the principal character
by which chemists assure themselves of its presence
in the intestines, &c., submitted to analysis. Witscher-
lich, of Berlin, has invented an ingenious apparatus for
this purpose.—.Phipson on Phosphorescence.
A MAD RAILWAY RIDE.—The guard on duty at the
Donington station on Saturday night last was astonished
to see a man on horseback trot along the line by the
platform. The officer directed him to the highway,
and allowed him to depart without giving his name or
address. On examination of the line it was found that
the horseman had broken open a gate and so got on the
line, that he had traversed it when a goods train passed,
that he had been within a foot of going over a bridge
nearly thirty feet high, and in one place had been down
a steep embankment, where his horse had been
struggling violently. This adventurous forsaker of the
road for the rail has been discovered in the person of a
farmer, who will hear more of his trip.—Stafordshire
Advertiser.

LOUIS NAPOLEON'S MOTBER.—Hortense grew up to
be one of the most beautiful ladies in Europe. The
Duchess of Abrantes thus describes her when seventeen
years of age:—' She was fresh as a rose, and though her
fair complexion was not relieved by inueli colour, she
had enough to produce that freshness and bloom which
constituted her chief beauty. A profusien of light hair
played in silken locks around her soft and penetrating
blue eyes. The delicate roundness of her slender figure
was set off by the elegant carriage of her head. But
what formed the chief attraction of Hortense was the
grace of her manners. She had wit without the smallest
ill-temper. I have seen many princesses in their own
Courts and in Paris, but I never knew one who had any
pretension to equal talents with Hortense.'
Sir Joshua Jebb has unfortunately endeavoured to
soothe the public concerning the rapid increase of garot-
ting and similar crimes by statistics which are partly
irrelevant, and partly false witnessts for .the facts to
establish which Sir Joshua Jebb cites them. • He says
crime is diminishing, because in 1861 there were
only 123,049 members known to belong to the
criminal classes, while in 1860 there were 131,024
members of these classes; in other words, fewer by
7,975 than in the previous year. We can scarcely
believe Colonel Jebb's statements to be bona fide. The
compiler of the Judicial Statistics, from which these
numbers are taken himself explains away the diminu-
tion. In many districts, he says, there had been a
police custom of entering among known thieves and
depredators' all once con-dcted of crime, even though lead-
ing an honest life in the year in which they were thus cata-
logued. This practice was intcrdicted by the authorities,
and mainly, no doubt, in consequence of this change of
practice we have a diminution of 9,732 in this class, a
considerable larger number than Sir Joshua Jebb's total
decrease. Does this zealous administrator of convict
law think that the public needs a little opiate to its
excited imagination, and that for that purpose false
figures will do as well as true, if they have a reassure-
lug look? The figures of 1861 have very little in any
case to do with the present outcry, since the complaint
is that ticket of-leave men—' Jebb's Own,' a contem-
porary has dubbed them,—are making very active play
in 1862. If it were true it would be little comfort for
us garotted martyrs to know that a year ago the crime
had begun to decrease; but if there be anywhere a
visionary imagination to which Sir Joshua Jebb's
statement gave hope that he was at last incu-
bating in his dreary nest some promising result of his
convict system,—we are sorry to be compelled to state
that the egg is addled.—Spectator.
SAD FATE OP Two CHILDREN.—Two sisters, named
Lee, have been missing from their parents' home at
Clovelly for more than a week. The woods, the cliffs,
the sea shore, the lanes, and fields, for miles around had
been gone over and over again in search of them, and
people were beginning to surmise there had been foul
play, or that they had wandered in the dark over the
cliffs and fallen into the water; but it was determined
to make another effort before abandoning all hope.
This was done on Thursday last; and in the wood near
Mouth Mill the bodies were found by four of the
county constabulary, who formed a portion of the ex-
ploring party. There the unfortunate dead sisters lay,
partially covered with leaves. The bodies were re-
moved by the police, and on Friday an inquest was
holden on view of them, before R. Bremridge, Esq.,
one of the coroners for Devonshire. The position of the
bodies and their appearance, taken in connection with
all the circumstances known relating to their loss, indi-
cate that after they were seen on Colonel Pane's land on
Saturday week they wandered in the wood, were
overtaken by night, and died from exhaustion and ex-
posure.

TILE ACCLIMATIZA.TION SOCIETY OF
GIiE.AT BRITAIN. --

The quarterly meeting of the council was held at the
offices of this society, 3, Duke-street, Adelphi, on Tues-
day afternoon at three o'clock.; Mr. L. Mackinnon in
the chair. The secretaries having reported the death of
the Marquis of Breadalbane, the president of the society,
the following resolution was proposed and unanimously
• carried That the council has received with deep
regret the sad. intelligence of the death of the most noble
the Marquis of Breadalbarie, the president of this
society, to whose aid, countenance, and advice the
society has been from its very commencement much
indebted? It was then moved and carried—' That a
special general meeting of the society be called on the
15th day of December, for the purpose of electing a presi-
dent, and discussing other matters connected with the so-
ciety.' By a vote of a former Council meeting the sift of
£l5O had been granted from the funds for the purpose of
getting from Australia a supply of the wonga-wonga and
bronzewing pigeons, the Murray cod, and a few wombats.
A communication having been received from Mr. Edward
Wilson, kindly offering to place at the disposal of the
society the machinery of the Acclimatization Society of
Melbourne, for the purposes of obtaining and transmitt-
ing to the society specimens of these creatures,_ it was
determined to hand over the Money so voted to Mr. Wil-
son for transmission to the Melbourne society, in full
confidence that the Council of that society will do its
best to lay out the money of the British Society to the best
advantage. Measares were decided upon for obta"ning
from Berlin a supply of that desirable fish the lucio perm,
for the purposes of ,breeding, and Mr. Buckland was
authorized to make arrangements and incur a limited
amount of expenditure that for purpose. The Secretaries
reported the receipt of a present of a great variety of
vegetable and other seeds from Algeria, -presented to the
society by M. Teston' the Commissioner of French-
Algerian colonies at the International Exhibition.
These seeds will be distributed among the members at
theTroTer season. 'Since the last meeting of the council
the society has made considerable progress. Forty-two
new members have joined since the: beginning of the
month of August. The stock of Chinese sheep is in
a thriving condition; all that were offered for sale
were readily purchased, and there is a -demand for
more. Lord Powerscourt, one of the purchasers re-
ports the birth of four lambs to one of his ewes. To the
small stock now in the bands of Mr. Bush, on behalf of
the society, five lambs were added in the month of Sep-
tember. The turkeys, which arrived from Honduras in
the month of September, laid 20 eggs, which produced
nine birds, seven of which are now in good condition. Re-
ports from several members give a good account of the
dieseorea batatas, which have been dug in excellent
condition where the soil has been rich and light, and
therefore favourable to their growth. In these cases
the larger tubers have been housed for consumption,
and the smaller ones laid by in dry places for replanting.
A present from his Excellency Sir George Bowen the
Governor of Queensland, in the form of a pair of the
talegalla (or mound-building turkey of Australia) is
shortly expected. The birds were shipped on board the
Montgomery, and may be expected to arrive soon. A
promise has, been received from the French 'Societe
d'Accli;natation of sorghe seeds, to be sent over in the
spring. They will be distributed among the members.

RECENT WILLS ~4117 D BEQUESTS.

The will of the Honourable Mrs. Lamb, sister-in-law
of Lady Palmerston and the late Lord Melbourne, has
been proved in London. This lady had but a small
amount at her own disposal, which she has charged
with annuities, having previpusly settled the bulk of
her property on her nephew, Colonel Spencer Clifford,
at his marriage. _
_ _

The will oI Sir. George Houlton, Knight, of 'Farley
Castle, Somerset, Ensign of her Majesty's Body Guard,
has just been proved, in the London Court by Lady
Moulton, the relict and sole executrix, to whom Sir
George has left the whole of his property, real and
personal and of every description, for her own Sole use
absolutely. Sir Ge6rge was formerly Captain in the
43rd Foot, - and had served with distinction in the
Peninsula and in America, and was in his 71st year.
The Will bears date Feb. 3, 1862.
The will of William Barker, Esq., formerly of Mark-
lane, and Manor-street, Chelsea, but late of Barnes-
green Surrey, was proved in London, on the 27th ult.,
by Thomas Man Bridge, Esq., of Layton House, Putney,
the sole executor and trustee. The personalty. was
sworn under £20,000. The will was executed in 1860,
and is of more than ordinary length, owing to the num-
ber of bequests and the directions given therein. The
principal legatees are his executor and his (the testator's)
cousins, Alexander Bassett, of Cardiff, surveyor; and
Robert Cr. Bassett, of Southampton, solicitor. To each
of these three parties he leaves a freehold estate and a
legacy of £4,.000, appointing his executor also residuary
legatee of his entire property. There are legacies to
his friends, godchildren, and others varying in'arcount ;
many charitable bequests; and legacies to all his
domestics. To one female servant who has been in the
family many years, a legacy of £lOO and an annuity of
£52, and to another an annuity £2O. The testator also
leaves £lOO to be added to a sum of £3OO already invested
by him for the support of a school at Ludgershtill, Bucks,
in union with the National Society for the Education of
the children of the F.arming and Labouring Poor of that
parish; and the interest of £3OO to be expended in keeping
in repair his family tomb, and any remainder to be given
to the poor of Wimbledon. The following twelve charit-
able institutions have legacies, viz.—The Brompten. Con-
sumption Hospital, £200; the Society for Promoting
Christian Knowledge, Society for the Propagation of the
Gospel in Foreign Parts Incorporated Society for Build-
ing and. Enlarging Churches and Chapels, National
Socidy,for the Education of Poor Children in the Prin-
ciples Of the Church of England, and King's College
Hospital, each £100; Chelsea, Bronrpton, and Eel crave
Dispensaries, £5O each; and small bequests to the
National and Infant Schools, Chelsea.

TURF SCANTA.LB.—A Court of Inquiry, composed of
the senior officers, Colonels Lambert, Wynyard, lion.
R. Curzon, and Bruce, of the Grenadier Guards, has
been sitting for some days, to report upon some of the
proceedings which, under the designation of 'Turf
Scandals, have acquired such an unfortunate notoriety.
We are anxious to avoid saying anything indicating a
premature conclusion as to the guilt or innocence of the
accused, but we may at once express our conviction that
this inquiry was highly necessary for the reputation of
the regiment and the brigade to which it belongs. We
also deem it not unnecessary to say that we trust the,
inquiry will be conducted in so close and searching a
manner that the result will be completely satisfactory to
the gentlemen of the regiment who are so deeply inte-
rested in the preservation of its good name.—Army and
Navy Gazette.

LAMENTABLE ACCIDENT.--AS the drag of Sir Velters
Cornewall, one of the masters of the Herefordshire
hounds, was leaving Hereford on Saturday night, about
seven o'clock, a terrific accident happened to it, which,
it is feared, placed at least one life in jeopardy. The
vehicle, containing Miss Cornewall and a party of
friends, was driven by the coachman, and was on its
way to Meccas Court, about eleven miles from Here-
ford. The night was foggy, and it •appears that the
coachman, relying upon his sight, did not make use of
his lamps; but when about two miles from the city,
and going at a rapid pace, they were met full tilt by a
brewery dray returning home. The force of the colli-
sion was such that the break was dashed to pieces, and
the bed of the brewer's dray broken from the shafts.
The dray horse galloped into the city with the shafts
attached to the harness. The occupants of the carriage
were thrown out with great violence, and Miss Corne-
wall, a very amiable young lady, received injuries the
extent of which is not yet known. The leg of one of
the horses was broken.

The New Zealand chiefs have rivalled the Poet
Laureate in an elegy on the death of the Prince Consort.
Their poetry is not quite of the same kind, but even in
the English version it is pathetic and melodious, as well
as quaint. The lament begins with an address to the
Queen. We have just heard the crash of the huge-
headed forest tree which has untimely fallen ere it
attained its full growth of greatness. Oh, good lady,
pray look with favour on our love. Although we may
have been perverse children, we have ever loved you.,
Then the Maori muse glides into the inner personality of
the Queen, and utters her descant from that centre. She
bewails the Prince who had sheltered her from the
sorrows and ills of life, the pet bird' whose sweet
voice welcomed her glad guests; the pet bird caught
in the forests of Rapaura ; ' the pillar that did support
her palace, and that is now transplanted to the skies;
the noble form that stood in the prow of the war-canoe '
inciting others to noble deeds. She ends with reproach-
ing the helpless physicians whose remedies, and the
helpless priests whose prayers, could not avert the blow,
for I have lost my love; no more can he revisit this
world.' The poem expresses at once the dependance of
the desolate woman and the pride of the powerful
Queen. Even in the mid-stream of grief the Maori
poet never forgets that the Prince was in rank the
inferior of his mourning Wife—' the pet bird caught for
her in the forests of Rapaura '—thus proving, perhaps,
that civilization rather subdues than enhances that keen
sense of princely dignity which is so strongly engraven
on all savage tribes.-Bpectator.

MtNIFICENT LEGACIES.—To the Leeds charities and
the Bradford Infirmary, Mr. Abraham Musgrave, of

General Infirmary, the Leeds House of Recovery, and

£lO.OOO to each.

articles.text:
AMERICAN SYMPATHY WITH THE
LANCASHIRE OPERATIVES.

' On every occasion, without, so far as we have ,015--
served, a solitary exception,. the utterances of the
operatives and working- men of England and Scotland
the classes which are •by far -the most affected by the-
war—have been of the same kind,
,and have uniformly
expressed a deep sympathy with the cause which, they
secretly feel, is the cause of the ;people and of them
selves, after all. Orators explain to them that inter-
vention will bring cotton to the mills, work to their
hands, bread to themselves, and their starving families.
And the operatives all :I.eelare against intervention.
Adroit secession agents and :secession newspapers tell
them of the enmity for them, and their country enter-
tained in the North, of the infernal glee with which the
northern people contemplate their sufferings, and of the
malign purpose of the North to . insult, harass, and
subject them to untold woes for years to come. And,,
feeling' that this must all be. false, they applaud once
more for the Union Cand -the North. We suggest
whether it would not be well for the American, people to
give some substantial expression' of the sympathy enter-
tained for these our, ,only friends in England, in this
their day of terrible distress. For terrible, indeed, their
sufferings now are. The accounts, which reach us from
Lancashire and other manufacturing districts of the
prevailing and spreading want, famine, and suffering
are heartrending. The number of unemployed persons
now receiving charitable relief in Lancashire alone is
close upon two hundred thousand. The amount of
wages of which the poor of-the district are depriTel, by
the stoppage of mills, is over half a million dollars a
week. But figures can give no conception whatever•of •
the extent and depth of the pervading *ant. Every
week now, too, it becomes worse. The applicants for
relief increase in awful ratio. The cold, dismal, dreaded
winter is upon them, and it seems almost hopeless to
try to keep thousands from positive starvation. The
employers of these unfortunate- men have done well in
aiding them. And they have been assisted by the
wealth of England. The colonies have contributed
munificently. Montreal, Toronto, and other cities in
Canada have scat forward contributions. Wherever the
story of their woes has reached practical sympathy has
been evoked. But all is insufficient. The distress still
grows, and more aid is called for. Would it not be a
magnificent thing for the people of these States, even
in this, our great day of national trial, to send these,
our poor friends in England., a contribution—to offer
them a ship load of corn and wheat out of the God-,
given bounties of our land? Our country is rent by an
unpreced )nted war, but it could spare a gift of a hundred
ship loads of produce. .And we cannot believe that the
Confederate pirates which the• English have let loose
upon our commerce would burn or sink any one of
these bounty ships. Send over the ship with the
American flag at its peak, and let its benefactions be
bestowed upon our suffering and famine-stricken friends
with a bounteous hand.—New York Times.

articles.title: EMIGRATION OF FACTORY OVERLOOKERS.
articles.text:
EMIGRATION OF FACTORY OVER-
LOOKERS.

On Saturday morning a meeting of unemployed fac-
tory overlookers took place at St. John's-hall, Manches-
ter, when Mr. Lang, the honorary secretary, read a letter
from Mr. Jordan, emigration commissioner, requesting
the association to select overlookers with families equiva-
lent to the number of 75 adults, who would be sent off
at once as the first batch of a large number to follow to
Queensland. Mr. Lang stated that the association was
now ready to send off 100 families every two months as
soon as the necessary means were obtained. A letter
from a gentleman at Paris, having property in Algiers,
and who had offered to take five families to send out
and settle them on his land, was read. The letter said:
'I have given orders to my agents to build small farm-
houses on the estate, the buildings being ten yards by
five -and-a-half yards inside. They are to be semi-de-
tached, with an oven for baking to each two ; the build-
ings to stand upon twenty-five acre plots, with portion
of timber. They will be only carcases, with a substan-
tial roofing, but without doors, windows, or flooring.
The emigrants' after due selection, will have to finish
them, and in the meantime will have to live in my
own farms, working 'partly for themselves and partly
for me. These farms I will sell to them at the rate of
11. per acre, pail yearly for fifty years' including the
buildings, so that they will immediately be landowners.
A tobacco crop of moderate average yields 10/. per acre.
I will furnish them with draught oxen, ploughs' and
lend them the necessary seeds. Twenty-four plots are
already occupied, so that they will soon see the way of
raising good crops. The timber in some places being
oak, is worth 21. or 3/. per acre, and the brushwood
turned into charcoal finds a ready sale on the spot. Now'
if you will select five families capable amongst them to
finish the farms and settle down in them, I- will in the
course of a fortnight, or. three weeks be hi London, and
defray their expenses to Algiers' provided the expenses
do not exceed 100/. and also that the Men do undertake
to repay me the advance at a future time. I must give
a bond to the government to feed them as long as they
are in Algeria, so they need not be afraid. Pray see
that the people be of good character, and have tools. A
plasterer, plumber, carpenter and painter amongst them
would do well.' It was stated that eleven families were'
ready to go to Algeria at once, out of whom the writer-
would have the opportunity of selecting, five.

The Scotch papers report an accident, which, though
it involved only one life, contains more of the true
elements of human horror, strikes more sharply on the
fine chords of :human terror, than many a great and
meaningless catastrophe. Thomas Loch, a dock
labourer, was working on a ship, just beached near
Wigtown, when she heeled over, and the bulwark fell
on his chest. The tide was fast coming up, and it was
evident that in an hour the wretched man would be
drowned, unless the weight could be removed from his
chest. All the place turned out to help, but the weight
was immovable, and the tide flowed on remorselessly.
A clergyman stepped forward in to the water, and
prayed with the unhappy victim. A napkin was at
his own request placed over 'his face that he might
not see the tide, and so, apparently without complaint,
he lay till the waters closed over his head, while the
townsmen, gathered round in helplessness, sobbed
aloud. Could not,the timber resting on him have been
hewn away ?—Spectator.
THE FIRE AT DIA GICFRIARS. ROBBERY OF TRH
Hos. G. C. NORTON.—During the prevalence of the
destructive fire on Thursday, the Hon. G. C. Norton
found himself unable to pass the Blackfriars-bridge in a
cab which he had engaged to convey him to the Albion
Tavern, and he, in consequence, alighted, and proceeded
on foot. During his progress the pressure of the crowd
became so great as to endanger the limbs of a female,
and the life of an infant she bore in her arms. Mr.
Norton with that humanity which characterises him,
appealed to the bystanders in so effective a manner that
a passage was made for the mother and child, both of
whom ultimately reached position of safety. On
reaching the Albion Tavern Mr. Norton missed his
purse, a long bead one, containing two Bank of Eng-
land notes of £5 each, a cheque on Messrs. Coutts, dated
some time back, and wrapped up in a piece of paper, a
diamond in the rough, believed to be of considerable
value, but still more estimated from its being the gift of
an old and esteemed friend. The bank notes were
marked J. Kingsbury, 14th Nov.,' with the initials
G. G.' As a matter of course, the payment of the
cheque has been stopped. Mr. Norton had taken out
his purse to pay the cabman his fire on discharging
him, and believes he returned it to his trousers-pocket,
but there is a p,obahility of his having dropped it, and
of its having fallen into honest hands, and if so the
finder may know from this narrative to whom the purse
and its contents belong.

It is a noteworthy- circumstance that during the
mayoralty of Mr. Cubitt, considerably more than a
quarter of a million of money, in the whole, tio wed
spontaneously into. the Mansion House from time to
time towards one public object or another. The figures,
as they appear in the official records, are subjoined.
During the first year, including the severe winter of

the mutiny. Again, the public subscription was com-
menced under Mr. Cubitt's auspices on the 14th of

orphans of the unfortunate men who perished in the

was paid into the hands of the late Lord Mayor between

two .months. For the surviving relatives of the men
who lost their lives by a similar catastrophe at Gethin,

and the 21st of April. Lastly, on Saturday week, when
Mr. Cubttt's tenure of office expired, the Lancashire
Relief Fund at the Mansion House amounted to
£125,000 in round numbers; making a grand total of
-1316,779, of which £200,098 was subscribed in the

MATIMIONY.--The following capital parody of Ham-
let's soliloquy is from the _Knickerbocker Magazine for
October
To wed,, or not to wed—that is the question.;
Whether 'tis happier in the mind to stifle
The heats and tumults of outregeous passion,
Or with some prudent fair in solemn contract
Of matrimony join. To have—to hold—
No more—and by that ' have ' to say we end
The heart-ache, and a thousand lovef-sick pangs
Of Celibacy—'twere a consummation
Devoutly to be wished. In nuptial band
To join, till death dissolves—ay, there's the rub;
For in that space what dull remorse may come,
When we have taken our solemn leave of liberty,.
Must give us pause. There's the respect
That slacks our speed in suing for a change.
_Else, who would bear the scorns and sneers which
bachelors
When aged feel—the pains and fluttering fevers•
Which each new face must give to roving fancy,.
When he might rid himself at once of all
By a bare Yes? Who would with patieuce bear
To fret and linger out a single life,
But that the dread of something yet untried,
Some hazard in a state from whose strict bond
Death only can release, puzzles the will, •
And makes us rather choose those ills we have
Than fly to others which we fancy greater?
This last reflection make us slow and wary,
Filling the dubious mind with dreadful thoughts
Of curtain-lectures, jealousies, and cares
Extravagantly great; entailed on wedlock;
Which to avoid, the lover checks his passion,
And, miserable, dies a BACHELOR.

ON MAKING A WILL—I have known good Christian
men, who throughout their lives were remarkable for
their unselfishness and consideration of others, cause
much inconvenience, if not sorrow, to those they loved,
by neglecting to make their wills. It seemed as if they
were afraid of shortening their lives by so doing. But
we do not invite death by preparing for it. On the con-
trary, an illness from which we might recover, if free
from anYiety,. may be made fatal by an addition of
worldly care. When a man feels the death-sweat on his
brow, he has enough to think of without being compelled
to devise, execute, and assign. We are commanded to
take no thought for the morrow; but we create and
provide thought for the morrow if we leave undone
so grave a business a the disposal of the things
we have received of God, and for the right distribu-
tion of which we feel ourselves responsible. It is no
sufficient answer to say that our property is not in a dis-
posable shape. If our affairs are so disarranged that we
could make no bequests, if we don't know what we have,
or have not, the sooner we remedy the confusion the
better—however long we may live. But even supposing
that there is money invested which we could not easily
realise, there is always something in every well-regulated
business or income which we could leave in •order. A
man is not obliged to wind up his affairs when he makes
a will. He may make a dozen in succession, if he
pleases. He would always have some direction to give
if he was told he had to die the next day. If his life is
spared, he may at some future time leave these directions
in a fuller and more detailed shape; supposing, however,
he is cut off suddenly by an accident, or is taken with a
fever which unfits him for business, the sorrow for his
death will be accompanied by regret for his previous
neglect. No doubt money or legal provision is not the
medicine for a mourning heart; but the memery of the
Christian will be all the sweeter in his home circle if
he makes a just arrangement for those who remain in it.
The influence he had upon his family for good during his
lifetime will be confirmed by this final evidence of his
thoughtfulness and fairness. They will feel that they
succeed to a man who loved righteousness and justice to
the last. But if he dies without a will, they inherit,
whatever he leave, a possible source of jealousy and dis-
content. —Sunday at Home.

NAPOLEON AND THE AUSTRIAN EmPEROR AT VILLA-
inANcA.—At seven o'clock a.m., the two monarchs met
at Villafranca, in a house in Contrada Cappuccini,
belonging to a Signor Gandini Morelli- Bugna, who had
inherited it, together with a large landed property, from
a priest devoted to Austria. What passed at that meeting
(which lasted a little less thah an hour) nobody can
exactly tell. It has been stated, however, that the two
emperors conversed, sometimes in Italian, but more
frequently in German. During the conversation Louis
Napoleon, as if mechanically, picked to pieces some of
the flowers placed in a vase before him, the petals of
which were found scattered about on the floor at the
'side of the table where the landlady of the house had
noticed that he sat. When the sovereigns left. the house
and appeared in the streets, to.present to each other the
officers of their staffs, the younger looked pale and em-
barrassed—the elder gay and at ease. The proud
leeeendant of the Hapsburgs doubtless felt bitterly the
humiliation of that moment. Louis Napoleon, on the
contrary, had Satisfied what was thought to be one of
his greatest desires—the dealing in person with a legiti-
mate emperor. Nothing was written by the two
monarchs at that meeting. The inkstand and paper
which had been placed on the table were not touched,
and they may still be seen exactly where they were
originally set down.—ltal9 under Victor Emmanuel.

THE ENGLISH SOLDIERS.--What must be admired in
the battle of Waterloo is England, the English firmness,
the English resolution, the English blood, and what
England had really superb in it, is (without offence)
herself; it is not her captain, but her army. Wellington,
strangely ungrateful, declares in his dispatch to Lord
Bathurst, that his army, the one which fought on June
18th, 1815, was a detestable army.' What does the
gloomy pile of bones buried in the trenches of Waterloo
think of this England has been too modest to herself
in her treatment of Wellington, for making him so great
is making herself small. Wellington is merely a hero
like any other man. The Scotch Greys, the Life Guards,
Maitland and Mitchell's regiments, rack and Kempt's
infantry, Pozzonby and Somerset's cavalry, the High-
landers playing the bagpipes under the shower of canister,
Ryland's battalions, the fresh recruits who could hardly
manage a musket, and yet held their ground against the
old bands of Essling and Rivoli—all this is grand.
Wellington was tenacious; this was his merit, and we do
not deny it to him, but the lowest of his privates and his
troopers was quite as soiid as he, and the iron soldier is
as good as the iron duke. For our part, all our glorifi-
cation is offered to the English soldier, the English army,
the English nation; and if there must be a trophy, it is
to England that this trophy is owing The Waterloo
column would be more just, if, instead of a man, it
raised to the clouds the statue of a people. —Les Aliserables.
By Victor Hugo.

Dont.s.—A doll is one of the most imperious wants,
and at the same time one of the most delicious instincts,
of feminine childhood. To clean clothe, adorn, dress,
undress,, dress again, teach, scold a clean,
nurse, lull, send
to sleep, and imagine that something is somebody —the
whole future of a woman is contained in this. While
dreaming and prattling, making little trousseaux and
cradles,, while, sewing little frocks and aprons, the child
becomes a girl, the girl becomes a maiden, and the
maiden a woman. The first child is a continuation of
the last doll. A little girl without a 11011 is nearly as
unhappy and quite as impossible as a wife without
children.—Les Atiscrables. By Victor Hugo.
FALSE FEELING OF THE POOR ABOUT WORKHOUSES.—
Although it is not a desirable thing for any person to
come into the workhouse, you should really consider
'what the workhouse is—a good house, good clothing,
and education for your children, and you eln walk out
of it the very moment you feel disposed. And, as to
separaton, begging your pardon, it is all humbug, be-
cause we are all separated from our children in every
grade of life; they are obliged to be knocked about and
separated from -as. They go to school, and to every
part of the world; and that braggadocio way of talking
about putting an end to your children's lives, rather than
they should be clothed and fed, and educated, when you
are distressed yourself, and cannot mAintain them, as
you are bound to do if you can, on account of your
being unfortunate enough not to get work, is exceedingly
wrong—very foolish talking indeed; very wrong.talking.
—Preface to Jerusalem the Golden.'
TIIE DUTCIL—The Dutch people are not such as you
have been taught to believe them to be. You have in
your mind a picture of Mynheer Van Dunck as he drinks
his brandy alio: water gaily; of Dirk Hatterick,
he murders Glossop.;. and William the Taciturn, who is
supposed to have enfranchised his country by his silence.
You conceive your Dutchman to be short, fat, broad-
faced, very heavyin the stern, and not unirequently
phlegmatic; sentetimes murderous, sometimes drunk,
and occasionally thoughtful and pltriotie„ All this is
wrong. They drink no more brandy than their neigh-
bours ; they are not much given to murder; and though
you may sometimes believe in their patriotism, you may
believe neither in their silence nor in their special
thoughtfulness. But above all, be careful not to fall
into that vulgar error as to their bodily proportions.
Your Dutchman of the present day is rather small than
otherwise—a compact, tidy man, with pleasant English
features, too often disgraced by a French hat above
them. Put on his head a hat made in England, and you
will take him for an Englishman a little under-sized.—
arnhal Magazine.

Governor has just sent to this country for twelve tons
of the same kind of seed, and the Sultan's Ambassador
in London, in seeking tlge assistance of the Cotton
Supply Association in the matter, remarks that the
well-known public spirit and energy of his Highness
render it certttin that, having interested himself in the
cultivation of cotton in the
.extensive and important
province under his administratwe.n, he will not relax his
efforts until they be crowned with success.'
DEATH OF MR. RIDGWAY, TIIE PUBLISHER—We
have to record the death of Mr. James Ridgway, the
well-known publisher, of Piccadilly, which event
occurred on •Thursday evening, at his seat, near Burton,
on-Trent. Mr. Ridgway was for many years connected
as publisher with the leading members of the Liberal
party. So far back as the time of the Catholic Emancipa-
tion in 1829, he published many of the most stirring
works in advocacy of that measure, and at a more recent
date, pamphlets which powerfully told in favour of a
repeal of the corn duties. For some years he was one of
the principal proprietors of the Globe newspaper, in the
management of which he took an active part. -
THE PRINCE or IVALES.—A telegram was receiyi.d. at
Buckingham Palace on Saturday last from Roe, by
which we learn that the Prince of Wales, together with
their Royal Righnesses the Crown Prince and Princess
of Prussia, was still sojourning in the Eternal City.
Beth the Prince of Wales and the Crown Princess of
Prussia were in excellent health. His Royal Highness
the Prince of Wales, attended by Lieutenant-General
Knollys and suite, will, on leaving Italy, land at Mar-
seilles, whence the Prince comes to Paris, and. after a
brief sejour at the Hotel Mirabeau, where His Royal
Highness is expected about the 28th inst., will at once
proceed direct to meet ht,- Majesty and the Royal
Family at Windsor Castle.

NOTICE.

AT a meeting convened by the Trades' Council
on Tuesday last, November 25th, representatives
being present from most of the metropolitan societies,
it was resolved that the members present form a
committee to be ealled the LONDON WORKING MEN'S
CENTRAL COMMITTEE, to collect subscriptions for
the distressed operatives in the North.
As this committee is now appointed and have corn-

meneed to work, I beg to inform those who have so
generously subscribed through the medium of the
BEE HIVE, that all future subscriptions received by
me will be handed over to the LONDON WORKING
MEN'S CENTRAL COMMITTEE, and announced under
that head, in order to avoid having two funds and
prevent mistakes. As the Working Men's Com-
mittee have appointed me to fill the office of treasurer,
subscriptions may still be sent by all parties as before
to this office, as the Working Men's Committee will
co-operate with the East Lancashire Committee, to
which all our funds hitherto have been forwarded.

I take this opportunity of returning my sincere
thanks, on behalf of my distressed brethren in the
North, to those who have so generously subscribed
to this noble object, and trust that now we have a
Working Men's Committee, composed of so many
branches of industry, that renewed efforts will be
made by the working classes, to raise a large sum to
relieve the wants of those who now stand so much
in need. I am, yours truly,
GEORGE POTTER.

Subscriptions may be forwarded to the office in
money, post office orders, or postage stamps, daily
or on Saturday evenings, from 7 to 9 o'clock.
