NOTICES TO CORRESPONDENTS,

CHARLES WILLIAMS.—We ttave rec-eiveci; letter from
Mr. C. Williams, of Liverpool, the Secretary of the
National Association of Plasterers, congratulating
us on the great improvements that have taken place
in our paper. Let working men only support us as
they should do, let them follow up the tide of success
which is now rolling in upon us, and we can
promise Mr. Williams and all other friends who
sympathise with as that the working classes shall
have a paper second to none in any of its depart-
ments. Mr. W. in another part of his letter refers
to the case of the secretary of the painters' trade last
week at the Middlesex Sessions, and desires other
parties to take warning.
TRADE UNIONS AND POLITICS. We have received
several letters; several highly approving, and some
few opposing the opinions containing the address we
published last week. We will endeavour next week
to make room for the most important of these letters.
A BRISTOLMAN' will appear in our next.
GEORGE CeunwELL.—tteceived.
HENRY BISUOP.—We have received a letter from Mr.
Bishop, who signs himself as 'Chairman of the Bir-
mingham Working Men's Lancashire Relief Com-
mittee,' calling us severely to task for omitting some
passages from his letter which we published about a ,
fortnight back, in reply to some remarks made by
Mr. Peacock, ot the East Lancashire Relief Com-
mittee. We only exercised that privilege which
every editor possesses of judging for ourselves what
portions of a correspondent's letter are fit for publi-
cation. We have no personal knowledge either of
Mr. Bishop or Mr. Peacock, and can have no feeling
on the subject. We thought it our business to omit

from Mr. Bishop's letter some passages containing
strong personal imputation, which would have
rendered us liable to prosecution for libel, and we
'did the same with Mr. Peacock's letter, and as we
-shall do with all letters sent to usiorinsertion when
we think it necessary. With respect to Mr. Bishop's
letter received this week we refrain from inserting
it, not wishing to encourage a paper warfare between
two gentlemen engaged in the same holy cause. As
doubts, however, have been expressed as to Mr.
Bishop's exact position, and that of the committee he
represents, we think it but fair to give him the
benefit of the following passage we extract from his
letter. He says lam a true working man;
the committee I represent is a bona fide working
man's committee. The men who represent our
workshops are not selected by the employers; our
collections are not in any way enforced by the
authorities of the establishment; there is no show
about our proceedings.'

SATURDAY, NOVEHBER 29, 1862.

SUMMARY.
FOREIGN.

FRANCE opposes the election of Prince Alfred
as King of the Greeks, by all the machinery of
politics with whieh the French Government is
familiar from former transactions. The Greeks
are not dismayed by this opposition, but scatter
biographies and memoirs of the Prince over
their land, and through their population, by
thousands. These proceedings are favoured by
the Greek houses, in this, and in other countries,
whose partners suppose that the future influence
of the Prince would secure the independence of
their nation.
The alliance of" the Western nations" is not
at present worth much. It has sustained many
fractures, and is much weakened. Greece, Italy,
and the States, North and South, all supply
shadows, which seem to settle into a continuous
umbrage.
Italy suffers still from inundations, and the
south of France from hurricanes, and both life
and property have been lost at Marseilles dur-
ing the week, through these fierce winds.
The Italian Parliaments are occupied with
discussions, arising out of the Garibaldi move-
ment, and the occupancy of Rome. The finance
of the kingdom is in a critical state, and another
loan of twenty millions sterling is necessary and
is proposed. The Austrian Parliament have
reduced the military section of the budget, and
do not apparently expect an early renewal of
hostilities. Great suffering by famine is ex-
perienced in Montenegro, as the consequence
of the late war. The Prussian King maintains
the propriety of his course in declining to accept
the reduction proposed on the budget of his
cabinet by the Chamber of Representatives ;
but he resents the refusal of his contempbrary
of Hesse, to exhibit any budget to the Hessian
representatives. Prussia even threatens to
compel Hesse by force to follow constitutional
practice. The inconsistency is very glaring,
unless Prussia alleges that, on the principle of
the antique instruction issued in the nursery,
"look at everything, but touch nothing," the
representatives of a people_ are entitled to

ex-amine, but not to reduce-, the particulars of
expenditure for which they are taxed. A budget
may be as good for a puzzle or a to-, as any
other contrivance, but it is needless to make
war on the Hessian Prince, only because
he will not amuse his Hessians, according to
the fashion wherein King William wants to
amuse the Prussians.

The Russians are again said to have
experienced discomfitures in tunnelling their
path of empire through the Circassian Moun-
tains to the south. Russia in Europe is now
sealed up in ice. The hostilities round Herat
interest the Russians, whose politicians always
regard that city as one of the keys to India;
although the difficulty of marching an army
from India to Herat, or Herat to India, must
be calculated to cool the ardour of ordinary in-
vaders. Alexander of Russia has the same road
as Alexander of Greece, and it is not probable
that he would ever get farther into India.

Letters and pape-rs received by the last mails
from the East describe an intense confusion in
China; aggravated by our interference; while
in Japan new attacks on the Europeans have
been perpetrated.

Wars in South America are not easily decided.
Some time ago we heard that General Mos-
quera had conquered the enemies of freedom in
New Granada, and placed civil and religious
liberty on a secure basis. Now we hear again
that he has once more conquered these enemies;
and has, we hope, made the basis in question
sure for this time. The contest of the New
Granadians, against foes within and without, for
civil and for religious freedom has been persis-
tent, for the lives of men now becoming old
and steady. It is a contest that merits our
sympathy. Intelligence is now expected of
French progress in Mexico; it will be progress
to a new crime, after the manner at Rome.
General 111‘Clellan has been removed from
the command of the Federal armies on the
Potomac by. President Lincoln, who has in-
structed General Burnside to take the place.
I\i'Clellan has been ordered to his home in
Trenton, New Jersey, where he received an
ovation from the inhabitants. He is a Demo-
crat. The President is a Republican. The
Democrats were successful at the last elections,
and Lincoln becathe jealous of 111‘Clellan, who
has been mentioned as the candidate of the
Democrats for the next Presidency. That is
not the reason assigned, for General 111‘Clellan
is said to be removed for disobedience to the
orders of General Halleck, the Commander-in-
Chief, who required him to cross the Potomac,
and crush the Confederates at the end of October. ,
A part of General M'Clellan's army did cross
the Potomac, at that date, and were nearly all
drowned or killed; and he alleged his inability
to move all the army from defective supplies.
A month should not have elapsed before punish-
ing this error, if it deserved the name.
Burnside is moving slowly to the South, but
the Confederates retire, and no fighting has
occurred for some time in Virginia.
Gold ?mains at a premium of 32 to 33 in
New York. The consequence on fixed earnings
or income is a reduction of one fourth. Pro-
bably as goods are advanced more in selling
value than the actual difference between gold
and notes, the real reduction of earnings or
incomes is ONE THIRD. A great number of
trades have in consequence struck for an ad-
vance of wages in the northern towns. Their
requests have been conceded in several places,
and in a majority of instances at New York.

COLONIAL.
The oil wells of Canada attract continued
attention and repay it. Several companies
have now been formed in this country to work
them, and they have added materially to the
means of the province.
The gold quartz of Nova Scotia has become
productive, and rises into the importance of a
regular and remunerative trade.

A company, with a capital of one million
sterling, is proposed for the...formation of means
to irrigate, and otherwise to extend cultivation
in Southern Africa. The scheme embraces
the Cape Colony and Natal. Irrigation is the
agricultural necessity of ,South Africa. Rain
falls in adequate quantities, but it is wasted.
India attained its greatness by irrigation.
Mesopotamia in ancient times supported the
Assyrian and Chaldean empire, 'Babylon and
iNineveh, by irrigation. Ceylon in more recent
times maintained a population of fifty or sixty
millions by the same policy. This new com-
pany will give fresh prosperity to Southern
Africa.

readers could scarcely have supposed that
French mercenaries addressed them on this
subject ii the English language, .and avowedly
for English interests. Perhaps, indeed, the
secret association of master builders did not
employ Mr. SIDNEY SMITH to negotiate with

The people of Calcutta say that they have

Fund, which they propose to send to Lanca-

THE CAPITALIST'S PRESS AND THE
FRENCH GOVERNMENT,
THE Court of Queens Bench was on Tuesday
in part occupied with a case disgraceful to a
defunct member of the English press, and the
French Government. An aged, but once
respectable and talented, daily journal came to
the grave by many devious paths. Through
one of these bye-roads Mr. Sergeant GLOVER
took the "departing" by the hand. Mr.
GLOVER belongs to an honourable profession,
in which he has obtained some distinction and
a good position. If the journal could have
thought for itself, or the journals, for the re
were three of them, like a mother and two
daughters, no suspicion could have arisen that
Mr. GLOVER, "an English Barrister-at-Law,"
would lead them into ignominious paths. Our
readers are familiar with the address of one of
the three, the Morning Chronicle; although
the Morning News and the Evening Journal
have not left "distinguished memories" behind
them. When Mr. GLOVER entered the pub-
lishing trade, and became proprietor of these
papers, he fell into temptation by struggling
to make his own, or more than that, out of
them. He was supposed to be a pure patriot,
who joined the press only for public purposes.
The first supposition may have been correct,
and the second is not, perhaps, so, well esta-
blished.
According to the report of the proceedings
on Tuesday in the Court of Queens Bench,
Mr. GLOVER met with certain French gentle-
men, asseciated with the Count de PERSIGNY,
who is connected with M. BILLAULT, who was
one of the French Ministers, and by these
gentlemen the English Sergeant-at-Law was
induced to sell the services of his three journals
at £BOO a month for the purposes of BILLAULT
and PERSIGNY. M. BILLAULT was Minister of
the Interior for Louis NAPOLEON, and Count
de PERSIGNY was his ambassador at our Court,
while Mr. GLOVER was to be his agitator" in
London through the journals named. No
charges can be brought of personal wrong
against M. BILLAULT and Count de PERSIGNY
for their efforts to promote the interests of
their Government, but Mr. GLGVER occupies a
different position as an English barrister, gen-
tleman, and publisher. He might have
held all these positions, and published a news-
paper for the defence and explanation of the
Napoleonic system. The London American is.
,for example, an organ of the Federal party in
the States, and when we read its sensation
placards, we nearly all know that they are not
of sterling value. The Index, we believe,
represents the Confederates of the Southern
States, and we are also prepared to allow its
statements only a certain weight. So, if the
Frenchman in London were to appear under the
auspices of Mr. GLOVER, for the advocacy of
NAPOLEON'S plans, the public would not be de-
ceived by its contents. But all London
journals, established in the common manner,
are supposed to advocate the interests of this
country according to the opinions which their
conductors may form regarding these interests.
Differences of opinion exist on these as on
other subjects; but in buying a daily paper we
are not expected to guard against the possibility
of its being pensioned by the Emperors ALEX-
ANDER or NAPOLEON, or by President LINCOLN.
The Frenchman in this transaction began by
inducing Mr. GLOVER to deceive the publie,
and they have ended by deceiving him. For
a man engaged in a quiet business, the English
Sergeant-at-Law is remarkably simple and
stupid. He agreed to do secret work at EBOO
a month, and he ran up a bill of £14,000
without any payment in part or in whole. His
duties under the engagement comprised the
preparation and publishing of one set of
articles, and the publishing of sundry transla-
tions. He was to prepare articles translateable
into Parisian use; and he was to copy articles
published in France for the benefit of London.
The arrangement comprised an attempt to
cheat the British and French public. The
British readers of the Morning Chronicle and
its satellite, were to take its opinion on French
matters hs the unpurchased and unpurchaseable
sentiments of an English and intelligent poli-
tician. The French readers of these articles
were also expected to consider them unbought
certificates of NAPOLEON'S popularity in
London, and evidence to the excellence of that
Government which had gained the esteem and
favour of an important London journal; while
all these commendations were to be paid from
the French secret service money. These are
the particulars, and such were the objects, of
an arrangement ignominious to all the parties
concerned. Mr. GLOVER has brought the facts THE "BLOODY TIMES."

THE LANCASHIRE DISTRESS-HOW
TO HELP, AND WHERE TO SEND
RELIEF.

-WHILE the Confederates are contending for
independence, and the Federals for empire, and
wasting, in futile efforts to accomplish these,
oceans of blood, and mountains of treasure,
England is fighting the battle of famine, and
rousing her entire energies to the herculean
task of supporting the men of Lancashire, until
she can be independent of all strangers for
supplies of the raw material. We term the
task herculean, because look which way soever
we may, the truth confronts us with unvarying
conviction that at least two millions of human
beings will require to be fed, clothed, housed,
and warmed, for the next six or nine mopths.
The wages lost by this dense population will
already amount to millions; but assuming the
duration of the famine to extend till September
next, which is a proximate calculation, there
will be a loss in wages for Lancashire of twelve
millions. This is the opinion of all who are
competent to judge on this awful subject. The
question to be considered, then, will be, how is
this vast loss to be made up? If we add the
Lord Mayor's fund to the Bridgewater Hcuse
and all other extraneous charities, will they
reach one million? We very much question
it. The Poor Law is now expending at the
rate of £300,000 per annum, or upon an
average of one shilling and twopence per head,
and Mr. Farnall anticipates this source to be
exhausted by February. Lancashire itself has
done much, despite Professor Kingsley's asser-
tion to the contrary, and may fairly be said to
have contributed thus far about a million of
money in private and public charity; but we
rejoice to say that the largest sum contributed
yet has been from the working classes in all
parts of the kingdom and colonies. Paradox-
ical as it may sound, the poorest class has
hitherto contributed the bulk of the private
and public charities, and have put to the blush
the sub,criptions of the rich and wealthy.
The Queen has given £2,000; Lord Derby
£1,000; but the Australian colonists have
contributed £30,000, and are still sen ding their
generous gifts. This essential help from our
brethren is felt to be so great, and in Dublin,
Edinburgh, Leeds, York, Liverpool, Birming-
ham, and other influential towns and cities,
working men make the general sum significant.
Will the benevolent and trades societies aid us
in this important and essential service? If
they will, we on our part, as the advocate of
their interests, will not fail to perform ours.
At present the hard-earned monies of the
workmen are laid up in the banks by these
middle class committees, or doled out in trivial
sums to the starving multitudes. In many
instances used to purchase chep labour for the
cotton lords, and, in some cases, we could men-
tion, refused the poor co-operator or marked
workman, at the pleasure of a revengeful em-
ployer. All this cruelty, extortion, and wrong
would be avoided, by the working classes con-
tributing to their own "Relief Fund." This
fund will be dispensed by an Executive, formed
of respectable and intelligent workmen. It
will be managed in the most business-like man-
ner, and will distribute its funds weekly to all
sufferers in Lancashire, without distinction of
trade, creed, or politics.
A necessity has arisen for some special fund
of this nature, in consequence of complaints
thdo have reached us from some places of harsh
dealings with members of co-operative com-
panies, or persons who had been engaged in
trades' societies. We sincerely trust that such
cases are rare exceptions to a better rule, but
so much distress prevails that in providing to
our utmost for its general relief, it is only
prudent to have means of neutralising any
petty feeling of this nature wherever it may be
or has been unhappily manifested.

witness. We neither believe nor suppose that
this course has been ever adopted, but it could
be taken.

The Times, in addition to its own entreaties
for the execution of this woman, published
earnest remonstrances with Sir GEORGE GREY
for not taking another life. These letters were
ascribed
.to Professor KINGSLEY, and Mrs.
NORTON, and they were ably disingenuous.
On Thursday, the Times reverted to the
subject. The Home Secretary had said in one
letter "the result" of the inquiry "was far
from removing all uncertainty," and, adds the
Times, "a very good reason for leaving the
verdict undisturbed." That is to say, Sir
GEORGE GREY finding that farther ir quiry was
"far from iliTemoving all uncertainty" of the
woman's guilt, declined to permit her execu-
tion; but the fact, says the Times, that an
uncertainty of her guilt remained, and could
not be removed, "is a very good reason, we
should have thought," for hanging:the woman.
WILLIAM COBBETT selected an appropriate
name for the journal.

articles.title: CABMEN'S PUBLIC MEETING.
articles.text:
THE CABMEN'S PUBLIC MEETING.

THE cab drivers have decided upon holding their
great central aggregate meeting on Wednesday even-
ing next, at the Whittington Club Room, Strand,
and Lord Henry Cholrnondely, a nobleman, who
has taken great interest in the formation and pro-
gress of those useful institutions, the Cabmen's
Clubs, will take the chair upon the occasion. This
meeting is held for the purpose of explaining to the
drivers generally the proceedings taken by their
delegates, who were appointed to prepare a revision
of the present one-sided Hackney Carriage Act, and
to ask the support of the drivers towards the carrying
out of the necessary measures to obtain a redress of
the manifold grievances under which they labour.
Our opinion on the proceedings of the delegates has
been given on many previous occasions; they have
performed the task they have undertaken in the most
temperate and business. manner, reflecting the high-
est, credit upon them as men and citizens; and if their
fellow drivers do not rally on Wednesday next,
and stamp their approval of their conduct by their
presence and support, they will deserve all the con-
tumely that has been heaped upon them frcm Salis-
bury Square. The delegates cannot receive a greater
reward for their labour than to see the large room
of the Whittington Club filled to overflowing with
their "brother whips." We understand the pro-
prietors are invited to attend, and we are
informed that some of the most influential
amongst them have promised to be present. Thi,,
is as it should be; let proprietor and driver work
well together, and success is certain. The
hour of meeting has been fixed so as to lesst in-
convenience the public; and we trust every driver
will feel it a duty incumbent upon him to be present
at least during some portion of the proceedings. A.
golden opportunity is now before cabmen to elevate
themselves in the social snalc, which, if neglected
n3w, may not occur ag am n for many yeals.

articles.title: HOW TO OBTAIN CLOTHING FOR LANCASHIRE. TO THE EDITOR OF THE " BEE-HIVE."
articles.text:
HOW TO OBTAIN CLOTHING FOR
LANCASHIRE.
TO THE EDITOR OF THE " BEE-HIVE."

SIR, —lf you had been able to insert my last
letter at the time when it was written, I should
have claimed the merit of first suggesting the pro-
priety of relieving the day and night clothes of the
Lancashire operatives out of " mortgage," for one
may employ a respectable word on the topic, in
preference to supplying them with old clothes from
London. Day clothes are not likely ever to make
"good fits," that come in this manner, but there
could be no human doubt concerninc, the clothes
that each person tied up in a melancholy bundle, and
deposited for a sum not equal to the cost of making
them.

Night clothes are somewhat different. Blankets
and sheets fit any person, but all good housewives
prefer their own, and the benevolent are not assist-
ing common paupers in this tribulation, but hard-
working, industrious, and respectable families on
whom has fallen the bolt of judgment for national
follies and sins. Not being able to argue all points
like a professor of logic in the Scotch university,
whereat the London strong-minded female sought
this session to study anatomy; and, by the way, do
you not think it rather fast for English girls, of a
certain age, to propose for themselves the annoyance
of studying comparative anatomy, merely in a
scientific manner, among a crowd of young Scotch
medicals, no more staid personages, I suppose, thzn
we all should be ; well, but half-venturing a mere
female lady like " anathema," at parantheses, I
proceed with my confession, of no: being a logician,
and thereby being incapable of arguing points, I
fall back on woman's instinct, and say that we
should not have lived, as we have been living, many
of us, on stolen cotton. For this crime, and with
our light it was a crime, we are under suffering :
"Behold the hire of the labourers which is if you
kept back." Aye, truly behold it now, that same
hire, spent in the destruction of human life, spent
in dyeing red those bloody rivers of Maryland and
Virginia,spent in putting mourning on the backs and
life-long sorrow in the hearts of desolate orphans;
drooping parents, and grief-stricken widows; while
here in this city of ours, pampered, pensioned, and
luxuriously paid, agitators or lecturers are found like
the fiends from subterranean places to hound on
these stupid friends of ours in America; on to another
round; on to another tarn of blood; on to then
making of another cemetery; on and on, and on is
a continuous, desolating, exterminating strife. What'o
the good or u-e of these fellows id black coats and
spotlessly white neck ties, rather too loose by the
way are the ties, for they would be of better service
if they were a little tighter; what's the reason of
their haranguing people here in favour of other
people's being bayoneted or bulleted ? Can't they go
and be shot? Should they not volunteer to fAtte n
the banks of the James' river? Nothing of any
consequence would be lost, and something might be
gained.

Now if I could only get in a good scold at paren-
theses, I would be pleased, and I come gladly back to
the hire of the labourers; and we are spending our
portion of it in relieving distress, and in a loss of
profits and of wages, that is surely equivalent to the
savings of a long period, on the employment of slaves
to grow cotton.

As we have all partaken of the profit, such as it
has been, if any, even so should the nation partake
of the loss. The immediate sufferers should not
have been obliged to part with their books and their
clothes and their furniture to sustain life. As they
have parted with these necessaries they should have
them again. Why should little children be robbed
of their boots and flannels, their caps, shoes, or
stockings, their little Sunday finery for the chapel or
church, or the Sabbath School, or of their doUble
blanket in these freezing nights*, in order to pay
what is clearly and distinctly a national debt ?
Why should mothers be deprived of the household
goods that they pinched and struggled to bring
together, and keep together by severe economy,
because the nation have gone on in a fog of
"principle" and "talk" to the edge of a great pre-
cipice, and fallen over the jagged rock down into
the darkscine deep and miry slough ?
Give men, women, and children back again the
clothes that they should never have been compelled
to part with. Relieve the pawn brokers from the
pressure on their resources. One family ia London
belonging to that trade are said to hold half the
savings of the English county to which they origi-
nally belonged. At present the Lancashire pawn-
brokers, I fancy, employ in their business half the
profits of the cotton speculators for the year.
EvELYN LEE.
LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

articles.text:
, SECOND EDITION.—SATURDAY bloßimm..

ITALY.

Tuanv, Nov. 22.
The Italian Parliament has been sitting all the weeki
and the debate has been one of confidence in the Ra-
tazzi ministry. To-day Ratazzi made a long speech.
in defence of the policy of the administration. It is
thought probable the decision will be against the
Government.

articles.title: AMERICA.
articles.text:
AMERICA.

NEW Yon; Nov. 141 Evening.
The unfavourable rumours which were current at
the departure of the Arabia have not been confirmed.
Large numbers of persons have gone to Trenton to.
pay their respects to General Welellan. At a serenade
given in his honour he made a speech, in which he said
that whilst the army was fighting the citizens should
see that the war was prosecuted for the preservation of
the union, the constitution, and the nationality and
rights of the citizens.

Two of General M'Clellan's staff officers have been
arrested and sent to Washington. The charges against
them are unknown.

The advance of General Burnside's army has oc-
cupied Fayettesville, four miles from Rappahannock
Station. General Stonewall Jackson is reported to be
moving along the turnpike-road towards Cumberland,
Maryland. The Confederates, under Generals Floyd
and Bragg, are concentrating at Gordonsville.
It is again reported from Washington that the
French minister has demanded redress for General
Butler's treatment to Frenchmen at New Orleans.
Spain has also made demands against the Federal
government. It is supposed that the demands in both
cases will be complied with.

NEW YORK, Nov. 18.
The Confederate Governor of North Carolina haa
declined to hold any conference with the Federal
Governor, at the same time declaring that North
Carolina would fight to the last drop of her blood.
He referred the Federal .Governor to the Confederate
authorities at Richmond.

The base of operations of General Burnside's army
has been changed to Acquia Creek, from which place
the advance on Richmond is to be made by way of
Fredericksburg.

General 111'Clellan is being urged to become.
Democratic candidate to the Senate from New
Jersey.

The cause of the arrest of two of General M'Clel-
an's staff officers was that they were absent without
Leave.

INDIA, CHINA, AND JAPAN.

We have received papers from Bombay, dated
November 1; Calcutta, October 22; and Madras,
October 29.

The government of India in a long dispatch has
answered Sir Charles Wood's attack on the financial
department of Mr. Laing's budget. Admitting some
trlfiing errors, the policy of the budget is vigorously
defended.

From Ningpo we learn that General Ward has been
killed while operating against the Taepings in the
neighbourhood.

Hong Kong journals of October 15 report a serious
incident at Yokohama, where one of our countrymen-
(a Mr. Richardson) has been murdered in cold blood
and two others wounded while riding along the high
road from Yedo to Miako.
The following telegram was received at the India
office yesterday, Nov. 27 :

BOMBAY, Nov. 12.
Calcutta news to Nov. 11. The British Vakeel
in Cabul has arrived at Candahar. The siege of Herat
continues, and winter arrangements are in progress.-
A large meeting, at which the G-3vernor-General pre-
sided, was held at the Town-hall on Thursday, in
connection with the distresss in the manufacturing
districts.'

articles.title: PRUSSIA.
articles.text:
PRUSSIA.

BERLIN, Nov. 27.
The New Preussische (Kreuz) Zeitung of to-day pub—
lishes the reply of the King to an address of devotion
presented to him by a deputation from the cities of
Elberfeld and Marienburgh. The conclusion of his
Majesty's speech was as follows :--4 I am sorry that I
must now govern without a budget. I shall, however,
return to a regular course. In the meantime, the
representatives of the people, on their part, must help
to render this possible, and must not exercise their
constitutional rights, as by so doing they would para-
lyze my government and disarm the country. I
cannot surrender the rights of the crown.'

articles.title: GREECE.
articles.text:
GREECE.

ATHENS, Nov. 26.
Great demonstrations in favour of Prince Alfred
have taken place at Syra and Hydra. Tranquility
continues to prevail everywhere.

articles.title: GREAT FIRE IN TORONTO.
articles.text:
GREAT FIRE IN TORONTO.

QUEBEC, Nov. 15.
The entire block of buildings comprising the &sin
Hotel, Toronto, was burnt yesterday. It is reported
that several lives were lost. The insurances on the
property destroyed are very heavy, including 50,000
dols. in the Scottish, 12,000 dols. in the Liverpool and
London, 11,000 dols. in the Queen, and 15,000 dols. in
the Unity Insurance Companies.

DEATH OF DR. BERNARD.—We have learned with
regret that will be widely shared the death of the well-
known French refugee, whose trial for conspiracy
against the life of Louis Napoleon was an event in the
history of both countries. The unhappy gentleman
has for many months been suffering under a malady
of the brain, which terminated fatally on Tuesday
Inight, in the forty-sixth year of his age. We are
I requested to announce that his friends, English as well
as continental, are invited to meet at ..,he house where
ha died—No. 3, Percy-street, Bedford-square—at half-
past one on Sunday. and thence proceed to the
place of interment, Paddington Cemetery, Kilburn.
THE FATAL COLLIERY EXPLOSION NEAR NEW-
CASTLE-UPON-TYNE.—Yesterday morning the adjourned
oouteth,
l
inquest relative to the death of William Barnes and
fifteen other persons, who were killed by the explosion
in Walker Colliery, was held atscit„hceorltoanielrwfaoyr
Hs
Walker, before Stephen Reed, E
Northumberland. Mr. Matthias Dunn, the official
inspector of coal mines for the northern district, was
present, as were also Mr. Jobling, the principal
engineer at the colliery, Mr. J. E. Forster, and other
eminent mining engineers.. The origin of the explo-
sion has not been conclusively ascertained, but the pit
has resumed working on a small scale. After hearing
the evidence of a number of witnesses, the jury returned

AOCTDENTAL DROWNING.--On Saturday, at Ea g;yt
near Bolton, a number of boys were sliding on a sheet
of water, when the ice broke, and three of them (all
cousins) were precipitated into the water. One of them
succeeded in getting out, but the two others, named
Thomas Hardman and James Fielding, aged respectively
12 years and nine years, were drowned.
CLOSING OF COTTON MILLS IN LONDON.-013. the 25th
two extensive cotton mills, employing about six hundred
men and women—one situated in Golden. lane, and the
other at Hoxton—were closed on account of the scarcity
of the staple. Several other mills in the metropolis are,
it is said, about to be closed for the same reason, the
proprietors having already greatly reduced the number
of their hands, who have for a considerable period
worked only short time.

articles.title: TRADES' INTELLIGENCE.
articles.text:
TRADES' INTELLIGENCE.

GREAT MEETING OF THE LONDON
TRADES' DELEGATES.
(Reported specially for the Beehive.)

THE DISTRESS IN LANCASHIRE.
On Tuesday night a general meeting of delegates
from the Metropoli an Trades' Societies, convened by
the London Trades' Council, was held at the Bell Inn,
Old Bailey, to consider the best way in which the
united power of tile Trade Societies could be brought
to bear in aid of the Distressed Lancashire Operatives.
Delegates were present fzom the following societies :
Amalgamated Society of Carpenters; Running limes,
ditto; Silver Cup ditto ; Brickmakers, West-end
Bootclosers, Boilermakers, Basketmakers, Bookbinders,
Kensington Bootmakers, West-end Ladies' Shoe-
makers, Zincworkers, Tin Plateworkers, Silk Velvet
Weavers, Typefounders, Cigar makers, Silver Spoon-
makers, Progressive Society of Carpenters, City Boot-
makers, Friends of Freedom Society of Carpenters,
Adam and Eve ditto, Stonemasons, Parasol-makers,
Carvers and Gilders' Iron Shipbuilders, Windmill So-
ciety of Carpenters, North London ditto, Letterpress
Trinters, Ropemakers, City Ladies' Shoemakers,
:Plumbers, Brass Finishers, Chelsea Shoemakers. Dele-
gates were also present from the Trades' Newspaper
Company, and a deputation from the bookbinders at
Mr. Burn's, Hatton-garden.
Mr. Goddard (bookbinder), Chairman of the Trades'
Council, was called to the chair. He said it had often
been charged against trade societies that they were
always willing to spend large sums in strikes and
lock-outs; but he believed the result of this meeting
would show that while they were determined, as they
always had been, to spare no expense in defending the
privileges of their trades, they were at the same time
willing to assist to the utmost of their power in alle-
viating the distresses of their fellow-workmen in all
parts of the country. (Hear.)
Mr. Applegarth (carpenter) moved the first resolu-
tion, as follows That we, the representatives of the
various London trade societies' pledge our societies to
do all in their power, either by levies or voluntary
subscriptions, as each society may for itself determine,
to assist as promptly as possible, and in a permanent
way, our distressed brethren:in Lancashire.' He had
been an eye-witness to the distress and suffering now
existing in the cotton districts, having but recently
come from those parts, and he felt certain there would
be but one feeling in the meeting on the subject.
Mr. Sweeting (boiler maker) seconded the resolution.
The society to which he belonged had its headquarters
in Manchester, and his official position had made him
-well acquainted with the present state of the operatives
in Lancashire and Yorkshire.
Mr. Graham (carpenter), Mr. Reeves (basket maker),
Mr. Pethetbridge (carpenter), Mr. Fast (zinc worker),
Mr. Blass (boiler maker), Mr. Walker (bookbinder),
and Mr. Hornsby (carpenter), briefly supported the
. _

resolution on behalf of their respective societies.
Mr. Howell (bricklayer) said it was thought by some
that this was a question which did not concern trade
societies. That was a very mistaken notion. The
distress would be made a pretext for reducing wages.
He thought an extensive plan of emigration ought to
be at once adopted, but as this was a debateable point,
he would not at present press his views on that subject.
Mr. Connolly (stonemason) said, there could not be
a more pitiable sight than a strong man willing to
work, but unable to find employment, to keep himself
and family from starvation. Working men were alone
to blame for many of the evils under which they suf-
fered—evils traceable, in most cases, to misgovernment,
and before the working men could hope to better them-
selves, they must look more after their interests in this
respect. The Government of this country were to
blame for the present state of things; as statesmen
they must have known that a war with or in America
would stop the supply of cotton, and it was their
duty to have provided against a contingency such
as has arisen. (Cheers.) The aristocracy of this
country, or a large portion of them, had pro-
longed the lamentable war now raging by their
undisguised sympathy with the slaveowners and
slave dealers of the South. Had they not done so, the
war would long since have terminated in favour of the
North, cotton set at liberty, and the slave emancipated.
(Loud cheers.) The cottonocracy of Lancashire had not
done its duty; some few had done their duty, but the
great mass had been found wanting, while many had
made immense fortunes by trading on the starvation
of the operatives, in buying up and exporting cotton.
(Hear, hear.) It was the duty of the government at
once to step in and save the operatives in the North
from famine and pestilence; for what was 2s. 2d. per
week to keep a man? He supposed they meant to wait
until the working classes were debilitated by want,
and swept off by pestilence. The neglect of the govern-
ment and the cottonocracy was, however, no excuse
for their neglecting their duty, and he trusted great
and substantial relief would be the result of this meet-
ing. (Cheers.)
The resolution was then put and carried unani-
mously. •
Mr. G. Potter (manager of the BEEHIVE), moved the
next resolution as follows That this meeting re-
solve itself into a committee, to be called "The London
Working Men's Central Committee," for the purpose
of collecting subscriptions for the relief of the dis-
tressed operatives in the North. That London be
divided into districts, and a subcommittee appointed
in each district to act in concert with, a,nd send their
subscriptions through the London Central Committee.
That a chairman, treasurer, and secretary be elected,
and a central office at once taken; and that the com-
mittee shall be empowered, if necessary, to send a
deputation to Lancashire, for the purpose of seeing the
funds properly and equally distributed.' He thought
that the duty of every working man was to come
forward at the present time and give some assistance
to those suffering ones in the north. It might be
asked why they wanted a Working Men's Central
Committee? He would tell them. Because work-
ing men were not satisfied with the proceed-
• ings of the Mansion-house Committee, who had
• just invested £4OOOO of the subscriptions they had
I received, a large portion of which had beencontributed
! by working men in Consols, instead of distributing it
' amongst the workmen, who were perishing for lack of
food and clothing. The Manchester Central have also
a large sum kept in band.. He was not assuming too
much, when he said those sums would be yet
43,- largely increased, and that at the termination of their
mect,lesbours, they would have many thousands in hand.
lisui."T, his should not be, precedents were not wanting to
-Iprove this. The amount collected for the Patriotic
resi Fund was not expended, and a considerable sum was
SL‘ still in hand ; of the India Mutiny Relief Fund there was
many thousand pounds in hand; and for the famine
in India, a large sum was collected, and instead of
being used for the purpose for which it was subscribed,
there is now in hand £BO,OOO. Other instances might
be mentioned, where funds had been collected, and
instead of being distributed,had been invested in some
way or other. Now he would. no bring discord
among any class at the present time; but it was
a fact that many working men were not subscrib-
ing at all, because thcy would not send their
subscriptions through the Lord Mayor's Committee,
and by appointing a Working Men's Central Committee
many working men and trade societies might be in-
duced to subscribe, and the result would. be a larger
amount collected to distribute to their distressed
brethren. He would divide London into districts,
and appoint a sub-committee in each district, so that a
large amount might be collected in all parts of the
metropolis. He would call a general meeting of the
working men of London, at some large hall, such as
Exeter-hall, and endeavour to show the working men
the necessity to help in this work. There was a
golden opportunity now presented to the working
classes to show to the country that, whilst they com-
bined and contributed to dphold wages and obtain a
fair remuneration for their labour, they could also com-
bine and contribute largely towards the relief of their
poor unfortunate fellow-toilers in Lancashire. (Loud
cheers.)
Mr. Petherbridge (carpenter), seconded the resolu-
tion. The working classess as a body, and trade
unionists especially, had no confidence in Lord Mayor's
or any other committees from which working men were
excluded. The mode in which the funds already sub-
scribed were distributed, was not satisfactory. Relief
was wholly or partially withheld from men who had
made themselves conspicuious in trade matters. He
*hought it was the duty of working men not only to
r subscribe to the relief of the present distress, but to
see that their subscriptions were properly applied.
The subscriptions had not hitherto been distributed in
the way that working men would like to have seen, and
it therefore behoved working men to have their own
committee, and distribute their own subscriptions. He
had no desire to Oppose the committees now:in existence,
'but to supplement them. (Cheers.)
Mr. Murray (boot closer) cordially supported the
resolution. It was now high time the working classes
took the matter in hand for themselves, and not let the
proprietors of newspapers, as the Daily Telegraph and
Lloyd's, make political capital out of the money they
were subscribing. The middle classes would not pay
in their subscriptions to a working man's committee,
and why, then, should they desire to swell their lists
with the contributions el working men?
" 'r. Butler (tin-plate worker) explained the position
^44 trade, which in the North was mainly dependent
lotton trade. They had, therefore, been cora-
-1 put or v in their Ecciety to keep their

Mr. Wakelin (bootmaker) condemned the mode in'
which relief was at present administered. His society
would not contribute any funds through the present
channel, but would support the committee contem-
plated by the resolution.
Mr. Walker (bookbinder), Mr. Hornsby (carpenter),
Mr. Martin (cigar maker), Mr. Killingback (press-
man), and other delegates, having supported the reso-
lution, it was carried unanimously.
A resolution was then adopted, that the services of
the committee and officers should be gratuitous, but
that the secretary should be paid for all time actually
lost.
Mr. Killingback (pressman) was appointed as presi-
dent, Mr. Potter as treasurer, and Mr. Applegarth as
secretary, of the committee.
It was also arranged that the whole committee
should meet on Wednesday evening, Dec. 3, at the
BEEHIVE Office, 2, Bouverie .street, Fleet-street, and
that a sub-committee should meet at the same place on
next Saturday evening, Nov. 29, and every succeding
Saturday evening, from 7 till 9 o'clock, to receive sub-
scriptions; and that subscriptions could be paid daily
to the treasurer at the above office. It was likewise
resolved that all monies paid into the committee be
acknowledged weekly in the BEEHIVE Newspaper.

TRADES' GARIBALDI DEMONSTRATION.
The Chairman said the next business on the paper
was to hear a deputation from the Trades' Garibaldian
Demonstration Committee, consisting; of Messrs.
Cremer, Burgess Smith, Castle, and Crabb. The
Trades' Council had been applied to by this committee
for that purpose, and they had thought it their duty
to place the subject on the business paper, to give
those gentlemen an opportunity of being heard. The
Council, as a body, gave no opinion at present on the
matter, but were in the hands of the delegates.
Mr. Cremer, on behalf of the deputation, stated its
object, which was to enlist the sympathy of the dele-
gates, that they might urge on their trades the
necessity of their taking a part in the demonstration
intended to be given to the great and noble Garibaldi
on his approaching visit to this country. There was
no intention to give this demonstration either a
religious or political character, but simply to do honour
to a man of progress, an advocate of social freedom,
and a devoted friend of the working man. (Cheers.)
Mr. Connolly was opposed to the subject being
entertained. They might attempt to disguise it, but it
was intended to make it a religious question—a
demonstration against Catholic faith. (Cries of No,
no).' That was his opinion. They were about to
honour Garibaldi because he had attempted, he was
happy to say in vain, to destroy the temporal power of
the Pope. (Question.) There were numbers of Irish
Catholics in their trade societies who would strenuously
oppose any such demonstration being made by the

trades. -
Mr. Murray, as a Catholic, entirely dissented from
Mr. Connolly. He thought that religion had nothing
whatever to do with the question.
Mr. Killingback said he had been deputed by his
society to support the demonstration. There were
many Irishmen in his society, but they did not look on
it in the same light as Mr. Connolly. (Hear.)
Mr. Howell said religion had nothing to do with the
matter. He neither knew, nor did he care, whether.
Garibaldi was a Protestant or a Catholic. He only
knew him as a friend of liberty, as one who bad risked
his life, and shed his blood, in the cause of freedom.
Moreover, he was the president of the trades' guilds of
Italy; institutions similar to our own trades' unions;
ano, therefore, in welcoming him, they would be wel-
coming a brother unionist. (Cheers.)
Mr. Wakelin was opposed to the matter being taken
up by the trades' societies.
Mr. Hornsby, to bring the question to an issue, I
would move the following resolution •—‘ That we, the
delegates here assembled, viewing the entire conduct
of the great patriot Garibaldi as calculated to instruct,
to free, and to otherwise elevate the whole of the
working community, deem it our imperative duty to
use our utmost exertions to make the proposed demon-
stration worthy of so noble a man.'
Mr. Howell seconded the resolution, which, after
some further discussion, was put to the meeting and
adopted by a great majority.
On the motion of .Mr. Petherbridge, a vote of
thanks was given to the trades' council for having
convened the meeting, which was suitably aoknow-
ledged by Mr. Odgers, the secretary, and the meeting
concluded.

articles.title: CO-OPERATIVE INTELLIGENCE.
articles.text:
CO-OPERATIVE INTELLI-
GENCE.

STAINLAND CO-OPERATIVE SOCIPTY.—The half-yearly
meeting of this society was held on Tuesday evening,
at Holywell-green school, Mr. Hodgson, the president,
in the chair. The minutes of the directors' meetings were
read by Mr. George Akroyd, the Secretary, which showed
not only what business had been done by the board of
directors, but also how much clear gain there was for
the half-year. The profits were found to be £5O Os. 10d.,
which would leave a bonus of 104-d. in the pound. Mr.
Hodgson was again re-elected, as well as Mr. J. Stott
for treasurer, together with a few directors, and the
meeting separated at a rather late hour.
HULL CO-OPERATIVE PROVIDENT COMPANY.—A tea
meeting in connection with the opening of the new
central store belonging to this company, in Lowgate,
which recently took place, was celebrated in the
Sailors' Institute, Waterhouse-lane, on Monday even-
ing, when about 350 members of the company with
their friends were present.
ST. CUTHBERT'S CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.—The close
of the third year of this co-operative society was cele-
brated by soiree, which was held in the schoolroom
attached to the Rev. Mr. Wilson's church, Fountain-
bridge. The large schoolroom was quite filled by the
members of the society and their friends. Mr. Caw.
chairman of the society, presided, who gave a short
address, in which he alluded to the success which has
attended the society since its formation.
CHATHAM CO-OPERATIVE INDUSTRIAL SOCIETY.---Mr.
Miller appeared on Saturday in Vice-Chancellor
Wood's Court in support of the petition of a creditor
of this society to the extent of £3CO3 praying that its
affairs, which have become embarrassed, might be
wound up under the direction of the court. Mr. H.
Smith appeared on the other side. The Vice-Chancellor
granted a winding-up order.
THE BARNSLEY BRITISH CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.—
On Monday, a public tea-meeting, in connection with
the above society, was held in the Market-street
School-room, when addresses were delivered by Mr.
Robert Steel, of Manchester, Mr. Holmes, of Leeds,
and other gentlemen. The report, which was read by
Mr. Lawton, stated that the original capital of the
society was only £35; yet at the end of the first quarter
a dividend was realised of 10d. in the pound. In the
second quarter a dividend of Is. in the pound was
declared; and the receipts since the commencement of
the society had amounted to £1,375.

articles.text:
FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.

FREEMASONS.

GRIND MASONIC CEREMONY AT HEREFORD.-Art in-
teresting ceremony connected with the Masonic Grand
Lodge of Herefordshire took place at Hereford on
Monday. It consisted of the celebration of the cente-
nary festival of the Palladian Lodge, No. 141, held at
the Green Dragon Hotel. The interest of the occasion
was considerably enhanced by the presentation of a
magnificent medal to the highly esteemed Right Wor-
shipful the Provincial Grand Master, the Rev. Doctor
Bowles, of Staunton Lacy, Salop, and the delivery of
a brilliant oration on Masonry by the Right Worship-
ful the Deputy Provincial Grand Master, the Arch-
deacon of Hereford, Dr. Richard Lane Freer.

articles.text:
ODD FELLOWS (S.M)

NEWCASTLE.—On Tuesday evenlng die brethren of
the Royal Collingwood Lodge assembled at Bre-ther
John Ireland's, Queen's Head, Gallowg&te, Newcastle,
when after the report for the past quarter had been
read, P.G. Stephen Savage presented P.G. James
Scott with a chaste silver medal, bearing a suitable
inscription as a mark of respect for the manner in
which he had conducted the Lodge during his presi-
dency. The token was acknowledged in brief but feel-
ing terms, and the remainder of the evening was spent
in a highly agreeable manner.

FORESTERS.

LONDON.—On Monday last, Nov. 24th, Brother
Knowles, of Court Hathfield, 2,018, gave an amusing
and instructive lecture on the 'Davy safety lamp and
coal mines,' at Court -St. John, 3,906, National School
Rooms, john-street,Tottenham-court-road. The lecture
was given in a plain and intelligible manner, with a'
number of practical illustrations, that would be
creditable to any scientific man. The Court-room was
filled with members of the Order, who gaveunmistake- ,
able proofs of their approval and gratification. Too
much praise cannot be bestowed on Brother Knowles,
the more particularly so, he being a self-educated man,
for his exertions in endeavouring to impart to others
the knowledge he has acquired. The members of
Court St. John, 3,906, respectfully solicit the attend-
ance of Foresters on the second and fourth Monday in
each month, at the aboue School•rooms, believing that
the holding of Court meetings at such places, is
calculated to elevate and improve the usefulness et our
noble institution. _ _

the evening was spent harraoniously.

articles.title: SHIP BUILDING TRADE.
articles.text:
THE SHIP BUILDING TRADE.

In the Times of Thursday appears the following
contradiction, 'by authority,' from Woolwich dock-
yard, of a statement which has appeared. in that
paper :
'ln the Times on the 15th inst., it was said that "the
mechanics who had been employed in bending the
armour plates for the Royal Oak were to be despatched
to Woolwich to bend the slabs for coating the Cale-
donia, and that the officers from Chatham were
to superintend the process." It may be stated
that the shipbuilders at Woolwich have had
special advantages beyond those of other yards
to make themselves acquainted with the .process
in all its details, from their proximity to the
Thames iron factories, which they have been in the
habit of visiting. Many of them have likewise super-
intended and assisted in the construction of iron ships,
and have studied the preparation of plates in the ,prin-
cipal manufactories throughout England and Scotland.
The plate-bending and fixing at Woolwich, it may be
added, is progressing in the most .satisfactory manner.
About 30 of the slabs have already been fitted to the
Caledonia's sides, under the supervision of the officers
of the yard, and by the mechanics belonging to that
establishment only.'
The authorities at Woolwich dockyard may be
satisfied with the present state of affairs, but it is ques-
tionable whether the public will look upon thirtgs
the same satisfactory light when they come
thoroughly to understand that they are paying treble
for the work now being done by shipwrights, to what it
is alleged it would cost if done by iron-men, and that
the work is also executed in a very inferior manner.

RE VIE ROCKALL FISHING AND FISH MANURE COM-

This was a petition for winding up the shove corn.
pany, praying also, under the ro-ent .T,,int Steck Com-
panies Act, the appointment of an tlicial iquidator.
The question was mooted whether the official liquida-
tor ought to be appointed upon the application of the
petitioners only, without giving other parties
interested an opportunity of objecting to the person
proposed.—The Vice-Chancellor was of opinion that
he ought not to make an absolute appointment which

DISGRACEFUL VENALITY OF AN ENGLISH
_ _ _

DAILY PAPER.
GLOVER V. PERSIGNY AND BILLAULT.
(The Morning Chronicle and the French Government).
The plaintiff, Mr. Serjeant Glover, had been pro-
prietor of the Morning Chronicle new:paper in 1856-7.
The defendant, Count Persigny, was the then French
Ambassador to this country, and M. Billault was
the French minister of the Interior. The plaintiff
brought this action to recover the sum of £14,000 for
work and labour in writing, and procuring to be in-
serted in the Morning Chronick, and other papers in
this country, certain articles by the orders of the
defendants, praising up the French Emperor, his
Government, and its acts. In the plaintiff s affidavit
he swore that he was employed in England by M.
Billault as the agent of the Count Persigny, by whom
the employment was confirmed.—Mr. Gray now moved
for an order to rescind other orders, so that the plain-
tiff might be compelled to proceed with his action. Mr.
Hodgson, for M. Billault, pitted the affidavits of that
gentleman against those of Serjeant Glover, as to the
authority given for articles in the Morning Chronicle.
Serjeant Glover swore that M. Billault had ratified
the arrangements made by persons representing them-
selves as his agents; M. Billault swore that he had
never done anything of the kind. The tenor of Mr.
Hodgson's argument was that M. Billault was more
worthy of belief than Serjeant Glover.—The Lord
Chief Justice, however, said, as it was a case of oath
against oath, and as he had no right to assume that
one party was more likely to commit perjury than
another, he should grant the rule asked for by the
plaintiff.—[Some pretty exposures of Napoleonic in
trigues and English newspaper rascality may be there-
fore expected.]

articles.text:
COURT OF EXCHEQUER. •
(Before Mr. Baron Martin and Special Juries.)

WOODVARD V. PETO.

attorney.

_
This was an action brought by a labouring man,
employed in the Victoria Docks in loading a barge,
against Sir S. Morton Peto, Bart., M.P., for bodily
injuries sustained by him in consequence of the alleged
negligence of the defendant's servants. While the
plaintiff was engaged in loading the barge the shoot'
slipped and falling upon him injured his head and side
and prevented him following his occupation for several
weeks. Besides the loss of wages he had to pay six
guineas for medical attendance. Ultimately the plaintiff
was nonsuited, in consequence of its appearing from
the evidence that the person responsible for the acci-
dent was actually in the employ of the stevedore, and
not in that of Sir S. M. Peto, the defendant.

COURT OF BANKRUPTCY.
RE GUEST.-AN UNFORTUNATE CABMAN.
This was an application for an order of discharge
by the bankrupt, who was described as a cab driver, of
Lampton Mews, Westbourne-grove. The debts are
£llO, assets nil. Mr. Holt supported the bankrupt.
Mr. Aldridge appeared for the official assignee. The
bankrupt was examined, and said that he was a cab
proprietor formerly. He purchased a cab for £4, and
three horses for £6 l'Os. The Commissioner (sur-
prised) : £4 for a cab, and £6 10s. for horses! That
was cheap. Mr. Aldridge: And they realised alto-
gether £9. Mr. bolt: It was a night cab. The
Commissioner: Does that make any difference ?—Mr.
Graham (official assignee) : Oh, yes, the horses were
fit for the knacker's. (Laughter.) The order of. dis-
charge was granted.

AMALGAMATED CARPENTERS' SOCIETY.
HARRY JUNIPER, T. F. EVANS, WILLIAM WYATT,
JAMES PAYNE, AND WILLIAM GODLNG, v. JAMES
LEA.
This case had been adjourned on two previous
occasions with the view of an ai rangement between the
parties, but which, it appeared, could not be carried
out, and it now came on for trial.
Mr. T. Salter, instructed by Mr. Buchanan,
appeared for the plaintiffs, and Mr. Joyce, instructed
by Mr. Goodie, for defendant.
Mr. Salter, in opening the case, said: This was an
action by the plaintiffs, as the local executive council
and trustees of a society called the Amalgamated
Carpenters' Society, against the defendant, the late
secretary of the society, to recover certain books and
other property of the society, unlawfully retained in
his possessicn. The action was brought under the
Friendly Societies' Act, sections di and 42. The
society had been established in 1860, and the
defendant had acted as general secretary until
June, 1862, when the period of the annual elec-
tion of officers took place. At this time the defendant
was ineligible for re-election, being in arrears with his
subscriptions, and the delegates who was then assem-
bled decided that the election of general secretary
should be left to the branches, the defendant still
acting as secretary pro tem. In the meantime, how-
ever, it was found that the defendant's conduct
with respect to some of the branches into which
the society is divided, had not been of a character
conducive to the interests of the society at large, and
a large number of the members resolved to oppose his
election, and accordingly selected four other candi-
dates, all of whom, as well as Mr. Lea, went
the poll. In due course the polling papers were re-
turned, according to the rules, to the defendant, as
secretary, to cast up and report the numbers to the
council at the next meeting. It came to the know-
ledge of the council, however, that the defendant,
having looked over the papers and found he was in a
minority of 4, procured 11 additional votes in an illegal
manner, which gave him an apparent majority of 7.
The council thereupon declared the election null
and void on this ground, dismissed the defendant
from the office he was temporarily holding, and issued
forth papers for a fresh election, which took place in
•thie course, and Applegarth was returned. The de-
fendant and his friends, taking advantage of certain
technicalities, with respect to the powers of the local
and the general council, refused to recognise the elec-
tion of Applegarth, and the defendant obtained the
eleetionrtof a general council at a time of the year
not recognised in the rules, which gave him the ma-
jority of votes. Applegarth, however, under the
advice of the majority a the local council (at that
time the only recognised and legally elected govern-
ing power of the society), refused to acknowledge
either the general council or its decision. The de-
fendant was returned by his friends, and had since
retained possession of the books and property of the
society, and assumed the functions of its general secre-
tary, on the faith of this illegal election. The great
tnajority of the members, being desirous to put an
end to this state of affairs, the plaintiffs, as the local
council trustees and governing power of the soci-
ety at the time these transactions occurred, decided
to bring this action for the recovery of the books, &c.,
that they might be placed in the hands of the real
secretary—Applegarth. Upon the facts then stated
he relied for the order of his Honour that the books
should be given up to the plaintiffs.
Mr. Joyce, for the defendant, who had only just
entered the court at the close of Mr. Salter's remarks,
said he objected; that his honour had no jurisdiction
in this case, but if he said that he had, then he ob-
jected that the present plaintiffs were not the proper
parties to bring this action. While taking these objec-
tions he was prepared, if his Honour decided against
him, to meet the case on its merits.
His Honour overruled both the learned counsel's
objections. He held that he had ample powers to deal
with and decide the case, and that the plaintiffs were
the proper parties to sue. He wished, however, in the
interest of the society, to throw out a suggestion.
Would each side agree to appoint one person thoroughly
well acquainted with all the facts to meet him in his
private room, having with them all necessary books
and documents, and calmly and dispassionately go into
the whole case, without any legal quibbling on either
side. If each will agree to this, and be bound by his
decision, is would be much more satisfactory than
obtaining a triumph grounded upon legal technicali-
ties, and possibly save much future expense and litiga-
tion.
The counsel, having consulted withleir respective
clients, said they were much obliged to hisHonour for the
interest he took in the case, and had counselled their
clients to act upon his suggestions. It had been

The question of costs also to be left to his

Honour.
Mesars. Cremer and Lee then retired with his
Honour to his private room, and the subject was
fully gone into, and all documents relating to it sub-
mitted. At the conclusion his Honour said he would
give the matter his careful consideration, and deliver
his judgment in writing in a few days.

CENTRAL CRIMINAL COURT.
OLD COURT.—(Before Mr. Justice Byles.)
ALLEGED WIFE MURDER.
Henry King, 38. carpenter, was indicted for the
wilful murder of Sarah Anne Day, by stabbing her
with a chisel. Mr. Ribton appeared for the prosecu-
tion. The prisoner was defended by Mr. Serjeant
Ballantine (specially retained) and Mr. Kemp.
The learned counsel (Mr. Ribton, Q.C.) :in opening
the case for the prosecution, said he believed there
would be no doubt that the unfortunate deceased lost
her life through the act of the prisoner, and he be-
lieved the only question they would, in the result,
have to decide was whether the offence amounted
to the crime of wilful murder, or to the lesser one
of manslaughter. He then proceeded to state the
facts of the case, and from this statement, and the
evidence adduced, it appeared that the prisoner had
married the deceased two or three years ago; but
there was some doubt whether it was a legal mar-
riage, and it seemed that they did not live happily
together, and had separated. They had lived toge-
ther for some time in Westminster, but a short
time before the fatal affair took place the deceased
had left him and gone to lodge at a house in Tower-
street, in the Westminster-road. Before the deceased
left the prisoner's house ho was heard to say, that if
he did not find her at home when he came back he
would murder her, and afterwards do for himself. The
deceased, however, it appeared, did leave him, and
went to live with her mother in Tower-street, West-
minster. About five weeks before the deceased left the
prisoner to live with her mother, the prisoner quarrel-
led. very much with her during tea time, and she told
her mother that, if she was not out of the house by
the Friday, he would have her life and break every-
thing in the place. The deceased left the house on the
Friday, and she afterwards went back to him, but left
him again and went to her mother. The prisoner
went to the house several times, and annoyed her very
much, causing a mob to collect round the door. On
October 18, the day the occurrence took place, the
prisoner went to the house and saw the deceased. She
occupied a room on the ground-floor, and a police-
constable named Cook, a friend of the mother's, was
there in private clothes, and heard part of the conver-
sation which took place between them. Deceased said,
Well, Harry, what brings you here?' And he
asked her if she intended to return, and. she said
No, King, you have never acted like a man to me,
and no persuasion will induce me to return.' The pri-
soner, who is by trade a carpenter, at this time was
holding a hammer, a scow driver, and a chisel in his
right hand, and he put the hammer in his left hand, and,
advancing his left foot, he made a violent stab at her
with the screw driver and chisel, which he had in his
right hand, with considerable violence, and inflicted
two wounds, one of which was four inches deep. The
deceas&d screamed out, Oh, I'm stabbed,' and Cook,
the constable who was present, as soon as he heard
deceased say she was stabbed, immediately seized his
arms, but
.he struggled and got away. The deceased
woman was tall en to bed, and medical assistance called
for, but she died the next day. The medical evidence
was to the effect that she died from internal haemorr-
hage. The prisoner, upon getting away from Cook,
left the house, and went to a public-house, where
Cook afterwards apprehended him. When he was
taken into custody, he first said that the deceased was
his wife, and afterwards that she was not, and said
that she had been having improper familiarites with
other men, and that the constable Cook knew all about
it, and had taken her away from him, or some words
to that effect.
The witness Cook was cross-examined at very con-
siderable length by Serjeant Ballantine, who elicited
from him that after he had been called in, in the
execution of his duty, to interfere between the prisoner
and the deceased, he was in the habit of constantly
visiting her and taking his meals with her, and that on
the day the occurrence took place he had been in the
room alone with her for an hour and a half. It also
appeared that after the transaction he was suspended
from his duty, and subsequently dismissed from the
police.
Serjeant Ballantine made a powerful address to the
jury on behalf of the prisoner.
At the request of Serjeant Ballantine, a statement
made by the prisoner before the magistrate was put in
and read. It was as follows
'There was a good deal more passed than he (Cook)
has stated. I called at the hornie for a pair of stockings,
and I positively swear that a had no intention of doing
her any harm; neither did I know that I had done so
when they turned me out of the house.'
A great number of highly respectable witnesses, who
had known the prisoner many years, and some of
whom had employed him, were then examined, and
they all spoke ot him in the highest terms, and said
that they had always regarded him as a kind and
humane man.
Mr. Justice Byles having summed up, the jury re-
tired to consider their verdict, and on their return the
foreman replied, 'We say that the prisoner is not
guilty, and that is the unanimous opinion of the jury.'
The prisoner was ordered to be discharged from
custody.

(Before Mr. Baron Bramwell.)
THE GAROTTE ROBBERIES.--It having been under-
stood that the arrangements of the authorities in-
volved the trial in this court of the very many
prisoners charged with the offence known and desig-
nated as 'garotte robberies,' the court was densely
crowded, not only by the witnesses in each case, but
also by many other individuals who, though subjected
to outrages of that class, had not been enabled through
the intervention of the police to bring their asailants
to justice.
George Roberts, 33, tailor, and James Anderson, 27,
painter, were indicted for violently assaulting Ryk de
Sueur, and stealing from his person a watch, his pro-
perty, in Bloomsbury-square, at 6 o'clock on the even-
ing of Oct. 26th. Both prisoners had been previously
convicted, Roberts no less than 15 times. Verdict—
Guilty.
John Redwood, 22, braccinaker, was charged with
having, in company with divers others, feloniously
assaulted John Roper, with intent to rob him in
Holborn. Several previous convictions were proved
against the prisoner. Verdict—Guilty.
James Mo watt, 31, smith; John Allen, tailor; and
Lawrence Sherriff, 27, traveller, all well-dressed men,
were indicted for feloniously assaulting Will jam John
Northcott with intent to rob him in Long -acre, on the
12th of November. Both prisoners had been several
times previously convicted. Verdict—Guilty.
Charles Toms, 18, labourer, was indicted for robbery,
with violence, on David Moxdale, and stealing from his
person a watch in Cow Cross-street, Clerkenwell, on the
26th of October. Several previous convictions stood
against the prisoner. Verdict—Guilty.
John Painter, 22, labourer, and Charles Thompson,
22, joiner, were indicted for feloniously assaulting
Samuel Prior with intent to rob him, upon the morn-
ing of the 2nd of Novembor, at 2 o'clock, in the Hay-
market. The jury found them both Guilty, and the
police said that taey had known the prisoners for a
long time as the associates of thieves.
John Painter, 22, labourer, and Charles Thompson,
22, joiner, were indicted for feloniously assaulting
Samuel Prior with intent to rob him in the Hay-
market on the 22nd November.—Guilty.
William Smith, 24, labourer, Gibson Burley, 22,
sailor, and George Needham, 22, sailor, were indicted
for a robbery with violence of George Rowell, and
stealing from him a handkerchief and a flannel shirt at
Woolwich.—Guilty.
Thomas Redshaw, 20, harness-maker, James Dixon,
20, clerk, and Charlotte Redsha,w, 19, spinster, were
indicted for feloniously assaulting William Beamish,
and stealing from him part of a watch chain and is. 6d.
in money, in the City-road, on the night of Sept. 29.
—Guilty.
Joseph Hall, 30, labourer, and Robert Leat, 25,
smith, were indicted, together with a woman unknown,
with feloniously assaulting Edwin John Burt with
intent to rob him in Fenchurch-street on the 21st
inst.—Guilty.
Richard Hurley, 23, and William Windsor, 19, were
charged with committing a robbery, with violence, upon
Frederick James Bush, in the Old Bailey on the 17th
, inst.—Guilty.
Edward Marks, 41, John Lane, 18, James Butler,
18, and John Ford, 18, were charged with robbery,
with violence, upon Michael Murray, at Chealsea, on
the 3rd inst.—Guilty.

The following Southern news is given in

'I have news from Richmond up to the 6th. General
Lee arrived in Richmond about two weeks ago, and has
been there ever since. Ile has resumed his position as
General Commanding-in-Chief, and acts as military
adviser to the War Department. General Joe Johnson
succeeds General Lee in the active command of the rebel
armies north of Richmond, and now has his head-
quarters at Culpepper. " Stonewall " Jackson's corps
d' armee has been increased to 50,000 men. The advance
of the army of the Potomac was known in Richmond, and
the situation well understood. The rebel plan of
. operation was said to be to mass their forces on the
Rappahannock, and then fight the greatest battle of the
war. The Now Merrimac is completed, and has been
below Fort Darling for several days, with steam up and
her full complement and crew aboard. She is ready for
a fight, and may be expected at the mouth of James
River at any moment. She passed the obstructions in
James River coming down.; but, owing to their peculiar
nature, it is impossible for her to get back to Richmond.
If worsted in an encounter with our navy she can only
seek protection under the guns of Fort Darling.
Officers in the rebel service have been detached by the

A dispatch from Louisville, of the 9th, says
There was no assault on Nashville up to Friday
evening. Nothing has been heard of General Polk. On
Wednesday night the rebel pickets on the Murfreesboro,
M`Minnville' and Franklin Pikes commenced skiimish-
ing. Eight hundred of Stokes's cavalry charged upon
Stern's cavalry, and drove them within five miles of
Franklin. Meanwhile, a rebel force, supposed to be
Morgan's, made a dash on the new railroad bridge, north
of Nashville, but were repulsed. Union loss in the
various skirmishes, one killed, 13 wounded, and three
missing; M'Cook's advance reached Nashville on the
afternoon of the 6th. It is reported the rebels have
evacuated Murfreesboro and M‘kinnville and gone to
Chattanooga; also that General Joseph E. Johnson had
arrived at Chattanooga and assumed command of the
Department of Tennessee and North Alabama. Breck-
imidge's command is at Chattanooga. Deserters from
the rebel army say Bragg was obliged to destroy most
of the property captured by his forces in Kentucky to
prevent its falling into Buell's hands.'
The following order has been issued in consequence of
the recent investigation into the surrender of Harper's
Ferry:—
'War Department, Adjutant-General's-office,
Washington, Nov. 8.
General Orders, No. 183.
1. The Military Commission, of which Major-
General David Hunter, United States' Volunteers, is
President appointed to meet in the city of Washington
on the 25th of September, pursuant to Special Orders,
No. 225, of the 231 of September, 1862, to investigate
the circumstances of the abandonment Of Maryland
Heights, and the sun-ender of Harper's Ferry, have re-
ported that Colonel Thomas H. Ford, of the 32nd Ohio
Volunteers, conducted the defence of Maryland Heights
without ability, abandoned his pesition without SPE-
cient cause, and has shown throughout such lack of
military capacity as to disqualify him in the estimation
of the Commission for a command in the service. The
said Colonel Thomas H. Ford is, by direction of the
President, dismissed from the service of the United
State.

'2. The Commissionb aving rep ortecl that the behaviour
of the 126th New York Infantry was disgraceful, and
that Major W. H. Baird; for his bad conduct, ought to
be dismissed the service, Major Baird, of the 126th New
York Volunteers, is, by direction of the President, dis-
missed from the service of the United States.
3. The commission having reported that Brigadier-
General Julius White, United States' Volunteers acted
with decided capability and courage, had its approbation,
and having found nothing in the conduct of the subor-
dinate officers brought befort", the commission, they are

'4. The military commission of which Major-General
Hunter is, president is dissolved.

Repeated cases, which lady°. lately Came before the
magistrates, of persons accused of stealing goods exposed
in the front of drapers' shops, have attracted our atten-
tion, from the frequency of their recurrence, and the
manner in which they have been commented upon and
`treated. by the magistrates generally. We know that
the practice of exposing large and miscellaneous quanti-
ties of goods, especially in low neighbourhoods, in the
front of shops, has plenty of precedent to recommend it;
but notwithstanding this, we look upon it as most ob-
jectionable one, and as offering a greater premium to
crime, and temptation to theft, than any other practice
extant. We are not living now in the time of Alfred;
the days are passed whoa gold bracelets could, be hung
with safety by the side of the open highway without
danger of appropriation by the passers-by. ' The
Englishmen of the nineteenth century may be more
civilised and enlightened than those of the ninth, but
according to the tradition of that, and Our experience of
this, they are hardly so scrupulously honest-7-7'7w
