The following appears in the Times:—
. .
Egypt and the Soudan are supplied with slaves kid-
napped from the tribes of the White Nile to the amount
of many thousands per annum.
The head-quarters from which .the expeditions
annually start -is Khartoum, the capital of the Soudan,
situated at the junction of the Blue with the White Nile.
At Khartoum is a Governor-General, the European
Powers being represented by English, French, and Aus-
trian Consuls. The black population of this town is
composed of the dregs of the human race: they are
principally employed in the White Nile trade by the
merchants—the latter being Europeans, Turks, Syrians,
and Arabs. The produce of the White Nile is confined
to slaves and ivory. In former years ivory was
generally obtained in exchange for glass beads,
copper rings' and lance heads; but competition has
so inundated the tribes with these articles and raised
the value of ivory that it is now imposskble to procure it
by such exchange. Cattle are now the only medium of
barter. It being impossible to convey cattle- from
Khartoum for this
.T.urpose, the trade of the White Nile
has resolved itself into piratical expeditions, and is thus
simply conducted :—The merchant in Khartoum sends
&party of from 80 to 200 armed men in large sailing
vessels well •supplied with ammunition and with a
certain amount of copper rings and glass beads for pay-
ment to natives who act as porters in conveying ivory
to the boats. Upon arrival among a tribe rich in cattle,
they attack a village by surrounding it and firing upon
the inhabitants, killing or putting to flight the men and
capturing the women and children and cattle. The
latter now form the merchant's "stock in trade; the
women and children are fastened together and driven off
to the boats as slaves. Some thousand head of cattle
being thus secured, they are driven by the armed force
into the interior, among tribes rich in ivory, who—if
too powerful to be openly attacked—are bartered with,
and the ivory is conveyed to the boats. By this barter
the trader's supply of cattle being exhausted, he leagues
himself with a neighbouring trible hostile to the last,
and with them he invades his recent customers and
steals back all the cattle, giving one-half to his new
allies, and bartering the other half for ivory. This affair
being concluded, he is again without cattle; thus, he
makes a fresh alliance, and, if possibly, he robs his old
allies; thus the same cattle are frequently stolen and
exchanged several times, their produce in ivory being
carried to the boats, together with the captives from the
various razzias.: -The vessels being loaded with slaves and
ivory retire to the trader's fortified establishment, where
both cargo and. slaves are deposited; in the meanwhile
the piratical boats depart upon further expeditions.
The voyage being completed, the ivory is brought to
Khartoum. The wages of the crew are paid in slaves, at
about one-third of their actual value, thus giving the
men a zest for the trade. The slaves remaining at the
depot are draughted into the Egyptian possessions, and
sold as opportunities offer, theirnecks being secured on
the march in a long cleft pole, to *Well they are also
handcuffed. The frightful atrocities committed by the
troops of banditti thus employed by the' traders of
Khartoum are beyond description; but I will not at
present descend to details, it being sufficient to declare
the existing state of the White Nile trade, which can-
not be generally known in England. So infatuated are
the wretches of Khartoum for the lucrative sport of
man-hunting that I can procure no men for escort upon ,
my southern expedition, as they will not engage to an
Englishman known as an anti-slavetrader. The British
flag, in some instances,, covers cargoes of slaves on the'
waters of the White Nile. JASIES W. BAKER.
Khartoum, Sept. 20.

The typographers GE Paris, who were condemned tos
different punishments in consequence of a strike, have
made their advocate, M. Berryer, a preSent, unique in
its execution, and remarkable for the ingenuity of the
thought. They have printed on vellum the or4tions of
Bossuet, and have produced a book in a style of magnifi-
cence unequalled for typographical excellence. In order
that no other copy should exist, the forms were im-
mediately broken up.

A Preneh court-martial at Rome has-just condemned.
two Roman peasants to death for the miuder of a
soldier, named Bruneau„ of the 19th Regiment. The
soldier, with two of his comrades, was caught in. the
fact of stealing grapes in a vineyard at Viterbo—a very.
favourite pastime as it seems with the French garrison
there. The owners of the vineyard, who bear the
formidable names of Saturnino, Terribili and Valentino
Terribili, were watching their property, with a loaded
gun, aud it was proved that one of them. did shoot the.
French soldier, in a very cold-blooded* manner. After
the murder the culprits took refuge in Cardinal Beclini's
carriage, and were conveyed, by him to a sanctuary' in
which the .Roman government pretended. that ;their
persons were inviolable. The French cordmander-in-
chief, however, intimated to Cardinal Antonelli that
he should recognise none of this medimval nonsense in
a case where French subjects were concerned. The
Terribilis were dragged from the sanctuary and brought'
before a court-martial. The Capuchin monks made
great efforts to suppress evidence in the case, but the
French military authorities got quito enough to satisfy
the court-martial. The men are condemned to death,
and the sentence will,, doubtless, be executed; The
officer acting as judge-advocatepressed for an example,
as, he said, the prisoners were actuated by hatred to
the French army, and not by a desire to protect their
grapes. What- a singular jurisdiction is that of the
French court-martial in this case r. The eldest son of
the church—who protects the temporal power—cannot
trust the Pope to do justice upon his own subjects for
vulgar civil crimes, but tries Roman citizens by court-
martial, as if the- French army were in an enemy's
country.

HIGHWAY ROHDERIES,—That the City has been un-
disturbed during the period of these aggravated outrages
in the rest of the metropolis we must attribute to the
vigilance of the police. If there is any special tempta-
tion to plunder in any locality, it must be here, among
the banks, jewellers' shops, and richly-stored warehouses.
But the felonious part of the population have a quick
perception for the weak points of our protective measures,
and they select those districts where the police supervi-
sion has become lax, partly, perhaps, through the ab-
sorption of police power at the Exhibition, but partly,.
also, we must think, from some decline in the adminis-
tration. Mr. Commissioner Harvey's proposal for a
supervision of the tickets of leave might result in a
clearer knowledge of the working Of the system than
any of the speculations hitherto indulged, or than even
the bitter experiences of aessions and police-courts. It is
a question, not if we cannot hasten the restoration to
liberty of the convietesk ruffian, but, if after a certain
number of convictions, ...>a law should ever relax its
grasp of him. One theory is as worthy ofProof as a a other.
Ilk- is a mistaken kindness to let these gaol birds loose to
prey upon society as before it might be real kindness to
keep them safe for the whole term of their natural lives;
when, by repeated acts of infamy, they have forfeited all
claims to the possession of personal liberty. The awful
cost of such a system would be the first objection started,
perhaps, were it ever seriously discussed, but even that
could not be consideseed'an insuperable objection to the
adoption of severer measures; for a thief costs the
community a hundred times as much while he follows
his vocations undetected than the cost of his keep in
prison; and it is, moreover, high time we made better
use of convict labour, so as to render prisons self-sup-
porting. Six-feet burglars with the strength of giants
ought to earn more than their keep in gaol, and the task
for reformers is to discover how to make them do so.
THE BEGGARS OF Moscow.—ln Moscow exist about
40,000 beggars by profession—rather a strong propor-
tion in a total of 380,000 inhabitants—who chiefly ply
their trade in the shops and galleries of the Vrostinnoc
Dbor, a kind of Oriental bazaar. On every step you
fall in with women carrying their children via' them,
with persons dismissed from hospitals, with burned-out
people from the neighbourhood, and that particular
species of the Russian beggar who appeals to your
generosity on behalf of recruits and the starving families
they have left behind them. The most impudent
of all are discharged officials and soldiers, who are
generally drunkards, covered in rags, and decorated
with orders and clasps. Then, again you meet old
women carrying open coffins with them, and begging
alms to defray the cost of burial. Other women, of the
same stamp, applying to you in the name of a bride,
who would like to be married, but wants a dowry.
Peasants will stop you, to enable them to buy a new
horse, the old one having gone to the wall by some
accident or other; soldiers in full uniform, who have
broken a glass in the barracks, clamour for a trifle to
replace the departed one. To the secular members of
the fraternity is admixed a strong proportion of
monks and nuns, walking in the sombre garments of
their order, and asking a mite for the erection of a new
church, the restoration of a chapel, or such like pur-
poses. All point imperatively to the boxes, plates,
coffins, prayer-books, and altar-covers they present to
you, with an entreating gesture. Pilgrims and pil-
grimesses, too, who have vowed to go to Palestine, to
the Soloviski Monastery, to the grave of the sacred
Tychon, will accost you, each enlarging with great
emphasis and considerable fluency upon the holy
object of their journey.—Letter from St. Petersburg.

articles.title: T.HE GREAT IVAPOLEOW'S END:
articles.text:
T.HE GREAT IVAPOLEOW'S END:

[From There History of the Consulate:l
The end of April had arrived, and every moment in-
creased his danger and suffering. Ilehad no relief from
the spasms, vomitings' fever, and burning thirst.
Napoleon was relieved by, occasionally drinking some
drops of fresh water breught from the foot of the peak
of Diana, the spot where he had wishedto have a dwell-
ing erected. I wish,' he said, if it is possible, that I
should be buried on the banks of the Seine, or
at Ajaccio, in my family domain, -or should my body
be fated to continue prisoner, at the foot of the
feuntain whose waters have afforded me some relief.'
This his friends promised with tears, for they no longer
concealed from him a state he so well understood him-
self. You will return to Europe,' he said to those who
surrounded hint. • ',Yon will return bearing withyou the
reflection of my glory, wittz the honour of your own
fidelity. You will be 'esteemed and happy. I go to
meet Kleber, Desaix, Lames,— Massena, l3essieres,
Duroc, Ney ! They will come t 6 meet me. They will
experience once more the intoxication of human glory.
We shall speak of what we have done. We shall talk
of our profession with Frederick, Turenne, Coßde,
Caesar, and Hannibal.' Then pausing, Napoleon ad`ded,
with a peculiar smile, 'Unless there should be as great
an objection in the upper spheres as there is here below
to see a number of soldiers together." This badinage,
alternatine. with the most solemn discourse, produced a
profound effect upon those present.

On the Ist of. May the agony seemed to commence,
and he was in constant torture. On the 2nd and 3rd
Napoleon was in high fever, and suffered from continual
spasms. Whenever his sufferings abated, his mind was
as radiant as ever, and he spoke with clearness and
serenity. During one of these intervals, he indicated,
under the title of first and second revery, two notes on
the defence of France in ease of an invasion. On the
3rd he became delirious, and 'mid his ravings these
words were distinguishable, My son. The army.
Desaix.' It would seem as though he had a last vision
Of the battle of Marengo recovered by Desaix. The
agony continued during the entire of the 4th, and the
noble countenance of the hero was terribly distrted.
The weather was terrible, it was the bad season at St.
Helena. Sudden gusts of wind tore up some of the
planted trees. On the sth of May there was no doubt
but that the last day of his extraordinary life had
dawned: .A 11 his servants, kneeling round his bed,
watched the last flicicerings of the vital flame.
These were unfortunately attended with bitter suffering.
The English officers, assembled outside, listened with
respectful interest to the accounts the servants gave of
his agony. Towards the decline of day, his life and
sufferings decreased together; the cold extending from
the extremities became general, and Death seemed about
to seize his glorious victim. The weather had become
silent and serene. About twenty minutes past five,
when tEe sun was setting in waves of light, and the
English cannon gave the signal for retiring, those around
the bed perceived that the patient did not breathe, and
cried out that he was dead. They covered his hands
with kisses, and :Marchand, who had brought to St.
Helena the cloak the First Consul had worn at Marengo,
laid it over, his body, leaving only, his noble head un:.
covered. The convulsions of the death agony, always
so painful to witness, were succeeded by a majestic tran-
quillity of expression. That face, so wondrously beau-
tiful, now restored to the slenderness of -youth, and the
figure clad in the mantle of Marengo, seemed to prpsent
again to the witnesses of that foliating scene, General
Bonaparte in the meridian of his glory.
In obedience to Napoleon's instructions, his body was
opened, and from the examination. it Would appear that
cancer in the stomach
,'was, the principal cause of his
death. The liver was slightly diseased, which shows
that the climate had some, though not a determining,
influence on his general health. There is no doubt but
grief and suppressed despair, joined to want of exercise,
hadaccelerated,the progress of the disease and shortened
his life, though it would be impossible to say by how
years. The- inspection of the body revealed several
wounds, some very slight, and, three very distinct. ~Of
these three, one was in his head, one on the right-anger
of the left band, a third in the left thigh, the last a very
deep wound resulting from a bayonet
,trust received at
the siege of Toulon. Of these-wounds the origin of the
latter alone can be historically ascertained. From the
measures taken and the
,exact description made of -the
body, it appears that Napoleom was five feet two inches
(French measure), the body well-proportioned, the feet
and hands remarkable for the regularity of their form,
the shoulders-wide, the chest well developed, the neck
a little short,,but bearing firmly and erect the largest
and best formed head ever submitted- to the investiga-
tions of science, and a ceuntenance whose beauty even
death respected, of which his contemporaries have pre-
served an ineffaceable remembrance, and of which
posterity will say, when comparing it with busts from
the antique, that it was one of the most beautiful that
God had ever made to manifest the workings of genius.
His life, solaregnant in action that it seems to comprise,
centuries, did not last more than fifty-two years. MM.
de Montholon and Marchand dressed him in the uni-
form he preferred, that of -the Chasseitra of the Guard,
and placed upon his puissant head the little hat he was.
accustomed to wear. A single priest and a few friends
prayed. for some days beside his inanimate body..

We observe that dresses do not appear to,have de-
creased, but rather increasedrin length and voluminosity.
Trimmings are still extensively worn round the bottom of
the skirt; skirts are in many cases full, plain, and
gored,. with each seam trimmed. A full plain skirt with
a simple plaiting of narrow ribbon at the bottom is
still in favour. if we may judge by the promise
held out, the mantles and jackets for the coming
season ate exceedingly elegant, and, in many cases,
costly from their rich trimmi:ags. One of the handsomest
is a mantle called ‘Bobergli.' It is of the richest
Lyons velvet, splendidly trimmed; and. its folds
look quite impervious to the cold. Mantles are still
worn very large and sweeping. Some of the jackets are
exceedingly stylish and pretty, especially one called the
‘Hongroise.' Bonnets are comfortable, looking—
though much loaded with trimming flowers, do not
appear quite so much in favour for the winter season.
They yield in many instances to feathers, which are
very fashionable, and bows of velvet, &c., fastened with
jet.ornaments or slides. We notice, also, two or three
morning dresses—the body plain in every case, with
epaulets, gauntlets, and front trimmings. An evening
dress also is pretty, but has nothing new iii it. —The
_Drapers' Week,ly News. -

; A case fortunately of rare—we believe it is of un-
precedented occurrence—in the aiutals of English jour-
nalism, was brought before the Court of Queen's Bench
on Salm-lay. Mr. Sergeant Glover was the proprietor
of the Morning Chronicle for a few years; and he has
brought an action against Count Per.signy and M. Bil-
lault for payment of certain sums of money in re-
muneration for articles which Mr. Glover caused to be
inserted in his journal at the request of the defendants.
Glovers allegation is that he was engaged to the work by
M. Billault, then a member of the French embassy, as
agent for the Count de Pelsigny, then Minister of the
interior, who also subsaquently confirmed the engage-
ment. Though Serjeant Glover commenced the action,
there appears to have been some delay in proceeding
with it, as the a'nplication was on Saturday made on the
part of the defendants to compel the serjeant to go on
with his action.

The probabilities of Prince Alfred being elected Kin.
of Greece are so great that La France has an article
drawing attention to the subject, and pointing out the
evil results that would ensue if one of the great Western
Powers should- -seek to obtain a preponderance in the
East to the prejudice of the others. The latest news
from Athens confirms -what has before been stated, that
the English Government are altogeth-r neutral, and have
further given instructions to the English Alinister at the
Greek capital to refrain from endeavouring in any way
to influence the election. The elections to the National
Assembly will commence on the 6th, and terminate on
the 10th of December. Several of the celebrated refugees
who have returned to Athens have received a brilliant
ovation. Tranquility continues to prevail throughout
the country.
A curious instance of opposition has taken place at
Pisa between the government and the party of action.'
It is stated that during the night a marble slab had been
set up at the spot where Garibaldi was landed, com-
memorating that event, and mentioning that he was
wounded at Aspromonte. That circumstance was con
sidered by the authorities as intended to cast a slur upon
the army, and on the following day a picket of car,
bineers was sent to pull down the slab, and put another
in its stead, with the same inscription, except the words,
wounded at Aspromonte.' But, lo! notwithstanding
the vigilance of the police, on the night after the govern-
ment slab was taken away, and one identical withlhe
first one put in its stead. The correspondent of the
Opinione of Turin, who relates this says that whil3 the
carbineers were at work, Madame Mario (Miss White)
might be seen at the window of the hotel inhabited by
the general, watching them in great apparent agitation.

articles.title: AGRICULTURAL PROSPECTS.
articles.text:
AGRICULTURAL PROSPECTS.

This week opened with a bright, clear, and fine day„,
after a little rain during the previous night; but Mon-
day, too, was fine' with no frost in the past night;
barometer high, up to 30.20.
Field-work would proceed steadily in all the late dis-
tricts, the wheat going into the ground inthe finest order
possible, and good progress was made. The accounts
speak most favourably of the plant, where the seed had
been got in early in October. We heard one farmer
observe that he wished he had sown more of Hallett's,'
for this looked the best of any he had sown this season,
and he had planted giessingland; Browick,' and
'Rough Chaff,' besides "Rivett's.' The latter is now
being got into the ground, as about the last sown of the
season, but its growth is not extended, being confined
much to the Roothings of Essex. In parts of Hertford-
shire many farmers plant the Nursery up to April, but
this season a good deal has been committed to the ground
in October.

Tuesday was slightly inclined to rain, but it held up;
wind N.W. ; thermometer 42 deg, barometer 30.30.
Again field would go on favourably. Our advices from
Lincolnshire on that day say 'the weather has been
exceedingly cold and frosty since our last repeet '
Wednesday was a dull looking day, with ocf.ei.
slight drizzling rain; wind N.E., the night 4,-
cloudy.
r Upon the whole the weather has- been racr,
able for thrashi,pg grain, a stiffish breeze , frequee.tiy
blowing, but the farmers are not disposed to bring this
grain to market freely whilst the wade remains so
depressed, and with such an immense import•of foreign
continued from week to week. The deliveries have
therefore fallen off in the agricultural districts, and they
will probably keep much in the straw for the benefit of
the cold penetrating March winds, which will improve
the condition greatly- By that time, too, the markets
may have been cleared of the great bulk of foreign, as
both Baltic and American supplies will no doubt have
greatly fallen off. These may be the last important
arrivals from the north of Europe for the season, as soon
the winter will block up the ports.
The deliveries of barley are, of course, on the increase,
as this is now being thrashed in preference to wheat,
and the markets are filling. llaltsters having bought
pretty freely in some parts, will not go on so anx-
iously, but select what they want for their present
use as prices suit them. Those who will have none
but the best will not probably get into stock very readily,
and they must pay a good• price for a choice sample,
whilst the intermediate qualities will sell lower in pro-
portion, from their being.the most abundant of any,
ranging in price from 355. to 375. per qr. Grinding,
sorts are of the smallest number of any, and sell toler-
ably well in consequence. French and Saab e qualities
come in slowly, and sell steadily, when approved of by
the maltsters, at fair prices, but not to en-Courage the ina-
porters to buy freely, as price free on board leave no
margin for profit.
The weather for the remainder of the week was
favourable for the field—cold without being frosty. On
Saturday at midday the thermometer stood at 30 deg.;
barometer at 29.80, steadily falling, with more the ap-
pearance of snow than rain. Still taking the month of
November thus far, it has been a fine month, passing us
nicely on towards December without much severity, and
giving the farmers a good opportunity to clear up the
wheat sowing.—Nov. 22.

articles.title: TOWER OF LONDON.
articles.text:
THE TOWER OF LONDON.

Few persons are aware of the strictness with which
the Tower of London is guarded from foes without and
treachery within. The ceremony of shutting it up
every night continues to be as solemn and as rigidly
precautionary as if the French invasion were actually
afoot Immediately after tattoo all strangers are ex-
pelled; and the gates once closed, nothing short of such
imperative necessity as fire or sudden illness can pro-
cure their being re-opened till the appointed hour ,next
morning:
The ceremony of locking up is very ancient, curious,
and stately s A few minutes before the clock strikes
the hour of eleven—on Tuesdays and Fridays at twelve
—the head warden (yeoman porter) clothed in a long
red cloak, bearing in his hand a huge bunch of keys,
and attended by a brother warden, carrying a gigan-
tic lantern, appears,in front of the main guard-house,
and calls out in a loud voice, 'Escort keys.' At
the words the - sergeant of the guard, with five or
six men, turn out and follow him to the Spur, or
outer gate; each sentry challenging him as they pass
his post :
'Who goes there?'
• 'Keys.
The gates being carefully locked' and barred—the
warden wearing m solemn an aspect and makino• as
much noise as possible—the procession returns,'and.the
sentries exact the same explanation and receive the same-
answer as before. Arrived once more in front of the
main guard.house,the sentry there gives a loud stamp
with his foot, and the following conversation takes place
between him and the approaching party—
'Who goes there?

6-Keys.r •
'Whose keys F.

'Queen Victoria's keys.'
Advance Queen Victoria's keys, and all is well.'
The yeoman porter then exclaims—

Goil bless Qdeen Victoria.'

The main guard devoutly respond Amen.'
The officer on duty gives the word Present arms,'
the firelocks rattle, the officer then kisses the hilt of his
sword, the escort fall in among their companions, and
the yeoman porter marches majestically across the.
parade 'ground alone to deposit the keys in the lieu-
tenant's lodgings.
The ceremony over, not only is all egress and ingress
tot,illy precluded, but those within being furnished with
the countersign, anyone who, unhappily forgetful, ven-
tures feom his quarters unprovided with this talisman is
sure to be made the prey of the first sentinel whose
post he crotses.—City Press,

articles.title: PRUSSIAN LAW"S ON DUELLIRG.
articles.text:
PRUSSIAN LAW"S ON DUELLIRG.

The National Zeitung contains a report of a trial of a
principal and his second in a case of threatened hostile
proceedings, by which it will be seen that the Prussian
laws afford but little proteetion to duellists. The follow-
ing is an abstract of the proceedings
M. von Schimmelpfennig, an actor, considered him-
self to have been offended by the Russian Baron von
Brunner, and commissioned a brother actor, M. Ore-
linger, to summon the baron to mortal combat. This
challenge the baron: declined to comply with. Some
days afterwards Von Schimmelpfennig met the baron
in the garden of the Victoria Theatre, accompanied by
two ladies connected with the establishment, and de-
clared that if he declined to fight he would strike him.
The baron again refused to fight, and was assaulted by
the actor. On this a threefold charge was made against
the latter—first, of having incited another to fight a
duel with deadly weapons; secondly, of having incited
another to commit a breach of the peace; anethirdly,
of having committed an assault. Orelinger, the 'friend,
was also included in the charge as bearer of a cartel,
but was acquitted on the ground that he had not spoken
of any kind of deadly weapon in communicating the
challenge • but the two ladies deposed that a duel was
spoken of by Schimmelpfennig, and he was accordingly
found guilty, and sentenced to three months' imprison-
ment.'

THE. GORILLA NOT YET CAUGHT. —The English and
French papers have contained a ,paragraph announcing
the arrival of a live gorilla by an African vessel at
Liverpool. On the strength of this, a scientific gentle.
man from the Zoological Society started by express
train, with his pocket full of gold, to acquire the
valuable specimen for the gardens in Regent's Park.
A speedy telegram, however, at once announced to those
disappointed enthusiasts who believe, with Dr. Grey,
that gorillas are as plentiful as sheep on Salisbury.
plain, that the so-called gorilla was nothing more than
a poor chimpanzee, an animal often been in England
before.

THE SAN CARLO OF NAPLES —ln this famous the-
atre there have been great disturbances lately, the
people being indignant with the new company. A
Naples letter says :---‘ Justly irritated, the people have,
it is to be regretted, violated all the convenanees, and
scenes have occurred which have never been before
witnessed since San Carlo was built. On Sunday
night the new company attempted to make them-
selves heard again; but all in vain, for their voices
and the orchestra were drowned by howlings and
every species of insult and disapprobation. This
continued till near the end of the secred act,
when such was the uproar that the curtain dropped,
and did not rise again for the opera. A commissary

by a carbineer, placed himself near the stage; but, so
far from calming, this increased the fury of the
people. All rose to a man, shouted, howled, wh'stled
with their keys and fingers, until the officers were com-
pelled to retire, utterly discomfited. Another commis-
sary, a good-natured looking person, then walked
slowly up with his hands in his pockets, and shrugged his
shoulders, imitating byithis pantomime, "'Well, go on;
it can't be helped." This had the effect of restoring
good humour, but until this occurred there appeared to
be every "chance of a serious row, and people left their
boxes and their seats in the pit. It must not be omitted
that cries were uttered for the " Sopraintendente !"
and it is lucky, perhaps, for him that he had left the
night before to take his place in Parliament. It is not

CRUISE OF TILE

41ZIE,L. ,

Captain Oldfield, of her Majesty's steam sloop Ariel,
who has been cruising off the West Coast of :Afriete,
itcceeded in capturing no less than 26, slave dhows
within the last twelve months. Several had slaves on
-board—one 54, one 82, and two others 100 each. One,
which was taken with a cargo of slaves on board in
March last, at the very entrance to Zanzibar harbour
(the Sultan of Zanzibar having given authority to
search suspected vessels), produced a pass from the
Sultan, but his Highness decided that she had no
claim to his protection having been guilty of violat—
ing his ordinance prohibiting the slave trade and the.
treaty with Great Britain; she was therefore ad-
judged in open durbar a lawful prize, and the negroes
were sent to Seychelles, and the crew distributed,
among vessels bound out of the Sultan's dominions. In
the following month the Ariel chased a dhow, which
made for the land near Brav' e and the crew escaped and
left the vessel drifting into the surf with nearly -100
slaves on board; her position rendered it impossible to
remove them, and the boats of the Ariel were in the
most imminent peril, that commanded by Captain Old-
field being swamped, and the crew with difficulty saved,
while the shore was lined with armed men, who /
with muskets and spears attacked the boats and
such of the slaves as attempted to make for
them. The dhow soon afterwards became a -
total wreck. The slaves escaped to the shore, where
they were seized by the armed men, apparently Somali
Arabs, and the dhow being deserted her destruction
was completed by shelling her. She appeared to be
from 150 tons to 175 tons burden. The casualties in
the course of the cruise seem to have been but few, In
one instance a lieutenant of the Ariel having seized .a •
dhow, from which the crew had just escaped by
swimming to shore, placed a prize crew and native pilot a
OR board, and proceeded to sea with the dhow in com-
pany; but when within thirty miles of Zanzibar the
dhow, without any assignable cause, unless treacherously
scuttled by the native pilot, sank, with the loss of two
of the prize crew and the pilot himself. In another in-
stance a sub-lieutenant seized a dhow at anchor in port
Clink chak with a crew of 15 Arabs and six slaves' and
it being necessary to follow another vessel the dhow
was left in charge of a single seaman, the only hand
that could be spared; unfortunately, on returning, the .
dhow was found deserted by the crew, who had carried
away the slaves, and our seaman was found mortally
'wounded. An encounter took place in Mombas harbour,
in April, Lieutenants Clark and Fellowes cruising in
the Ariel's cutter and pinnace, with a tender in charge,
having put in for water, leaving the tender outside.
Observing a large dhow at anchor in the harbour,
they went alongside, and asked for water, which
was refused. By another dhow, of Buddeen
'water was again refused. They boarded the latter
dhow, and observed that she was a slaver and had
evidently recently landed a cargo of slaves. The two
lieutenants landed, and informed the Governor of
Mombas of the fact of the Budden dhow being a slaver,
'whereupon the Governor accorded them his permission
to seize her. Accordingly, about 4 p.m.' they proceeded
in their boats to seize her, when they. found that since
their first visit she had been run ashore. A heavy fire
was opened on the boats, both from the dhow and from
the shore. The officers, however, succeeded in boardina
the dhow, but were not able to get her off in consequerm
of the tide falling fast. While on board, they had tar
opPortunity of seeing that she had a slave deck and othe:
slave fittings. They then returned to their boats, and wea
.pulling back, when, without cause or provocation, thi
large dhow before mentioned opened a heavy fire upot
the boats, and wounded Lieutenant Fellowes and tap
of his men. As the dhow was obviously strongl'
manned and armed, the officers did not think it prudei
to risk their men's lives by . attacking her, mor
especially as she received a strong reinforcement fron
the shore. They, therefore, stood out to rejoin tilt
tender, on board which was a 12-pouneler. That gut
was transferred to the pinnace, and at half-past
.2 on the following morning, when the tide had
risen sufficiently to float the slaver, the boats again made
for the harbour. On entering it they found that the
slaver had been moved up the river into a position so
close to the town that she could not be attacked with-
out injary to private dwellings, and probably imperilling
the Protestant mission station. The officers then made
for the dhow which had fired upon them on the previous
evening, in order to take possession of her as a pirate,
when she again opened a heavy fire on the boats, whica
was replied to with the 12-pounder. After 10 minutes'
engagement some of the pirate crew were seen to, leap
overboard, and others, including the wounded, to escape
in their boat. On boarding her the officers found he deck
stained with blood, but none of their crew dead or alive..
Some swords and muskets we found lying about, the rest
of her armament having apparently been curried off in the
boat by the crew. The dhow had neither papers nor
colours, and appeared by her build to belong to some of
the Persian Gulf piratical hordes. The boat towed out
the dhow, but at the entrance of the harbour she struck
upon a sunken reef, and was set on fire and abandoned,.
the boats having lost their anchors in trying to get her
off. From information subsequently obtained there is
reason to believe that the dhow was the Futhel
of Sohar, in the Persian Gulf, and that she hal five o
her crew mortally wounded in the engagement ifith.tln
Ariel's boats. She measured 80 feet in length, 17 fee' '
in beam, 12 feet in depth qf hokls and had a poca:
measuring 25 feet in length, 13 feet in beam, and.. five
feet in death. She was of 190 tons burden.

articles.title: AIIT _ATMOSPHERIC TIDE..
articles.text:
AIIT _ATMOSPHERIC TIDE..

We notice in a South Australian paper, the Teregraph
some ingenious. speculations on the possibility of ar
atmospheric tide :
Is our atmosphere, like the waters of the ocean subjec'
to tidal influence? When we find so heavy and incom
pressible a fluid as water rising in a wave of some feet
height, and following the moon is it not rational to con
dude that the light elastic fluid atmosphere must b
similarly affected 1- If such be the case, and we see n
reaanable objection to such a hypothesis, we may sup
pose that a tide wave, not to be measured in feet, bu
in miles, will follow, or rather, accompany our lumi
nary. Some atmospheric commotion is always observabl
at the time of neW moon, and at this time the wit
is generally from the northward. This wave will a
count for the difficulty attending every attempt to Learn
exact tables of the refraction of the heavenly bodies.. We
. know that the state of the atmosphere has to be taken
into account in allowing for the refraction. If, with a
sextant, we take on several successive days the meridian
altitude of the sun, when he is low, about the time of the
winter' solstice, and at or near the change of the moon,
when the combined attraction is at the maximum, we
shall find, when we have made exact allowance for the
small daily difference in declination, and fixed the amount
of refraction by the table corrected for the density and
temperature of the air, that a variation in the angle of
altitude will still remain to be accounted for. This
may reasonably be referred to the atmospheric tide,
which would increase the amount of refraction in pro-
portion to its height. It may be objected that this tide
wave should affect the density of the air, and, conse-
quently, ought to be indicated by the mercury in the
barometer. But this would not follow; for, although
the wave would considerably increase the height of a
column of the atmosphere, yet this, being the effect of
the moon's attraction, would be supported by that
attraction, and, consequently, it would not affect the
density at the earth's suffice. We often find on ai
evening obscured by clouds, that, as the moon approache
towards her meridian passage, the clouds are dissipated
and the sky becomt s clear. This is another effect whicl
may be rationally referred to the attractive influence-el
that luminary on the atmosphere.

A STOUT CENTENARIAN.—A Castlewelian correspon-
dent informs us that, a few days since, he saw three
men digging potatoes in the neighbourhood of that town
—a father and two sons—but, strange to say, the father,
who has arrived at the round age of 96, took the lead in
the labour with a vigour most surprising. This fine old
man's father is dead only nine years, having lived to the
round age of 109 years. _

GROTVTII OF POPULATION.—In the first three quarters
of the present year the excess of births over deaths in
Great Britain has been 248,537, a natural increase
greater by 16,063 than in the first nine months of 1861.
Although marriages have decreased in England this
year, the marriage-rate has been maintained in Scot-
land, apparently indicating that the general prosperity
of that part of the kingdom has not been so seriously
affected by the war in America. The marriage-rate in
Scotland, however, is always greatly below that of
England—a remarkable difference between countries so
closely allied; nevertheless, the proportion of legiti-
mate births to the population is as high in Scotland as
in England, Scottish marriages being more fruitful than
English. There has been an unusual proportion of
male births in Scotland this year, rising in the third
quarter to 107 boys to every 100 girls; in several
country parishes the proportion has been 3 to 2, and
even 2to 1. Scotland has also differed this year from
England in another respect the mortality, low in
England, has in Scotland been high throughout the
year, owing to the unfavourable effect of the damp,
cold, rainy weather in that northern clime.
The Emperor Napoleon and his guests were out
shooting on Saturday in that part of the forest of Com-
piegne comprised between the Moulin and Croix St
Ouen roads, More than 1,400 head of game w
brought down.

!:E P.RINC.E OF WALES AT :ROAM

The visit of the Prince of Wales to Rome is described
in detail by a correspondent who sends a diary dated
from the 13th to the 18th of November. We make the
following extracts :

Nov. 13.
Yesterday morning, at half-past four o'clock, the
Royal yacht Osborne arrived off the port of Civita
Vecchia, and waited outside for the daylight to appear.
On board were their Royal Highnesses the Prince of
Wales and the Crown Prince and Princess of Prassia,
with their respective suites. The Osborne was convoyed
by two steam frigates, the Doris and the Magicietme,
commanded by Prince Leiningen. The frigates remained
outside the harbour, but the yacht entered at half-
past seven, a.m., when the British Vice-Consul, Mr.
Lowe immediately went on board, and was presented to
1 his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales by General
Knollys. The Royal party disembarked under a salute
from the fortress, and proceeded to the railway station,
whence they started at half past eleven, arriving at the
Eternal City at two p.m. They were met and oomph.-
, mented at the Roman terminus by the Prussian Minis-
ter, Baron de Nanitz, and the French General de Monte-
bello. Nine carriages conveyed the travellers and their
suite to the Caftarelli Palace, where they remained for
the rest of the day, the weather being extremely un-
favourable for lionising the city, even if they had not
required rest after their boisterous sea voyage. Their
Royal Ilighnesses are all in perfect health. The Prince
of Wales, with the same prepossessing manners, pre-
sents a• much more virile appearance than during his
visit to and residence in Rome three years and a half
ago. His Royal Highness is accompanied by General
Knollys, Colonel Teesdale, Dr. Hill, and the Hon.
Robert Mead. The Prussian suite is more numerous,
and the whole party amounts to about 30 persons.
Tie strictest incognito is observed by their Royal
Highnesses, as the Prince of Wales travels under the
title of Baron Renfrew, and is still in mourning,- and
will continue to be so until the end of December. He
proposes leaving Rome on the 23rd inst. • but the Prince
and rrincess of Prussia will 'prolong their stay here for
about a month.
Mr. Odo Russell waited on the Prince and Princess at
the Caffarelli Palace soon after their arrival.

This morning, at eleven o'clock, Mr. Gibson, R.A.,
was honoured with a visit from their Royal Highnesses
at his siudio.

Nov. 15

On Thursday evening Mr. Severn, the British Consul,
Ms. Gibson, and Mr. Wolff had the honour of dining with
the Prince and Princess of Prussia and the Prince o f Wales
at the Caffareili Palace. The weather continuing to be
unfavourable for excursions to the ruins and surround-
ing Campagna, the museums and galleries of the city
have afforded sufficient objects of attraction to the -royal
xrisitors. Mr. Wolff accompanied them to the Vatican
yesterday morning and gave them the benefit of his
artistic comments on the treasures of that unrivalled
collection. To day Mr. Odo Russell has been acting as
cicerone to their Royal Highnesses, and the dinner party
will include the Rev. Mr. Woodward, British chaplain
in Rome.

Nov. 17.

, It is not an event of which history offers us many
precedents, that the heirs-apparent to the two first Pro-
testant thrones in Christendom should have been simul-
taneously in Rome, and proceeded together to pay their
respects ta the supreme head of the Catholic Church.
This rare occurrence took place this morning. The
Princv of Wales and his suite, attended by the British
representative, Mr. Odo Russell; and the Prince and
Princess of Prussia with their suite, attended by the
Prussian Minister, Baron de Kanitz, left the Caffarelli
Palace in five, carriages about noon, and drove to, the
Vatican Palace, where they were received at the foot of
the great staircase by the Pope's major-domo, M. Bor-
romeo, and conducted to the Pope's suite of apartments.
The formality observed in the Papal Court on the re-
ception of persons of royal rank by his Holiness is, that
after passing through the various ante-chambers in
which the noble guards and household prelates are
stationed according to their respective ranks, thepersons
to be presented proceed alone from the last ante-
chamber into the audience-chamber, conducted only by
the prelate entitled Maestro di Camera, who opens the
door and kneels down, whilst the visitors, stepping
forward, find themselves in the presence of the Supreme
Pontiff, who on such occasions is entirely unattended,
and receives his visitors tete-a-tete. The diplomatists
and members of the suite who accompany the royal
personages wait in the last ante-chamber until, on a
given signal, the Maestro di Camera gives them access
also into the audience-chamber, where they are succes-
sively presented to his Holiness by the sovereigns, or
princes who have previously enjoyed their own. private
interview with the Pontiff.

In accordance with this custom, the Prince of Wales
and the Prince and Princess of Prussia entered the
audience-chamber without the members of their suite,
and were most affably reerived bYPio Nono. His Holi-
ness had formerly known- the Prince Consort, he had
known the King of Prussia, and had known the Prince
of Wales so lately, that there were plenty of topics of
conversation to be found hi family reminiscences,
besides the customary common-places of inquiries and
answers about traVelling and sight-seeing. The Pope
was charming, and kept up a brisk conversation
for about ten• minutes, when the gentlemen and
ladies of the princes' and princess's suite were
admitted and presentee to his Holiness. The whole
Party, on leaving the Pope's apartments, proceeded to
those of..the Cardinal Secretary of State, to pay him the
customary visit of restitution. Cardinal Antonelli was
not so cheerful as the Pope, nor did he look by any
means so well, for he is at this moment suffering from a
recent family affliction, the death of his mother, to whom
the Cardinal, as well as his brothers, was sincerely
attached. Such is the simple account of their Royal
highnesses' visit to the Vatican, a proceeding purely of
a private and complimentary nature, and, as such, satis-
(actor/ to all parties.
• Yesterday the Prince of Wales and his suite attended
Divine service at the English Church, outside the Porta
del Popolo, and this afternoon, together with the Prince
and Princess of Prussia, drove round the Pincian pro-
menads,*opping occasionally to listen to the perform-
ance of the military band.
-- -

• Nov. 18.
A few select guests join the royal dinner circle every
evening, but as the princes, the princess, and their im-
mediate suite amount to 11 persons, the invitations
usually comprise only three more.
Lieutenant Colonel Caldwell, a constant winter
resident in Rome, dined at the Caffarelli Palace on
Saturday.

TILE SER7EANT-SURGEONCY. - Mr. Cwsar Henry
Hawkins, F.R.S., has just been seleqted as serjeant-
surgeon to her Majesty, in the vacancy occasioned by
the decease of Sir Benjamin Brodie, Bart. This
gentleman has filled the president's chair of the B,oyal
College of Surgeons on two occasions, viz., in 1852,
and again during the past year. "
EPPING FOREST INCLOSURE.-Mr. Torrens proposes
in the next Session of Parliament, to call attention to
the reports of the Commissioners of Woods, Forests, and
Land Revenues for the years 1856,, 1857, 1858, 1859,
1860, and 1861, reporting that the Commissioners had
sold the rights of the Crown in various parcels of land,
situate within the forests of Epping, Woodford, Walt-
ham, and Wanstead ; and to move for a select com-
mittee to inquire what steps either have been or
ought to be taken to preserve the rights of recreation
and resort to the forests exercised from time imme-
morial by the inhabitants of the eastern parts of the
metropolis, as well as the rights of the poorer foresters,
which they have long enjoyed, of pasture, cutting
wood, recreation or other rights; and with a view of
obtaining compensation (either from the Crown or from
those persons who have benefitted by the possession or
purchase of the various lots particularised in the reports
of the Commissioners), for those who had enjoyed or
have been deprived of rights of the kind referred to,
also for those officers of the forests, who, by the sale of
the rights of the Crown within the forests, have been
deprived of any emolument or perqaisite. It behoves
all those interested in the preservation of these favourite
IsPote for the recreation of the public to bestir themselves
te strengthen the hands of Mr. Torrens.
Jim GERARD IN LIVERPOOL.—The celebrated
Tean traveller, M. Jules Gerard, whose exploits have
gamed him the designation of the lion-killer, has been
in iverPool for some days past. On Thursday he was
present at a civic banquet at the Town-hall; on Friday
he attended the ball of the 4th Brigade Lancashire
Artillery Volunteers on Saturday he was a spectator
of the launch
of the troopship Orontes, at the Birken
head Ironworks-
; and on Wednesday next he will be
present at a public meeting to be heid in the

an exploration journey into
Central Africa, and his
presence in Liverpool is with the object of promoting
that undertaking. Few persons are better qualified
than M. Gerard to engage in such an enterprise; his
long sojourn. on the African continent and the know-
ledge he has acquired of the language of its different
peoples and of the habits, will materially assist him in
the hazardous undertaking. His chief aim in this jour-
IleY will be to find a spot for the estakunnant of an
independent settlement. This will probably be found
in tM mountainous regions of the interior between
Sierra Leone and the sources of the Niger. The object

Europe and the interior of Africa. The funds necessary
for this undertaking
are furnished Partly by the mem-
bers of the African Exploration Society, partly by per-
sona who take an interest in geograPhY, in natural

articles.title: 6REECE.
articles.text:
6REECE.

A letter from Athens of the 15th, in the Salut Public
of Lyons, says
The situation of the country is not the same as it
was t week ago. .tillthe persons exiled for the affairs
at Nauplia have returned, and they are, without excep-
tion, ardent partisans of the candidateship of Prince
Alfred of England for the throne of Greece. In fact,
that name has become so popular that in many towne
the Prince's bust has been crowned by the people and
carried in procession through the streets. The old
parties, English, French, and Russian, have been re-
formed in this crisis. The English party is the most
turbulent, the most exacting and the most daring, be-
cause it comprises all the madmen who style themselves
the principal authors of the last revolution, and because
the Government feels too weak to oppose them. They
parade the bust of Prince Alfred, who is to bring to
Greece millions of pounds sterling, an increase of
territory, and to embrace the Greek religion. The
French and Russian parties as they are called, seem
to be slumbering. How, indeed, could they act?
They await, from France especially, from public
opinion at least, since diplomacy is silent, instructions
how to act. Meanwhile, at Syra, the most Mercantile
town in Greece, the merchants are shouting for Prince
Alfred, as Sing of Greece: They have crowned the
Prince's bust in several commercial clubs and have
paraded it through the town. There are the same
tendencies in Messenia, Achaia (Patras), Corinthia,
and all Acarnania (Missolonglii). At Athens, and
even at the Pirmus, the English party meet with no
obstacles. And if England should not officially declare
the Prince's election impossible, I consider the demon-
strations of the Greek nation as a kind of plebiscite,
which will overbear the decisions of the future Na-
tional Assembly.

articles.title: BRAVE ZA.N.
articles.text:
A BRAVE ZA.N.

A public meeting was held a few days ago at Camp-
beltown, Kantyre, to present a beautiful silver medal,
which had been voted by the National Lifeboat Insti-
tution, to James M‘Millan, a mechanic, upwards of 70
years of age, in testimony of his general services in
saving life from wrecks, and particularly for his gallant
exertions in rushing into the teal; and rescuing at the
imminent peril of his life, William Fordyce, belonging
to the ship Genova, of London, which was wrecked
during a heavy gale of wind-in Glenmanuilt Bay,
Kantyre, N. 8., on the 13th October last. The chair
was occupied by J. L. Stewart, aq., who was sup-
ported by some of the principal residents of the dis-
trict.
The Chairman said that the National Lifeboat Insti-
tution, which they represented on that occasion, did
more than any other society in fostering the courage and
daring of our coast population in saving life from ship-
wreck. It was one of the noblest societies to which
this great country had given birth. Its object was the
saving human life from the fury of the devouring
waves. Few of us (continued Mr. Stewart) are ac-
quainted with the horrors of that situation where man,
in his weakness, is left to contend with the elements
in their fury. May it never be the lot of any of us to
know them. Yet is to be hoped that all of us will be
ever ready, as you were, to risk even our lives to help
shipwrecked mariners, and rescue them from a watery
grave. I have much pleasure in coming here to-day
as president of this branch of the National Lifeboat In-
stitution, but the pleasure is much increased by the
fact that your father, who lived upon my father's pro•
perty and mine, was known as a strong and a brave
man. He never lifted his arm in his own cause but
many a time he had raised it with effect for the help, of
others, and especially for the weak. In words which
feel justified in using, I may say—
' Altho' his arm was strong to smite,

'Twas also strong to save'
You, James, have inherited from him this disposition
to succour the weak and helpless, and to risk your own
life for the preservation ot others. This is not the
first time you have done so. You saw this man cling-
ing feebly to a rock, and having lost his hold of it, was
certain to have been swept off by the returning surge
and while others younger men, were standing round,
you rushed into the foaming waves, and by your strong
arm and noble courage, God helping you as He favours
the brave, you brought him safe to land. It is a
pleasure to meet with a brave man, and to address him
as I now do you; and it must be no small satisfaction
to you that he whom you rescued from death was
likewise a brave man. Half-way across the Atlantic
the vessel in which Fordyce sailed as mate fell in with
the Genova, of London, water-logged, and deserted by
the captain and crew. With four other men Fordyce
volunteeredtotake charge of the Genova and bring her
into port. They encountered severe weather, lost
their sails ani tackling, and yet, notwithstanding all
the difficulties he had to contend with, he all but accom-
plished his purpose. By this brave act of yours you have
added 0 the value of your own life. You now live in
him whose life you have saved; and a life thus preserved
will, I doubt not, be guided by the same pi inciples of self-
sacrifice and courage which have animated yours. James,
to you who must feel how great a thing it was to
save a brother's life from the dangers and horrors of
that night, I need say nothing more. Take this parch-
ment, on which the National Lifeboat Institution has
recorded its high appreciation of your acts. Mr. Wat-
son, Lloyd's agent, will attach the medal to your
breast, and long -after your sons shall have returned
from laying you in the cold grave your medal will re-
mind them of what you were, and stimulate them and
their sons to acts of mercy, courage, and daring.
Mr. M'Millan returned thanks for the gifts he had
received and the honours that had been done him, and
said—Although I am now getting an old man, yet if
another wreck should occur, I hope I may still have
strength to be of service to my fellow-creatures.
The medal, which was handed round among those
present, was very much admired, the portrait of her
Majesty being most perfect on it, and they all expressed
their sense of the handsome manner in which the in-
stitution had recognised M‘Millan"s exertions.

The Temps' Press; Opinion Nationale, and Sleets
newspapers. have started a subscription with a
view to present a valuable gold box to Dr. Nelaton, the
eminent French surgeon, in testimony of his great skill
in the treatment of Garibaldi, and the successful extrac-
tion of the ball in consequence of that treatment. The
Journal des Debats has taken time to reflect about joining
the subscription..
QUICK PASSAGE TO MADRAS.—The auxiliary screw-
steamer Calcutta, belonging to the East India and
London Steam Company, waived at Madras early on the
21st Oct-, being 59 days out. She left the Channel on
August 17th i arriving at the Cape of Good Hope on 19th
Sept., in 33 days. She left there on 24th Sept., and
made an unparalleled run of 26 days to Madras, thus
performing the whole of the passage in the unprecedented
short time of .59 days. This is understood to be the
shortest voyage that has ever been recorded.
LOST IN A. SNowsronm —The Aigle of Toulouse
states that a shepherd, who was keeping his flock in the
mountains near Martra (Haute-Garonne), last week,
perceived two horses in harness lying dead under the
snow at the foot of a precipice. He at once informed
the mayor of what he had seen, and that functionary,
accompanied by several gendarmes, lost no timu in
proceeding to the spot, to search for the owner of the
horses, who was also supposed to have perished. At a
distance of about 300 paces they found a man and woman
in the snow, quite dead, closely locked in each other's
arms, and near them was a cart containing a woolcomb-
ing machine and other articles. On the cart was the
name 'Joseph Rouquier, proprietor, at Miraval-
Cabardes.' It appears that the unfortunate mill le,
Rouquier and his wife, on returning home from a fair at
Mamazet, had been overtaken by a snowstorm, and
finding it impossible to proceed with their cart, had
detached the horses in the hope of reaching the next
village but were unable to find their way, and all
perished together.
PERSONAL LIBERTY IN FRANCE.--' I have never been
more struck,' writes the Paris correspondent of the
Times, with the truth of the Emperor's words, when
alluding to the indifference towards individual liberty in
France, than in the case of the unfortunate woman
Rosalie Doise
, Whose evidence before the Assize Court
of the Somme I gave in my Letter of Friday last. Here
is a poor creature bullied by a judge and a gaoler
into the avowal of a crime which she had not committed,
and risking an ignominious death to escape the horror
of a long and secret imprisonment in a dungeon, and
to save her unborn infant, and, with a slight exception,
to direct public attention
)nly yesterday the Sieele
t 0
00t
such
a tchjou an
nrnal enormity. deigning
—not, however, in a leading article, but in its
weekly summary of unimportant news—takes a passing
notice of it. 'ls there not,' it says, some subject
for meditation in this horrible penalty of secret
imprisonment, and in this application of preventive
Punishment? When applied to persons Accused (but
not yet tried or convicted) it cannot fail to produce a
fearful influence on the imagination, and even on the
reason. How differently they act in England! The
accused, whatever be the crime with which he is
charged, defends himself in the open day, and is never
shut up from his friends and advisers. The formidable
apparatus with which our accused are encircled is an
old remnant of the Roman law which should be dimi-
nished, if not entirely don( away with. Suppose the
jury had not accompanied it verdict with extenuating
circumstances, this poor woman would have died on the
scaffold for a crime of which she was innocent.' Day
after day we have articles more or less prolix on Ita-
lians, Americans, or Mexicans; but not a syllable is
vouchsafed on a case which comes home to every
French citizen. Indeed, it may be said that with
all the revolutions which have taken place in France,
the liberty of the subject is the last that is ever con-

MURIalt.

The Court of Assizes of the Seine et Oise on Satur-
day tried a young man of respectable family (a Corsi-
can, and a relation of the Pozzo di Borgo), named
Pierre de Signori°, aged 24, a medical student, on a
charge of murdering a coachman, named Olivrot, at
Enghien-les-Bains, on the 11th of September last. A
young woman, named Bertin, aged 19, with whom the
male prisoner cohabited, was also charged as an accom-
plice. Early in the morning of Sept. 11, two men, when
going to their work, saw a man, in a sitting posture,
leaning against the wall of a house in the Rue de l'Ar-
rivee. On approaching him, they found he was
dead, and, as his clothes were bloody, they sus-
pected he had been murdered, and immediately gave
notice of the fact to the police. On examination, it
was ascertained that the man had received two stabs
in the chest, one of which had penetrated the left lung,
and must have proved almost instantly fatal. As no
marks of blood or of a struggle were found near the
spot, it was inferred that the deceased had been
murdered elsewhere, and afterwards deposited there.
The body was soon recognised as that of a coachman
named Olivrot, who had been cohabiting with the
female prisoner some weeks previously, but had
recently been discarded by her, to make way for a new
lover, the male prisoner. From the inquiry instituted
it appears that the two prisoners had gone to a ball
on the preceding evening, and had there met the de-
ceased, who was greatly excited, and threatened to take
vengeance on them both. An hour or two after the
prisoners had returned to the girl's lodgings the
deceased knocked at the door and demanded admit-
tance, which was refused, and he then went away,
but soon returned with a large paving stone to beat
in the door. Meanwhile, Signori° had risen and
dressed himself, and when the man forced an
entrance, a, struggle ensued between them in which
the prisoner received several contusions about the
head, and inflicted the wounds which caused his
antagonist's death. The evidence did not clearly
show whether the deceased had walked to the place
where he was found, or had been carried there by
the male prisoner. The medical man who made the
post-mortem examination could not undertake to say
that the deceased could not have walked the distance,
but he thought it improbable. M. Lachaud, who de-
fended the male prisoner, pleaded that the wounds
were inflicted in self defence, and adduced numerous
facts and arguments in support of that conclusion. The
Procureur-Imperial abandoned the prosecution against
the female prisoner, but maintained the accusation
against the male prisoner. After the President had
summed up, the jury retired to deliberate, and in ten
minutes returned into court with a verdict acquitting
both prisoners, and they were immediately discharged.

articles.title: LATE COUNT CArOUR.
articles.text:
THE LATE COUNT CArOUR.

The cause of M. Ratta.zzi,' writes a Turin correspon-
dent, has been greatly damaged by a recent shact but
pithy publication. You are aware that a few weeks
previous to the crisis which hurled Baron Ricasoli from
power, Professor Berti published those letters of Count
Cavour bearing the date ot 1856, which gave rise to so
much talk in and out of Italy, and which were printed
for the sole purpose of showing the great regard and
esteem of the deceased statesman for his colleague Rat-
tazzi. M. Aynard de Cavour, nephew and heir of the
count, with a view better to reveal the real mind of his
illustrious relative on the merits of the present Prime
Minister, yesterday gave outthe following note addressed,
I believe, to Farini, then Dictator in the 2dmilia, and
bearing a far more recent date than the documents in M.
Berti's pamphlet. I think it will be read with great in-
terest in England by those who recall the Italian vicissi-
tudes of that time :

' " Dec. 25, 1859.
4 "I Will Dot 'elate to you the history of my appoint-
ment as Italian representative to the Congress (of Zurich).;
all the intrigues, all the lowest arts were set at wcrk to
render it impossible. Dabormida and La Marmora,
however, have no hand in these. It will be easy for you
to guess who the authors of them were. If they did not
carry their point, they succeeded ill adding.difficulty to
my most arduous mission, by revealing the antipathies,
the raneours, and base jealousies with which certain
persons honour me. . . . I accepted, nevertheless, be-
cause, had I refused, I should have had necessarily to
proclaim an antagonism fatal to Italy; but, by accepting,
I feel that I have made the greatest sacrifice a public man
may make to his country, not only by consenting to bear
cruel insults in silence, but also by accepting a mission
from a Government which inspires me neither with
esteem nor confidence.

"C. CAVOUR.'
The effect of this letter was all the greater on the
public who read it, as it was too well remembered that the
readiness to self-sacrifice of CavOur availed Italy but
little, and that the intrigues of his enemies prevailed
against him so far that, in spite of his acceptance, another
man was sent to the Zurich Congress.'

On the :16th Mr. Consul Severn had an interview
with Cardinal Antonelli at Rome, for the purpose of
requesting his eminence, as Prefect of the sacred
Palaces, to grant permission for photographs to be
taken of such of the frescoes in the Vatican by Raphael,
especially those in the Loggia, as may be advantage-
ously reproduced by that mode of representation. It
is well-known that the stanze and others of Raphael's
important frescoes are too faded to admit of photogra-
phic reproduction. The cardinal acceded to the consul's
request the more readily as he was informed that the
photographs were destined to complete a collection
which the late Prince Consort had been forming for
some time before his death.

DEATH OF THE COUNTESS GRANVILLE.—We regret
to have to record the death of the Countess Granville,
mother of the Lord President of the Council. The late
Countess was the second daughter of William, fifth Dime
of Devonshire, and was consequently sister of the late
Countess of Carlisle and the late Duke'of Devonshire.
She married, on the 24th of December, 1809, Granville,
first Earl, by whom she leaves Lady Susan, married to
Lord Rivers; Lady Georgiana Fullerton, wife of Mr.
Alexander George Fullerton, of Ballantry, County
Antrim; George, the present Earl Granville; and the
Hon. Edward F. Leveson *Gower, M.P. Her ladyship
was in her 78th year.
THE CITY BANK, MANCHESTER.—A meeting of the
creditors ot the City Bank (with which the name Jonah
Andrew is intimately associated) was held on Monday,
in order to.adopt a common course of agreement among
the creditors. It was agreed that a thorough and
searching public investigation should be made through the
medium of the Bankruptcy. Court,' and ultimately the
meeting was adjourned to the 10th of December, on
which day the assignees will be appointed. One gentle-I
mon stated that Andrew had assigned to his relatives a
great portion, if not the whole of his property, and it
was the business of the creditors to know what had be-
come of the money. It was also stated that Andrew's
liabilities would be £20,000, an estimate which was
considered by others to be much under the mark, and the
resolution pledged the meeting to contest the title of the
property assigned by the bankrupt.
Mn. CHISHOLM ANSTEY.—This gentleman, who, it
will be remembered, was suspended from his office of
Attorney-General of Hong Kong by Sir John Bow-
ring, has after a long inquiry, and at the end of a
lengthened correspondence, just received the amen*
honorable from the present Colonial Secretary. The
important paragraph of the Duke of Newcastle's letter
is as follows :—`l am directed to inform you, that the
Duke of Newcastle is perfectly ready to express his
opinion that the truth of the charges, of which you
were the principal author, brought against Mr. Cald-
well, before the Commission of Inquiry of 1858, has
been substantially established by the recent investigation
before the Executive Council, so far as the culpability
of his connection with Ma-Chow-Wong is concerned;
consequently, that it cannot now be said, in the words
of the letter addressed to you by order of Governor Sir
John Bowling, that "none of those charges have been
satisfactorily proved." His Grace will go further, and
say, that in forcing on a public inquiry into that officer's,
conduct you did in that respect render a material service
to her Majesty's Government and the colony of flung
Kong.'

REMOVING A ME3IBEE. OF AN EXECUTIVE COUNCIL.
The following dispatch is published in the Tasmanian
Mercury for Sept. 23 Downing-street, 26th Decem-
ber, 1861.—Sir —I have the honour to inform you that
I have receiveda letter from Colonel Broughton R.E.,
complaining of his having been removed from Broughton,
seat
in the executive council without any formal charges
aglinst him, and without a hearing. You will have the
goodness to explain to Colonel Broughton that he was
not removed on account of being accused of an offence,
in which case he would have been entitled, as he repre-
sents, to have distinct charges preferred against him,
and to enjoy an Opportunity of making a defence; but
on account of his constantly differing with his colleagues
and the governor, he was taken out of the executive
council, which is a council of advice, on the same grounds
on which a political opponent must have been removed
from it—viz. that his presence there could only be a
source of embarrassment and not of advantage to the
public service. No one can claim to sit as a right in an
administrative board with which he finds it impossible
to agree.--I have, &c., NEWCASTLE.'
MAKING MONEY.—In some Gossip from Richmond,'
a transatlantic paper states that the dollar and two-
dollar notes of the Confederate States are all signed by
young ladies, of whom many are beautiful and accom-
plished girls—ornaments of the society of the capital.
Several are young widows or orphans of those who have
lost their lives in battle, and a preference is given to
these in all appointments. They are engaged by the
treasury department at 600 dots. a-year, but the salary-is
about to be raised 50 per cent. Eaell clerk has to sign
2,000 notes a-day.

articles.text:
ATTEiIthTED' 'if WO' ER AT THE

LYCEUM THEATRE.

On the 25th, during the performance of the drama
Peep o' Day,' at the Royal Lyceum Theatre, a most
desperate attempt to murder the police-constable on
duty in the pit excited the greatest alarm amongst the
audience.

It seems that between nine and ten o'clock, a gentle-
man, who occupied a seat in the back of the pit, became
so excited with the performance that he continued his
applause to an unbounded extent, and so annoyed
the persons sitting around him that Police-constable
Brown, 566 A; had to request him to be quiet, or
else leave the house, whereupon he drew a large clasp
knife, with which he threatened to murder the first
man that approached him, and without any further
provocation sprang upon the officer, drew the knife
across his forehead and inflicted a number of stabs in
rapid succession on different parts of his body; and he
fell bleeding and insensible into the arms of Mr. John-
son, the messenger of the theatre. The would-be
assassin was and locked up at Bow-street Police-station.
Brown was taken to King's College Hospital, and
attended by Dr. Smith, where he remains in a pre-
carious state.

On the 26th, on the examination of the prisoner,
who gave the name of James Graham, at the Bow-street
police-court, a certificate was put in that the injured
man was unable to attend, and the prisoner—a man of
gentlemanly appearance—was remanded. The accused
has been in the habit of visiting the Lyceum Theatre
frequently. He indulged freely in drink, and was
partially intoxicated when he attacked the constable.

articles.title: SANDYFORD MURDER.
articles.text:
THE SANDYFORD MURDER.

. --
A correspondence between the Home Office and the
law agents of Mr. James Fleming has just beeß pub-
lished. The agents, on the 31st of October, wrote to
Sir George Grey in reference to the respite granted to
Jessie M`Lachla,n, drawing attention to the position in
which their client had been placed by this act, and ask-
ing the Home Office to express an opinion that the
alteration in the sentence was not intended to lead to
the inference that Mr. Fleming was otherwise than inno-
cent of the murder of Jessie M'Pherson. An answer
was received dated Whitehall, Nov. 4, in. which Sir
George declined to express any opinion on the matter.
On the 7th of November the law agents of Mr. Fleming
reopened the subject in a letter to the Home Office,
urging the necessity of ordering a renewed investiga-
tion in order that their client might be afforded an
opportunity of adducing evidence to test the truth
of any statements which may have been made at
the inquiry ordered by the Crown tending to eraai-
nate him. On the 14th of November, Mr. Clive, in
the name of Sir George Grey, intimated to the agents
that it was not in the power of the Home Office to
direct a judicial inquiry to be held into the guilt or
innocence of any person not charged with any offence,
especially when, as in the present case, according to
what he is informed is the law ,of Scotland, the person
on whose behalf you make the request, having been
examined as a witness in a criminal trial, cannot after-
wards be subjected to a criminal prosecution in respect
of the matter of such trial.' Mn Clive added Sir
George Grey instituted the inquiry to which you refer
under the very peculiar circumstances of this case in order
to assist him in deciding whetner sufficient doubt existed
as to the share which the prisoner, Jessie M`Lachlan,
had in the commission of the crime to justify a commuta-
tion of the capital sentence. The result satisfied Sir
George Grey that the whole facts relating to the case had
not been submitted to the jury at the trial, and that
sufficient doubt did exist en the point which I have
mentioned to justify him in recommending a commuta-
tion of the sentence to penal servitude for life. But
the result of the inquiry was far from removing all
uncertainty, nor could it be justly held to fix a share of
the guilt on any other person, especi illy when such
person was not represented at the inquiry.' On the
17th inst. the agents again addressed the Home Office,
expressing regret that Sir George Grey &if not feel it to
be in his power to direct further inquiry, urging that it
was not enough to say, that the result of the investiga-
tion had not 'fixed' guilt on their client; and calling
for an explicit declaration of his innocence or an oppor-

articles.title: LATE DUEL IN FRANCE.
articles.text:
THE LATE DUEL IN FRANCE.

The late fatal duel is likely to give ri‘T to further law
proceedings. It may be remembered that the presiding
judge before whom M. Gramont-Caderouse and his
seconds were tried for killing Mr. Dillon remarked
severely on an article in the Figaro, which, as he con-
sidered, aggravated the quarrel to such -2 degree
as admitted of no other settlement than single
combat. The editor of the Figaro, M. Ville-
messant, stated on that occasion that the article
in question was inserted at the suggestion of a third
party, wham he was not at liberty to name, but
as that person was in court he left, it to him to relieve
him from the imputation if he thought proper. T bore-
upon Colonel de Noe rose, and said that he was the
p,rson alluded to by M. de Villemessant. He described
a conversation which passed between them; but lie
positively denied that he had anything whatever
to do with the insertion of the offensive article, and
added that, as a soldier and a gentleman,' he could
not have done so.. The judge did not, or would not,
listen to any further explanations from M. Villemessant,
and pronounced a strong condemnation on M. Villemes-
sant.

M. Yillenaessant does not seem disposed to let the
affair end in that way. Ile has addressed a letter to
the judge, in which he declares that M. de Noe, this
soldier and gentleman,' not only suggested the article in
question, not only authorised its insertion, but took the
trouble to read and correct the proof sheet, and cven
added the expression ` comme etant de roture, more
offensive than the original term, plebeian,' applied to
Mr. Dillon. In support of his statement M. Villemes-
sant appends the written declarations of his secretary,
of the compositor, the corrector of the press, mi the
printer, through whose hands the proof sheet succes-
sivelyp.ssed.

Villemessant concludes thus:----4I have just con-
sulted my lawyer, who informs me, to my astonishment,
that an accused party cannot be proceeded against for
his allegations before his judges, seeing that he is not
on his oath. It is, then, to you, M. le President, to
your high impartiality, that I have the honour to
respectfully address myself, while you are still on the
seat where you addressed to me severe and unmerited
comments which still vibrate in my heart. And now,
M. le President, before whom does the shade of Mr.
Dillon rise ? And what are we to think of the word of
this soldier and gentleman?'
Colonel de Noe has in turn addressed a letter to the
papers, declaring that M. Villemessant's statement is
'quite incorrect in its tenour,' and that he has laid a
complaint before the proper tribunals.

articles.title: CONFIRMATION OF THE ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY.
articles.text:
CONFIRMATION OF THE ARCH-
BISHOP OF CANTERBURY.

On Wednesday, Dr. Longley, the Archbishop elect o:.
Cantetbury, attended in the parish church of St. Mary-
le-Bow, Cheaptide, to be present at the ceremony oi
confirming his election by the Dean and Chapter. Her
Majesty's mandate to proceed with the confirmation was
addressed to ten of the Bishops of the Southern Province;
and of these there were present the Bishop of London,
Dean of the Province of Canterbury, the Bishops of Win-
chester, Salisbury, Oxford, and Rochester. His Grace the
Archbithop was received by the Bishops, and by Dr.
Lushington, Dean of the Court of Arches; Dr. Travers
Twiss, the Vicar-General of the Province; Sir R. Phil-,
limore, the Queen's Advocate; and Dr. Shepherd, the
Registrar. The Litany service was read by the Rev.
Marshall Hall Vine, the rector of the parish; after
which the Archbishop. Bishops, and legal gentlemen
took their seats at a table placed in the middle aisle.
The schedule of election o Dr. Longley by the Dean
and Chapt r of Canterbury was presented, and the
Bishop of London, who act,d as president, decreed that
it should be enrolled. Proclamation was then made that
if any one had any objection to urge against Dr. Long-
Joy he was to come forward and declare it, and,
apparently, under the impression that there might be
some persons who had not heard it, proclamation was
again made, but with precisely the same result. The
Archbishop then took the oaths in the usual form, and
the proceedings terminated. No day is yet fixed for the
enthronement, which will take piice in Canterbury
Cathedral, soon after the Archbishoplas done homage
to the Queen.
